cases.system: Earthquakes, global shallow seismicity (Gutenberg-Richter law): seismic moment and rupture length
cases.law_or_distribution: log10 N(>=Mw) = a - b*Mw; equivalently N(>M0) ∝ M0^-beta with beta = 2b/3. Self-similar source scaling M0 ∝ stress drop * L^3
cases.variable_k: Scalar seismic moment M0 (N m). Secondary coordinate: rupture length L (km)
cases.reported_exponent: b ≈ 1, with regional values 0.8-1.2 (Huang & Turcotte 1988). Moment exponent beta = 0.63-0.67, called 'universal' for moderate events (Kagan 2002; Bird & Kagan 2004; Boettcher & Jordan 2004). Kagan (2010) argues beta may be exactly 1/2, with estimates inflated by 1-3%. Repo fit, USGS 2010-2024, M>=5.5: b = 0.998 [0.973, 1.024], giving beta = 0.666 [0.649, 0.683]. In rupture length: N(>L) ∝ L^-2b ≈ L^-2 (Aki 1981, D = 2b). The distribution tapers above a corner moment of about 10^21 N m
cases.alpha_uncertainty: About ±0.02 statistical; 1.63-1.67 across catalogues; 1.50 if beta = 1/2. In L: alpha_L = 1 + 2b = 3.0 ± 0.05
cases.conversion: beta = zeta_M0 = 2b/3, using M0 ∝ 10^(1.5 Mw); alpha = 1 + beta. For L, self-similar M0 ∝ L^3 gives zeta_L = 2b and alpha_L = 1 + 2b
cases.orthopolic_reading: The units are ruptures counted per unit time, so the orthopolic quantity is a flux: fault area ruptured per unit time per log size class. The shared total is the fault-surface area of the active system, i.e. the rupture 'slots' on a 2D plane. The resource per event in M0 coordinates is q ∝ M0^0.65 ≈ M0^(2/3) ∝ L^2, the rupture area. In L coordinates the density is ∝ L^-3, which reads as log-orthopolic in area L^2 or linear-orthopolic in volume L^3; this is exactly the user's k^-3 example. Moment itself is top-heavy (zeta < 1): the largest events dominate moment release, which is capped by the corner moment. So the shared resource is area, not moment

decompositions.resource: Rupture area A ∝ L^2 (fault-surface territory)
decompositions.composition: M0 = mu * mean slip * A, with mean slip ∝ (stress drop/mu) * L at constant stress drop. So M0 ∝ L^1 (slip) × L^2 (area) = L^3. Equal ruptured area per ln L gives N(>L) ∝ L^-2, hence q(M0) = M0^(2/3)
decompositions.independent_motivation: Ruptures are planar patches on faults, so the support they tile is 2D. Under self-similar (constant stress-drop) scaling, the number of patches of linear size >= L that fit on a surface scales as L^-2 (box counting in d = 2), without reference to any catalogue. Constant stress drop is measured independently: Hanks & Bakun (2002) find M = log A + 3.98, i.e. M0 ∝ A^1.5, for A <= 537 km^2
decompositions.theory_agreement: Aki (1981): D = 3b/c = 2b, so b = 1 means D = 2. King (1983) attributes b ≈ 1 to self-similar fault geometry, with a large share of deformation on minor faults. Pan et al. (2026 preprint) derive b from rupture-area power-law scaling combined with slip scaling, the same area × slip composition. Against it: Hirata (1989) found b anticorrelated with the epicentre fractal dimension, though that is a correlation dimension, not rupture area; Kagan's critical-branching beta = 1/2 is a competing, non-geometric mechanism
decompositions.testable_consequence: Width saturation. Above A ≈ 537 km^2 (Mw ≈ 6.7), Hanks & Bakun find M = (4/3) log A + 3.07, i.e. M0 ∝ A^2. If area stays log-orthopolic (zeta_A = 1), beta must fall to 1/2 (b = 0.75) for large continental events. If b stays ≈ 1, then zeta_A = 4b/3 ≈ 1.33; the repo fit for M >= 6.7 gives 1.36 [1.29, 1.44]. On current evidence the reading fails above the crossover. Pacheco, Scholz & Sykes (1992) report a b-value break at the seismogenic width, but its values were not retrieved here

decompositions.resource: Euclidean rupture volume L^3 under the linear measure (FD-SOC 'scale-free probability conjecture')
decompositions.composition: N(L) dL ∝ L^-d dL with d = 3, and energy E ∝ L^3. This is the same k^-3 density read the other way
decompositions.predicted_exponent: alpha_E = 5/3, b = 1.0 (identical to the first reading)
decompositions.independent_motivation: Aschwanden postulates that the probability of an avalanche of size L per unit L scales inversely with the d-dimensional volume. The motivation is scale-free avalanche statistics, not fault geometry
decompositions.theory_agreement: Aschwanden's FD-SOC (2012 onward) predicts alpha_E = 5/3 and reports earthquakes as consistent with it. The two readings give the same number here
decompositions.testable_consequence: The two readings separate only when the support dimension changes. For seismicity distributed through a volume (some induced or swarm seismicity), the area reading generalised to d_s = 3 predicts N(>L) ∝ L^-3 (b = 1.5), while FD-SOC still predicts b = 1. Not tested here; the Illinois/Decatur study found induced events departing from D0 = 2b

decompositions.resource: Fault-trace length for width-saturated ruptures (1D support)
decompositions.composition: Slots of length L along a 1D fault system give N(>L) ∝ L^-1. Under the L-model (slip ∝ L, width fixed) M0 ∝ L^2, giving beta = 1/2. Under the W-model (slip ∝ width) M0 ∝ L, giving beta = 1
decompositions.predicted_exponent: b = 0.75 (L-model) or b = 1.5 (W-model) for Mw > about 6.7
decompositions.independent_motivation: Once rupture width is capped by the seismogenic thickness, ruptures can grow only along strike, so the support becomes the 1D fault trace
decompositions.theory_agreement: Hanks & Bakun (2002) favour L-model scaling for large strike-slip events. Global b ≈ 1 up to the corner moment (Kagan) fits neither branch cleanly
decompositions.testable_consequence: Split catalogues above Mw 7 into width-limited strike-slip events and megathrust events, whose width keeps growing. The reading predicts b of 0.75 or 1.5 for the first group and ≈ 1 for the second

cases.source: Huang & Turcotte 1988 (paleoarchive PDF, via search); Aki 1981 as summarised there; Kagan 2002 GJI 148:520 and Kagan 2010 (scec.org/node/3413, scec.org/node/4180, arXiv 0908.1207); Hanks & Bakun 2002 BSSA 92:1841 (usgs.gov publication page); Pacheco, Scholz & Sykes 1992 Nature 355:71 (abstract); Pan et al. 2026 arXiv 2603.06892 (abstract summary); King 1983 (secondary summary); repo results/resource_choice.json. Abstracts and search summaries only; full-text fetch was blocked

cases.system: Fault and joint (fracture) networks: trace lengths in 2D maps, disc sizes in 3D
cases.law_or_distribution: n(l, L) = alpha * L^D * l^-a (number per unit length in a domain of size L); self-similar networks have a = D + 1
cases.variable_k: Fracture trace length l (m to km); in 3D, fracture disc diameter
cases.reported_exponent: Bour et al. (2002), Hornelen basin, seven maps from metres to about 1 km: a = D + 1 (self-similar). A separate set of 17 trace maps gives D = 1.56-1.79, which implies a ≈ 2.6-2.8 if a = D + 1 holds (this a is inferred, not reported). 3D fault networks (Swiss Alps study, Solid Earth 2025): 3-3.6, convention not checked. Bonnet et al. (2001) review: published exponents span the whole theoretically possible range, partly because of poor methods
cases.alpha_uncertainty: 2D traces ≈ 2.6-3.0; 3D ≈ 3-3.6 observed against 4 predicted for a dense space-filling network; single studies vary far more widely
cases.conversion: Density exponent a as reported; for self-similar networks zeta = a - 1 = D
cases.orthopolic_reading: The shared total is the map area (2D) or rock volume (3D) of the deforming domain; the units are fractures. Each fracture holds an exclusion or stress-shadow territory ∝ l^D, where D is the fractal dimension of fracture centres (D → d for a space-filling network). Log-orthopolic: every log-length class claims the same share of the domain, so N(>l) ∝ l^-D. This is a capacity (slot-count) quantity, not a stock

decompositions.resource: Exclusion territory l^D: the capacity of a D-dimensional domain for objects of size l
decompositions.composition: Count per ln l ∝ l^-D, with D = 2 for maps, 3 for volumes, or the measured centre dimension for clustered networks
decompositions.independent_motivation: In the dense regime a fracture stops growing when it meets a larger one; large fractures inhibit small ones, not the reverse. Each length class therefore fills the space left by larger ones in the same proportion: a self-similar packing of territories. The argument comes from fracture mechanics (stress shadows), not from the length data
decompositions.theory_agreement: Davy et al. (2010), 'universal fracture model': the dense-regime distribution is derived from the rule that fractures do not cross larger ones, with exponents fixed by D and one dimensionless parameter. Bour et al. (2002) found a = D + 1 empirically. The mechanism agrees with the capacity reading
decompositions.testable_consequence: Stereology: for the same isotropic network, the 3D exponent should exceed the 2D trace exponent by 1, and the 1D scanline exponent should be 1 below it. In 3D the dense regime predicts a = 4, so the reported 3D range of 3-3.6 is a direct test that currently falls short, pending a convention check. Below the dilute-to-dense transition (a few tenths of a km for faults, metres for joints), the exponent should depart from D + 1

decompositions.resource: Geological moment per fault (displacement × fault area)
decompositions.composition: Displacement ∝ l^n (n = 1 for self-similar faults) times area ∝ l^2 gives moment ∝ l^(2+n). Log-orthopolic in moment in 3D means count per ln l ∝ l^-(2+n)
decompositions.predicted_exponent: a_3D = 3 + n; this is 4 for n = 1, the same as the territory reading
decompositions.independent_motivation: For deformation to have no dominant scale ('brittle flow'), each log-length class must accommodate equal strain. King (1983) argued that b ≈ 1 requires a substantial share of deformation on minor faults
decompositions.theory_agreement: King (1983), self-similar fault geometry (from secondary summaries). It coincides with the territory reading in 3D only because moment and territory both scale as l^3 when displacement ∝ length
decompositions.testable_consequence: Where displacement-length scaling is non-linear (n ≠ 1), the strain reading predicts a_3D = 3 + n while the territory reading still predicts D + 1. The summed fault moment per log class in a mapped 3D network should be flat

cases.source: Bour, Davy, Darcel & Odling 2002 JGR 107(B6), doi:10.1029/2001JB000176 (abstract: a = D + 1); Bonnet et al. 2001 Rev. Geophys. 39 (abstract); Davy et al. 2010 JGR doi:10.1029/2009JB007043 (abstract); 3D range of 3-3.6 from a Solid Earth 2025 Swiss Alps study (se-16-641-2025); D = 1.56-1.79 from a reanalysis cited in search summaries. Search summaries only

cases.system: Impact craters on surfaces in saturation equilibrium (lunar maria small craters, Phobos, Deimos, mid-size icy satellites)
cases.law_or_distribution: Cumulative N(>=D) per unit area ∝ D^-2 at equilibrium (Gault 1970), at 1-10% of geometric saturation
cases.variable_k: Crater diameter D (m to km)
cases.reported_exponent: Equilibrium cumulative slope -1.8 to -2.0, provided the production slope is steeper than -2. Gault 1970: -2, from first principles and laboratory experiments. Hartmann 1984: -1.83 across several bodies. Lunar equilibrium density is 1-10% of geometric saturation (Xiao & Werner 2015)
cases.alpha_uncertainty: 2.83-3.0 (Hartmann -1.83 vs Gault -2)
cases.conversion: Cumulative slope zeta = 2 gives alpha = zeta + 1 = 3
cases.orthopolic_reading: The shared total is the surface area of the body; the units are craters, each holding an area ∝ D^2. Equilibrium means equal crater-covered area per ln D: each log-diameter class covers the same fraction (about 1-10%) of the surface. This is a capacity occupancy held constant by a balance between crater creation and obliteration

decompositions.resource: Crater area D^2 (surface territory)
decompositions.composition: Count per ln D ∝ D^-2 on a 2D support
decompositions.independent_motivation: A new crater of diameter D erases older craters inside an area ∝ D^2. A crater survives until comparable or larger craters have re-covered the surface around it once, so at steady state each log-size class occupies a fixed fraction of the 2D surface (cookie-cutter obliteration). Geometric saturation is the 2D packing limit for circles
decompositions.theory_agreement: Gault (1970) derived -2 from first principles and experiments; Melosh (1989) defined geometric saturation; Richardson (2009) gives an analytic model: the equilibrium slope is -2 when production is steeper than -2, and otherwise follows production. The mechanism (area-based erasure) agrees
decompositions.testable_consequence: (1) If the production cumulative slope is shallower than -2, no -2 equilibrium should form; Richardson's model confirms this. (2) Where erasure is not area-based (distal ejecta, diffusive degradation; Minton et al. 2019), the slope should depart from -2. (3) Along a 1D transect the same reading predicts the number of craters of size >= D crossing the line ∝ D^-1, since the crossing probability ∝ D

decompositions.resource: Excavated volume D^3 under the linear measure
decompositions.composition: Equal excavated volume per unit D
decompositions.independent_motivation: None: no mechanism shares excavated volume per linear diameter interval
decompositions.theory_agreement: No theory; it fits only because log-in-area and linear-in-volume give the same number
decompositions.testable_consequence: Makes no prediction for the transect test, whereas the area reading predicts D^-1

cases.source: Gault 1970; Hartmann 1984; Melosh 1989; Richardson 2009; Xiao & Werner 2015, as quoted in arXiv 1701.00471, 1509.06773, 2604.16223 and 1902.07746 (Minton et al. 2019). Search summaries only

cases.system: Asteroid belt collisional cascade (Dohnanyi 1969), main-belt size distribution
cases.law_or_distribution: dN ∝ m^(-11/6) dm, i.e. dN/dD ∝ D^-3.5. With size-dependent strength Q* ∝ D^s: dN/dD ∝ D^-((21+s)/(6+s)) (O'Brien & Greenberg 2003)
cases.variable_k: Body diameter D (km); also mass m
cases.reported_exponent: Theory: 3.5 in D and 11/6 in m; the exponent depends only on how the collision rate scales with mass (Williams & Wetherill 1994). Observed main belt: cumulative ≈ -2.5 for 100-1000 km (differential 3.5) and ≈ -1.8 for 10-100 km (differential 2.8). Sub-km high-latitude survey: cumulative 1.25 ± 0.03 (0.6-1 km) and 1.84 ± 0.27 (1-3 km). The distribution is 'wavy' below 10 km
cases.alpha_uncertainty: Theory exact at s = 0; observed differential slopes 2.3-3.6 depending on size range; strength-regime theory about 3.6-3.7
cases.conversion: Differential exponent in D reported directly. In mass alpha_m = (alpha_D + 2)/3 = 11/6, so zeta_m = 5/6
cases.orthopolic_reading: The shared total is the mass flux through the cascade: mass per unit time passing from large to small sizes. Each body contributes m × its catastrophic-disruption rate. The stock is not flat: mass per ln D ∝ D^0.5 (top-heavy) and cross-section per ln D ∝ D^-0.5 (bottom-heavy). The flat quantity, D^2.5, is mass × rate

decompositions.resource: Mass flux carried per body: m × disruption rate
decompositions.composition: q = D^3 × tau^-1(D), where tau^-1 ∝ cross-section D^2 × number of projectiles above the disruption threshold (∝ D^-2.5) = D^-0.5. So q ∝ D^(3 - 0.5) = D^2.5
decompositions.independent_motivation: In a steady cascade, mass is neither created nor destroyed at intermediate sizes, so the mass flux through each log size is constant. This is the transport identity B = F/v, with log-speed v set by the disruption rate
decompositions.theory_agreement: Dohnanyi (1969); Tanaka et al. (1996); O'Brien & Greenberg (2003). The mechanism (constant mass flux) is exactly this reading
decompositions.testable_consequence: Only the rate term should move the exponent. Strength Q* ∝ D^s gives (21+s)/(6+s): steeper in the strength regime (s < 0, about 3.6) and about 3 in the gravity regime. A cross-section ∝ D^b gives (15+3b+s)/(6+s). The observed shallower slope at 10-100 km and the sub-km oscillations are attributed to the strength-to-gravity transition

decompositions.resource: Stock mass m alone
decompositions.composition: q = m ∝ D^3
decompositions.independent_motivation: Mass is the conserved stock
decompositions.theory_agreement: Contradicted by Dohnanyi: conservation fixes the flux, not the standing stock per log size
decompositions.testable_consequence: None beyond the failure itself: the stock reading is refuted wherever the cascade is in steady state

cases.source: Dohnanyi 1969 JGR 74:2531, via arXiv astro-ph/0203371 and 1110.2503; O'Brien & Greenberg 2003 Icarus 164:334 (abstract), formula (21+s)/(6+s) via arXiv 2107.11389; main-belt slopes from Morbidelli et al. (c2pu.oca.eu) and arXiv 1308.3349. Search summaries only

cases.system: Interstellar dust grains (Mathis-Rumpl-Nordsieck 1977)
cases.law_or_distribution: dn/da ∝ a^-3.5, for 0.005 < a < 0.25 micron (graphite and silicate)
cases.variable_k: Grain radius a (micron)
cases.reported_exponent: 3.5, fitted to UV-visible extinction. Size limits vary between sources (graphite up to 1 micron in some versions). Shattering fragments in grain-grain collisions: about 3.3 (Jones, Tielens & Hollenbach 1996). Shattering models evolve toward an MRN-like 3.5 when fragment exponents are below 3.5
cases.alpha_uncertainty: About ±0.2; MRN is an empirical fit, and later models (e.g. Weingartner & Draine) are not pure power laws
cases.conversion: Density exponent reported directly
cases.orthopolic_reading: The same exponent as Dohnanyi. Mass per ln a ∝ a^0.5, so large grains hold the mass. Area per ln a ∝ a^-0.5, so small grains dominate surface and UV extinction. The flat quantity is a^2.5, which in a cascade reading is mass × shattering-collision rate

decompositions.resource: Mass flux through a grain-shattering cascade
decompositions.composition: q = a^3 (mass) × a^-0.5 (collision rate per grain); the same arithmetic as Dohnanyi
decompositions.independent_motivation: Grains in the diffuse ISM are processed by grain-grain collisions in supernova shocks and turbulence. A steady fragmentation cascade conserves mass flux
decompositions.theory_agreement: Jones et al. (1996) shattering gives about 3.3 for fragments, and later shattering models converge toward 3.5 (as summarised in arXiv 1303.3958). Dust is not as clearly in steady state as asteroids, since coagulation, accretion and destruction compete
decompositions.testable_consequence: Size-dependent grain velocities in turbulence change the rate term and therefore the slope. Coagulation-dominated dense clouds should be flatter (fewer small grains); shock-processed gas should approach 3.5

decompositions.resource: Geometric mean of area and volume, sqrt(a^2 × a^3)
decompositions.independent_motivation: None
decompositions.theory_agreement: None. It matches only because it was built from the exponent
decompositions.testable_consequence: None

cases.source: Mathis, Rumpl & Nordsieck 1977 ApJ 217:425, as quoted in arXiv astro-ph/0301488 and astro-ph/9910116; Jones, Tielens & Hollenbach 1996 ApJ 469:740, as used in arXiv 1303.3958 and 1001.2606. Search summaries only

cases.system: Global lakes (lake surface areas)
cases.law_or_distribution: dN/dA ∝ A^-tau, with tau = 2.14 for A >= 0.46 km^2 (corrected). Percolation theory predicts tau = 187/91 ≈ 2.055
cases.variable_k: Lake surface area A (km^2)
cases.reported_exponent: tau = 2.14 above 0.46 km^2, with shoreline fractal dimension 1.4 (Cael & Seekell 2016, as corrected in 2017; the original subset gave 1.97 above 8.5 km^2). A second dataset gives 2.13. Theory: 2.05, with shoreline dimension 4/3. A later review puts the lower limit of the power law anywhere from 0.001 to 1 km^2
cases.alpha_uncertainty: 2.13-2.14 across datasets; systematic dependence on the lower cutoff; no formal CI retrieved
cases.conversion: Density exponent tau reported directly
cases.orthopolic_reading: The shared total is the landscape (map) area; the units are lakes. In area coordinates the resource is A^1.06-1.14. Because A ∝ L^(D_f), with D_f = 91/48 the cluster dimension, this is A^(d/D_f) = L^2: the gyration territory each lake spans, not its water area. Lakes are log-orthopolic in territory

decompositions.resource: Gyration territory L^2 (2D capacity), with water area A ∝ L^(91/48)
decompositions.composition: Hyperscaling: the number of clusters of linear size > L per unit area ∝ L^-d, with d = 2. Then tau = 1 + d/D_f = 1 + 2/(91/48) = 187/91
decompositions.independent_motivation: Lakes are flooded clusters of a randomly rough landscape. Flooded regions of linear size L tile the 2D map once per log scale, while their water area is a fractal cluster mass. The argument is from percolation geometry, not the lake census
decompositions.theory_agreement: Cael & Seekell (2016) derive 187/91 from percolation; the hyperscaling relation tau - 1 = d/D_f is standard. The mechanism agrees exactly with the territory reading. The observed 2.14 is 0.085 steeper, and the authors call it 'similar'
decompositions.testable_consequence: Measure lake radius of gyration instead of area: the reading predicts N(>L) ∝ L^-2 exactly, independent of D_f. The shoreline dimension should be 4/3 (accessible perimeter); 1.4 was observed. A 3D analogue (karst voids from 3D percolation) would give 1 + 3/2.52 ≈ 2.19

decompositions.resource: Enclosed (hull) area including islands: a level-set loop reading
decompositions.composition: Loops of a rough surface with Hurst exponent H give zeta_A = 1 - H/2 <= 1 (see the islands case)
decompositions.independent_motivation: Lakes and islands are both level sets of topography
decompositions.theory_agreement: Kondev & Henley loop scaling. It cannot produce tau > 2, so the observed 2.14 favours the cluster (water-area) reading over the hull-area reading
decompositions.testable_consequence: Recomputing lake areas with islands filled in should move tau toward <= 2

cases.source: Cael & Seekell 2016 Sci. Rep. 6:29633 (PMC4937396), Corrigendum 2017 Sci. Rep. 7:42155 (PMC5304202); Cael, Biggs & Seekell 2022 Front. Env. Sci. (from repo). Abstracts and PMC summaries

cases.system: Islands (Korcak law)
cases.law_or_distribution: N(A > a) ∝ a^-B
cases.variable_k: Island area A (km^2)
cases.reported_exponent: B ≈ 0.65 on average, from about 0.5 (African islands) to about 0.75 (Indonesian islands), per Mandelbrot. Theory: B = D_e/2 with D_e = 2 - H (Sasaki et al. 2006), i.e. B = 1 - H/2. A 131,063-island compilation (Oline et al., arXiv 2512.16659) finds four Hurst-exponent estimates from island statistics that disagree; values not retrieved. An EPJ-H 2016 history disputes that the exponent is a fractal measure
cases.alpha_uncertainty: 1.5-1.75 across regions
cases.conversion: zeta = B, so alpha = 1 + B
cases.orthopolic_reading: The shared total is the map area of the region weighted by its relief. The units are islands, each holding q ∝ A^(1-H/2) = L^(2-H) = L^2/L^H: map area per unit vertical relief, i.e. the land an island class adds per unit fall of sea level (dA/dz). Each log-size class of islands contributes equally to the change in total land area when sea level moves

decompositions.resource: Area per unit relief, L^2 × (L^H)^-1
decompositions.composition: Count per ln L = (slots of size L in 2D ∝ L^-2) × (probability that sea level falls within the relief of an L-sized slot ∝ L^H). This gives N(>L) ∝ L^-(2-H), so q = L^(2-H)
decompositions.independent_motivation: An island of size L exists only where the water level cuts an L-sized patch of topography inside that patch's relief range, which scales as L^H for self-affine relief. Slot counting in 2D comes from geometry. H can in principle be measured from elevation profiles independently of island counts
decompositions.theory_agreement: Mandelbrot (1975): B = D/2 with coastline dimension D = 2 - H. Kondev & Henley contour-loop scaling: the probability that a point lies on a loop of size L ∝ L^(D(H) - (2-H)), giving loop number ∝ L^-(2-H). The mechanism (slot × level-hit probability) agrees; naming the resource dA/dz is new here
decompositions.testable_consequence: B should track independently measured topographic H region by region (B = 1 - H/2). The Oline et al. finding that four H estimates disagree is a partial failure. Low-relief terrain (H → 0) should give B → 1, consistent with lakes at 1.05-1.14. The change in total island area under a small sea-level change should be shared equally across log-size classes

decompositions.resource: Coastline length per island (Mandelbrot's B = D/2 read literally)
decompositions.composition: Perimeter ∝ L^(D_c), with log-orthopolity in coastline giving B = D_c/2
decompositions.independent_motivation: Weak: coastline as the shared resource (shore habitat, wave energy absorbed)
decompositions.theory_agreement: Conflicts with Kondev & Henley unless H = 1: a single loop has D = (3 - H)/2, not 2 - H
decompositions.testable_consequence: Measure H and single-island coastline D on the same archipelago. For H = 0.5, the area-per-relief reading predicts B = 0.75 and the coastline reading 0.625

cases.source: Mandelbrot 1975 PNAS 72:3825 and Korcak 1938, as quoted in arXiv 1303.1610; Sasaki et al. 2006 J. Phys. Soc. Jpn 75:074804 (via search summary); Kondev & Henley via arXiv cond-mat/0203593 and cond-mat/9907229; Oline et al. arXiv 2512.16659 (abstract); EPJ-H 2016 h150039. Search summaries only

cases.system: Landslides (event-triggered inventories, e.g. Italy, Guatemala, USA)
cases.law_or_distribution: Area pdf is an inverse gamma with power tail p(A) ∝ A^-2.40; volume-area V ∝ A^gamma
cases.variable_k: Landslide area A (m^2); also volume V
cases.reported_exponent: alpha_A = 2.40, proposed as universal for event inventories (Malamud et al. 2004); most datasets 2.5 ± 0.5. Volume-area scaling gamma = 1.1-1.3 for soil and 1.3-1.6 for bedrock (Larsen et al. 2010, 4,231 slides); 1.450 (Guzzetti et al. 2009). Volume pdf exponents 1.0-1.9, mean about 1.3, over 19 heterogeneous datasets including submarine and extraterrestrial (Brunetti et al. 2009)
cases.alpha_uncertainty: 2.0-3.0 across inventories; mapping resolution affects the tail
cases.conversion: Density tail exponent reported directly. Volume: alpha_V = 1 + (alpha_A - 1)/gamma
cases.orthopolic_reading: The units are landslides in one triggering event. Area is bottom-heavy (zeta_A ≈ 1.4), so most area is in medium slides. The candidate shared resource is mobilized volume: V ∝ A^gamma with gamma ≈ 1.4-1.5 makes volume per ln A nearly flat. The final resource would be area × depth, with depth ∝ A^(gamma - 1)

decompositions.resource: Mobilized volume V = A × depth, depth ∝ A^(gamma - 1)
decompositions.composition: q = A^1 × A^(gamma - 1); for self-similar bedrock slides (depth ∝ L), q ∝ L^2 × L = L^3
decompositions.independent_motivation: A landslide is an erosion event, and the eroded volume is the budgeted quantity. Failure depth grows with area as failure planes cut into bedrock, and the depth scaling is measured independently by Larsen et al. on 4,231 slides
decompositions.theory_agreement: No theory found that derives alpha_A = 1 + gamma. Malamud et al. (2004) propose 2.4 as universal without this mechanism
decompositions.testable_consequence: (1) Within a region, soil-dominated inventories should have shallower area tails (≈ 2.1-2.3) than bedrock-dominated ones (≈ 2.3-2.6). (2) Volume distributions in the same inventories should have alpha_V ≈ 2 (zeta_V ≈ 1). Brunetti et al. report volume exponents of 1.0-1.9 (mean 1.3), which contradicts this if taken at face value, though their datasets are not complete event inventories

decompositions.resource: Surface territory A (2D packing, d_s = 2, as for craters and lakes)
decompositions.composition: Count per ln L ∝ L^-2 with A ∝ L^2
decompositions.independent_motivation: Landslides occur on a 2D land surface
decompositions.theory_agreement: Fails: landslides are bottom-heavy in area. Using a 3D territory (L^-3) gives alpha_A = 2.5, which is the volume reading with gamma = 1.5
decompositions.testable_consequence: This failure is what points to a contribution from the third (depth) dimension

cases.source: Malamud, Turcotte, Guzzetti & Reichenbach 2004 ESPL 29:687 and EPSL 229:45 (abstracts and review summaries); Larsen et al. 2010 Nature Geosci. doi:10.1038/ngeo776; Guzzetti et al. 2009; Brunetti, Guzzetti & Rossi 2009 NPG 16:179 (abstract via search). Search summaries only

cases.system: Wildfires (USA, Australia)
cases.law_or_distribution: dN/dA ∝ A^-alpha (burned area per fire)
cases.variable_k: Burned area A (km^2 or acres)
cases.reported_exponent: Malamud et al. 1998: 1.3-1.5 (USA and Australia). Malamud, Millington & Perry 2005: 1.3-1.75 over 18 US ecoregions (88,916 fires, 1970-2000), with an east-west gradient. Clauset et al. 2009 (US federal lands, xmin about 6,300 acres): 2.2 ± 0.3, with a cutoff preferred. Drossel-Schwabl model fire sizes: 1.19 (Hergarten & Krenn 2011)
cases.alpha_uncertainty: 1.3-1.75 by region; up to 2.2 at high xmin; lognormal fits often better
cases.conversion: Density exponent reported directly
cases.orthopolic_reading: The units are fires. Burned area is top-heavy (zeta ≈ 0.3-0.75). The flat resource would be A^0.3-0.75, with no natural physical candidate. Estimator and region dependence (0.3 to 1.2 in zeta) prevent a fixed exponent from being assigned

decompositions.resource: Active fire front (perimeter) P ∝ A^(D_P/2)
decompositions.composition: Log-orthopolic in perimeter gives zeta_A = D_P/2
decompositions.independent_motivation: Weak: a fire consumes fuel at its front
decompositions.theory_agreement: None found
decompositions.testable_consequence: Requires an assumed D_P. It fits only the steep (western) end of the range

decompositions.resource: Forest-cluster size under size-biased sampling (forest-fire model)
decompositions.composition: Lightning strikes sites uniformly, so a cluster burns with probability ∝ its size: alpha_fire = tau_cluster - 1. Percolation clusters give 1.055; Drossel-Schwabl theory gives 1.19
decompositions.independent_motivation: Ignition sampling and fuel connectivity
decompositions.theory_agreement: Hergarten & Krenn (2011) derive 1.19 from accessible-perimeter scaling of percolation clusters. Modified rules raise it by about 1/3 toward observed values
decompositions.testable_consequence: Regions with strong suppression or fragmentation should differ in a predictable direction; the east-west gradient is unexplained

cases.source: Malamud, Morein & Turcotte 1998 Science 281:1840 (exponents via arXiv 1810.07868 and review summaries); Malamud, Millington & Perry 2005 PNAS 102:4694 (EGU abstracts, reviews); Clauset et al. 2009 via repo compilation; Hergarten & Krenn 2011 NPG 18:381 (abstract). Search summaries only

cases.system: River networks: drainage-area distribution and Hack's law
cases.law_or_distribution: P(A > a) ∝ a^-beta with beta ≈ 0.43; Hack's law l ∝ A^h with h ≈ 0.57-0.6; finite-size scaling gives tau = 1 + beta = 2 - h
cases.variable_k: Upstream contributing area A at each network site or link (km^2)
cases.reported_exponent: beta ≈ 0.43 for area and 0.45 for discharge (Rodriguez-Iturbe et al. 1992; La Barbera & Roth 1994). Energy-dissipation exponent 0.90. Hack's exponent 0.57-0.6 (Hack 1957; Gray 1961). Maritan, Rinaldo et al. (1996) link the area exponent to Hack's exponent and to elongation
cases.conversion: zeta = beta, so alpha = 1 + beta
cases.orthopolic_reading: The shared total is the basin area. The units are channel-length elements (sites) with upstream area >= a. Each unit holds the width of strip it drains, W(a) = a/l(a) ∝ a^(1-h). At every threshold, (channel length above threshold) × W = basin area. Hack's law read the same way: total area A is shared among main-stream length units l ∝ A^h, each draining width A^(1-h)

decompositions.resource: Drained width W = A/l(A)
decompositions.composition: q = A^1 × A^-h (area divided by Hack length). The number of sites with A >= a ≈ basin area / W(a)
decompositions.independent_motivation: Every channel element drains a strip, and channels carrying area >= a are spaced about W(a) apart. Their total length times W is the basin area, an exact accounting identity of the drainage network
decompositions.theory_agreement: Maritan et al. (1996) and Rigon et al. (1996) derive the area exponent from Hack's exponent and basin geometry. A 2024 HESS paper proves a link between the exceedance exponent and drainage density, the same identity. La Barbera & Roth (1994) predict 0.45 from Hack's exponent. The mechanism agrees
decompositions.testable_consequence: Composition: link energy dissipation ∝ A^0.5 implies an energy exponent of 2 × 0.45 = 0.90, which is observed. Random (Scheidegger) networks have h = 2/3 and should give beta = 1/3

decompositions.resource: Drained width in a random (Scheidegger) network
decompositions.composition: Same identity with h = 2/3
decompositions.independent_motivation: Random-walk network geometry
decompositions.theory_agreement: Exact for the Scheidegger model; real networks are optimal-channel-like with h ≈ 0.57
decompositions.testable_consequence: Shows the reading is predictive: changing the network geometry (h) moves beta by the predicted amount

cases.source: Rodriguez-Iturbe et al. 1992 WRR (via La Barbera & Roth 1994 PDF at pdodds.w3.uvm.edu); Rigon et al. 1996 WRR 32:3367 (On Hack's Law, digitalcommons.usu.edu); Maritan et al. 1996 PRE (abstract); HESS 28:3119 (2024). The tau = 2 - h form is from memory, though numerically consistent; search summaries only

cases.system: Solar flares (soft and hard X-ray; energy, peak flux, fluence)
cases.law_or_distribution: dN/dE ∝ E^-alpha_E, with alpha < 2 meaning large flares dominate the energy budget (Hudson 1991)
cases.variable_k: Flare energy or fluence E (erg); peak flux P
cases.reported_exponent: Hudson 1991: about 1.8. Aschwanden 2010: peak flux 1.72 ± 0.08, total flux 1.60 ± 0.14, duration 1.98 ± 0.35. Mean over 61 SOC datasets: fluence 1.66 ± 0.22, flux 1.78 ± 0.29. Nanoflare studies span 1.5-2.7 (Aschwanden et al. 2000: 1.79 ± 0.08). FD-SOC predicts alpha_E = 5/3, alpha_F = 9/5, alpha_A = 7/3 (observed area slopes 2.1 ± 0.3), alpha_L = 3
cases.alpha_uncertainty: ±0.2 across datasets; detection threshold and background handling shift values by about 0.2
cases.conversion: Density exponent reported directly
cases.orthopolic_reading: The units are flares (a flux: events per unit time). Energy is top-heavy (zeta ≈ 0.66). In length-scale coordinates N(>L) ∝ L^-2: log-orthopolic in area L^2 (flares as patches on a 2D surface: photosphere or current sheets), or linear-orthopolic in volume L^3 (Aschwanden). Energy ∝ L^3, the free magnetic energy in the volume above the footprint. This has the same structure as earthquakes: 2D territory, 3D content, so zeta_E = 2/3

decompositions.resource: Footprint area L^2 on the 2D photosphere, with energy ∝ L^3
decompositions.composition: Count per ln L ∝ L^-2 and E ∝ L^3, so zeta_E = 2/3 and q(E) = E^(2/3)
decompositions.predicted_exponent: alpha_E = 5/3; ribbon or footprint area alpha_A = 2 if A ∝ L^2
decompositions.independent_motivation: Flaring flux tubes are rooted in the 2D photosphere, so an active region's surface is the shared territory, while free magnetic energy fills the 3D volume above it. Moderate: the support could equally be 3D coronal volume
decompositions.theory_agreement: FD-SOC gives the same alpha_E by a different route (3D linear). No theory found for the 2D-footprint version
decompositions.testable_consequence: Footprint (ribbon) areas: this reading predicts alpha_A = 2.0, FD-SOC predicts 7/3 for fractal areas. Observed 2.1 ± 0.3 cannot yet discriminate

decompositions.resource: Euclidean volume L^3 under the linear measure (FD-SOC)
decompositions.composition: N(L) dL ∝ L^-3 dL; E ∝ L^3; flux ∝ fractal volume L^2.5; duration ∝ L^2 (diffusive)
decompositions.independent_motivation: Scale-free probability conjecture for avalanches in d = 3, plus diffusive spreading. It predicts several exponents jointly from one postulate
decompositions.theory_agreement: Aschwanden FD-SOC (2012-2025) agrees with mean observed slopes across 61 datasets
decompositions.testable_consequence: Joint prediction: the flux, duration and area exponents (1.8, 2.0, 2.33) must all hold together. Stellar flares in other geometries should keep the same numbers if d = 3

decompositions.resource: Energy itself (zeta_E = 1)
decompositions.composition: q = E
decompositions.independent_motivation: Energy is the budgeted released quantity
decompositions.theory_agreement: Nanoflare heating would need alpha > 2; most measurements fall below 2
decompositions.testable_consequence: Steeper slopes would be expected only at nanoflare energies

cases.source: Hudson 1991 Sol. Phys. 133:357 (doi:10.1007/BF00149894) via arXiv 2004.04399 and 1206.6097; Aschwanden 2010 (via search summary of arXiv 1006.4861 and 1010.0986); Aschwanden FD-SOC predictions and 61-dataset means via arXiv 2412.03481 and 2505.00748; Crosby et al. 1993 Sol. Phys. 143 (abstract). Search summaries only

cases.system: Stellar initial mass function above the turnover (Salpeter)
cases.law_or_distribution: dN/dm ∝ m^-2.35 (Gamma = 1.35 per log m)
cases.variable_k: Stellar mass at birth m (solar masses)
cases.reported_exponent: Salpeter 1955: 2.35 (Gamma = 1.35), above about 0.5-1 solar mass. Kroupa 2001: 2.3 ± 0.3 and 2.3 ± 0.7, and 1.3 below 0.5 solar mass (from repo compilation, not re-checked). Padoan & Nordlund core-mass slope: 3/(4 - beta) = 1.36 for turbulent spectral index |beta| = 1.8
cases.alpha_uncertainty: ±0.3 (Kroupa); cluster present-day slopes range more widely
cases.conversion: alpha = Gamma + 1
cases.orthopolic_reading: The units are stars or cores. Mass per ln m ∝ m^-0.35, so mass is bottom-heavy above the turnover. The orthopolic resource in m is m^1.35 = L^3: the volume of the turbulent parent region from which a core is compressed. Stars are log-orthopolic in parent volume (3D territory), not in their own mass

decompositions.resource: Parent turbulent volume L^3 (3D capacity), with core mass m ∝ L^(4 - beta)
decompositions.composition: Count per ln L ∝ L^-3 (self-similar turbulent structures filling 3D). Core mass m ∝ rho_0 L^3 M_A^-2 ∝ L^(4 - beta), from MHD shock jump conditions with velocity v(L) ∝ L^((beta - 1)/2). So Gamma = 3/(4 - beta)
decompositions.independent_motivation: Supersonic turbulence fragments clouds self-similarly in 3D, and core masses follow from shock compression and the measured turbulent spectrum. Neither step uses stellar counts
decompositions.theory_agreement: Padoan & Nordlund (2002) derive exactly 3/(4 - beta). It is contested because gravity is neglected (Padoan et al. 2007 identify two regimes); Hennebelle & Chabrier give related forms
decompositions.testable_consequence: The slope should depend on the turbulence spectrum: Burgers (beta = 2) gives 1.5, Kolmogorov (5/3) gives 1.29. Core mass functions in filament-dominated regions, where the effective packing dimension is below 3, should be shallower (2/(4 - beta) ≈ 0.9 for sheet-like fragmentation)

decompositions.resource: Stellar mass itself (zeta_m = 1)
decompositions.composition: q = m
decompositions.independent_motivation: Mass is the conserved stock; Bondi-type competitive accretion also gives about m^-2 (from memory)
decompositions.theory_agreement: Inconsistent with 2.35 ± 0.3 at about the 1-sigma edge; bottom-heaviness above the turnover is observed
decompositions.testable_consequence: None beyond the mismatch

cases.source: Salpeter 1955 ApJ 121:161 (Gamma = 1.35 via obspm dictionary and arXiv 1108.2287); Padoan & Nordlund 2002 ApJ 576:870, arXiv astro-ph/0011465 (abstract: 3/(4 - beta) = 1.36); Padoan et al. 2007 arXiv astro-ph/0701795; Kroupa 2001 from repo zeta-compilation. Search summaries only

cases.system: Dark-matter halo mass function, low-mass end (field halos and subhalos)
cases.law_or_distribution: dn/dM ∝ M^-alpha with Press-Schechter alpha = 2 - (n+3)/6 for P(k) ∝ k^n
cases.variable_k: Halo virial mass M (solar masses)
cases.reported_exponent: Press-Schechter low-mass slope -2 + (n+3)/6: -1.5 (n = 0), -5/3 (n = -1), -11/6 (n = -2); tends to -2 as n_eff → -3. Aquarius subhalos: -1.87 to -1.93 depending on mass range (Springel et al. 2008). A slope just below 2 keeps the total substructure mass finite
cases.alpha_uncertainty: 1.87-1.93 in simulations; 1.83-1.92 for n_eff from -2 to -2.5
cases.conversion: Density exponent reported directly
cases.orthopolic_reading: The shared total is matter: cosmic mean density × volume, i.e. Lagrangian volume. The units are halos, each holding mass M ∝ its Lagrangian volume L^3. In the n → -3 limit the system is log-orthopolic in mass (3D territory, zeta = 1). More precisely, excursion-set theory gives equal mass per unit peak height nu = delta_c/sigma(M): linear-orthopolic in nu, not in ln M

decompositions.resource: Mass per unit peak height nu (equivalently, q per ln M = M sigma(M)/delta_c = M/nu)
decompositions.composition: Brownian first passage: the mass fraction per d nu tends to a constant as nu → 0. With sigma ∝ M^(-(n+3)/6), the mass per ln M ∝ M^((n+3)/6), so d_log = 1 - (n+3)/6
decompositions.independent_motivation: Mass conservation (every mass element ends up in some halo as M → 0) plus Gaussian initial fluctuations. Only the linear power spectrum is used, not simulated halo counts
decompositions.theory_agreement: Press & Schechter (1974) and the Bond et al. (1991) excursion set. The mechanism agrees exactly
decompositions.testable_consequence: Scale-free simulations: n = 0 should give 1.5, n = -1 5/3, n = -2 11/6. Warm dark matter (small-scale cutoff) should flatten and turn over the low-mass end. Shear corrections change the slope (Audit et al. predict M^(n+1)), which is a discriminating test

decompositions.resource: Pure Lagrangian-volume (mass) orthopolity
decompositions.composition: q = M ∝ L^3, count per ln L ∝ L^-3
decompositions.independent_motivation: 3D territory: every mass element belongs to some halo
decompositions.theory_agreement: The n → -3 limit of Press-Schechter; real CDM gives about 1.9
decompositions.testable_consequence: The 0.1 departure is predicted by the spectral slope and is what keeps total substructure mass finite

cases.source: Press-Schechter slope from arXiv astro-ph/9704023 (Audit et al.) and Pfrommer lecture notes (pages.aip.de); Springel et al. 2008 MNRAS 391:1685, arXiv 0809.0898 (slope -1.87 to -1.93 via Aquarius team slides). Search summaries only

cases.system: Galaxy stellar mass function, faint end (GAMA, z < 0.06)
cases.law_or_distribution: Double Schechter phi(M) dM ∝ (M/M*)^alpha_S exp(-M/M*); faint-end alpha_S = -1.47
cases.variable_k: Galaxy stellar mass M* (solar masses), about 10^8-10^10
cases.reported_exponent: Baldry et al. 2012: alpha2 = -1.47, alpha1 = -0.35, M* = 10^10.66 (5,210 galaxies). Wright et al. 2017: alpha2 = -1.50 ± 0.01 ± 0.15
cases.alpha_uncertainty: ±0.15 systematic
cases.conversion: dn/dM ∝ M^alpha_S below M*, so alpha = -alpha_S and zeta = -(alpha_S + 1) = 0.47
cases.orthopolic_reading: The units are galaxies. Stellar mass is top-heavy, with most stellar mass near M*. The orthopolic resource in M* coordinates, M*^0.47, is approximately host-halo mass. Galaxies inherit the near-orthopolity of halos (zeta_h ≈ 0.9) through a steep stellar-to-halo mass relation. Final resource: stellar mass divided by star-formation efficiency, i.e. the baryon reservoir

decompositions.resource: Halo mass (baryon reservoir) M_h = M*/epsilon
decompositions.composition: q = M_h ∝ M*^(1/gamma), with epsilon = M*/M_h ∝ V_c^2 ∝ M_h^(2/3) under energy-driven supernova feedback, so gamma = 5/3. Halos have zeta_h ≈ 0.9 (previous case), so zeta_* = zeta_h/gamma
decompositions.predicted_exponent: zeta_* = 0.54 (alpha = 1.54) for energy-driven feedback; 0.68 (alpha = 1.68) for momentum-driven (epsilon ∝ V_c); 0.47-0.56 for SHMR slopes gamma = 1.6-1.9
decompositions.independent_motivation: Supernova energy ∝ M* must unbind gas with binding energy ∝ M_gas V_c^2 (a Dekel-Silk energetics argument). The halo slope comes from N-body or excursion-set theory
decompositions.theory_agreement: Dekel & Woo (2003): M*/M ∝ V^2 fits low-luminosity dwarfs. Abundance matching gives low-mass SHMR slopes of 1.6-2.2, steeper than 5/3 (Behroozi 2013; Moster 2013, as quoted), but abundance matching uses the GSMF itself, so it is not independent
decompositions.testable_consequence: Below the reionization scale, gamma steepens, so the faint end should flatten. For example, the Local Group SHMR slope of 3.1 at M* 10^7-10^8 implies zeta_* ≈ 0.3 (alpha ≈ 1.3) there. Since the halo slope is fixed, any change of alpha_S with environment or redshift must track gamma

decompositions.resource: Stellar mass itself (zeta = 1)
decompositions.composition: q = M*
decompositions.independent_motivation: Stellar mass is the stock
decompositions.theory_agreement: Observed 1.47-1.50: top-heavy
decompositions.testable_consequence: None beyond the mismatch

cases.source: Baldry et al. 2012 MNRAS 421:621, arXiv 1111.5707; Wright et al. 2017 (GAMA, z < 0.1); Dekel & Woo 2003 arXiv astro-ph/0210454 (M*/M ∝ V^2); SHMR slopes 1.6-1.9 and Local Group 3.1 from arXiv 1311.5492 and related search summaries. The Moster 2013 beta ≈ 1.38 was not confirmed

cases.system: Galactic cosmic rays below the knee
cases.law_or_distribution: Observed dN/dE ∝ E^-2.7. Test-particle diffusive shock acceleration (DSA) source spectrum E^-(r+2)/(r-1) = E^-2 for compression ratio r = 4. Leaky box: N(E) = Q(E) tau_esc(E), with tau_esc ∝ E^-delta
cases.variable_k: Particle energy or rigidity E (GeV to PeV)
cases.reported_exponent: Observed ≈ 2.7. DSA strong shock: 2.0. AMS-02 B/C ∝ R^-0.333 ± 0.014 (fit) ± 0.005 (syst) above 65 GV, i.e. delta ≈ 1/3 (Kolmogorov). Inferred source spectra: R^-2.3 to R^-2.5. SNR emission implies spectra steeper than E^-2
cases.alpha_uncertainty: About ±0.05 below the knee (proton spectra about 2.7-2.8; detail from memory)
cases.conversion: Differential spectrum exponent used directly
cases.orthopolic_reading: The source is log-orthopolic in energy injected per unit time (a flux), with equal energy per ln E. The standing Galactic population is not; it is log-orthopolic in energy × escape rate, the energy leaving per unit time (transport identity B = F/v with v the escape rate). DSA's E^-2 is a 'kinematic' orthopolity: escape probability per cycle equals fractional energy gain per cycle when r = 4

decompositions.resource: Energy escape flux: E × tau_esc^-1 ∝ E^(1 + delta)
decompositions.composition: d_log(stock) = d_log(source) + delta = 1 + 1/3
decompositions.predicted_exponent: alpha = 2 + delta = 2.33 with a DSA source and AMS-02 delta
decompositions.independent_motivation: Steady state of a leaky box: stock = injection × residence time. delta is measured independently from secondary-to-primary ratios
decompositions.theory_agreement: The leaky-box form (stock = source × residence time) is standard. The components do not sum: 2 + 0.333 ≠ 2.7, so a softer source (≈ 2.37) is needed
decompositions.testable_consequence: Source index = 2.7 - delta must be confirmed by gamma-ray spectra of supernova remnants, which are indeed steeper than E^-2

decompositions.resource: DSA source: energy injected per ln E
decompositions.composition: d_log = (escape probability per cycle)/(fractional energy gain per cycle) = 3/(r - 1), which is 1 at r = 4
decompositions.independent_motivation: Fermi acceleration at a strong shock; the ratio of loss rate to log-growth rate, as in Gibrat-type exponent formulas
decompositions.theory_agreement: Test-particle DSA (Bell 1978; Blandford & Ostriker 1978) gives exactly this. Sources inferred from B/C are 2.3-2.5
decompositions.testable_consequence: The effective compression ratio r ≈ 3.2 would give (r+2)/(r-1) ≈ 2.36, so 2.36 + 0.33 ≈ 2.7. Late-stage SNR shocks with r < 4 are a proposed explanation, but this is matched after the fact

cases.source: DSA index and E^-2.7 with leaky-box explanation via arXiv astro-ph/0409303 and par.nsf.gov 10344783 (search summaries); AMS-02 B/C: Aguilar et al. 2016 PRL 117:231102 (doi:10.1103/PhysRevLett.117.231102), Delta = -0.333 ± 0.014 ± 0.005. Search summaries only

catalogue.domain_patterns:
1. Territory rule (the strongest regularity). In at least six cases (craters, fault traces and 3D fractures, earthquake ruptures, lakes, turbulent cores for the IMF, dark-matter halos) the count per log interval of linear size scales as L^-d_s. Here d_s is the dimension of the space the objects tile: 2 for a planetary surface, a map, a fault plane or a landscape; 3 for a rock volume, a turbulent cloud or Lagrangian space. The orthopolic 'final resource' is then the territory L^d_s, not the object's own content. Any measured content k ∝ L^(D_k) then has zeta_k = d_s/D_k, i.e. alpha_k = 1 + d_s/D_k. This one rule gives:
- b = 1 (zeta_M0 = 2/3: moment ∝ L^3 on a 2D plane)
- crater equilibrium -2 (2/1)
- a = D + 1 for fractures
- 187/91 for lakes (2/(91/48), percolation hyperscaling)
- 3/(4 - beta) ≈ 1.36 for the IMF
- zeta_M → 1 for halos

A corollary can be stated before seeing data: content is top-heavy (zeta < 1) when it grows faster than territory (D_k > d_s: seismic moment, flare energy, stellar mass via the SHMR). It is bottom-heavy when it grows slower (D_k < d_s: lake water area with fractal D_f < 2; core mass ∝ L^2.2 in 3D). Exponents well above 2 (3, 3.5, 4) are a dimension count plus a correction: the integer part counts dimensions, the fractional part is a fractal or rate correction (91/48, 4 - beta, -1/6 collision rate, delta escape).

2. The k^-3 ambiguity is real and recurs. A density ∝ L^-3 appears in crater equilibrium, 2D fault maps, earthquakes with b = 1, lakes (in gyration radius) and FD-SOC flares. It can be read as log-orthopolic in area L^2 (2D packing) or linear-orthopolic in volume L^3 (Aschwanden's scale-free probability conjecture). The two readings separate only when the support dimension changes:
- 3D fracture networks: log reading predicts a = 4, linear reading 3.
- Scanlines or crater transects: the log reading predicts N(>L) ∝ L^-1.
- Volumetric seismicity: the log reading predicts b = 1.5.

Wherever a mechanism is known (crater obliteration, fracture exclusion, percolation hyperscaling, excursion-set halos), it is the log/territory reading. The linear-in-volume reading is so far only a postulate (FD-SOC).

3. Cascades are orthopolic in a flux, not a stock. The shared quantity is stock × rate, and exponents add:
- Dohnanyi and MRN dust: mass × catastrophic-collision rate, D^3 × D^-0.5 = D^2.5, so alpha = 3.5.
- Cosmic rays: energy × escape rate, E^(1+delta).
- River networks: area per unit channel length (drained width).

Because the rate exponents are measured independently (strength slope s, B/C delta = 0.333, Hack's h), these readings make risky predictions. They pass for rivers (beta = 1 - h, and energy exponent 0.90 = 0.45/0.5) and for the Dohnanyi strength dependence. They fail for cosmic rays (2 + 1/3 ≠ 2.7). DSA shows a different route to orthopolity: equal energy per ln E arises because, at compression ratio 4, the escape probability per cycle equals the fractional energy gain (d_log = 3/(r - 1)). That is a kinematic coincidence, not conservation.

4. Level sets: islands and lakes are one problem. Count = (slots ∝ L^-2) × (probability the water level falls inside a slot's relief ∝ L^H). The resource is L^(2-H): area per unit relief, the land exposed per unit fall of sea level. H → 0 gives zeta_A → 1 (lakes 1.05-1.14); H between 0.5 and 1 gives 0.75-0.5 (Korcak islands). The hull-versus-cluster distinction decides the sign of the deviation from 1: hull areas cannot exceed tau = 2, so lakes at 2.14 must be cluster-like.

5. Change of variable divides exponents; products of deterministic costs add them. Examples:
- The faint end of the galaxy stellar mass function is halo near-orthopolity (zeta_h ≈ 0.9) seen through M* ∝ M_h^(5/3) (energy-driven feedback): 0.54 predicted vs 0.47-0.50 observed.
- The river energy exponent is 0.90 = 0.45/0.5.
- Landslide area is volume orthopolity seen through V ∝ A^gamma.
- Seismic moment is area orthopolity seen through M0 ∝ A^1.5.

Many 'universal' exponents in this domain are a territory or flux exponent divided by a content scaling exponent.

Counterexamples and failures, which are informative:
- Wildfires: alpha is 1.3-1.75 by region and 2.2 at high xmin. Perimeter, size-biased-cluster and SOC readings each fit some region, and none is natural.
- Landslides: the area tail fits volume orthopolity (alpha_A = 1 + gamma), but published volume compilations give exponents of 1.0-1.9 (mean 1.3), not about 2. Surface packing (alpha_A = 2) fails outright.
- Large earthquakes above width saturation: area orthopolity predicts b = 0.75 (or 1.5 under the W-model), while data stay near b ≈ 1 (repo: zeta_A = 1.36 for M >= 6.7).
- Cosmic rays: the components do not sum.
- The IMF below about 0.5 solar mass and the galaxy mass function near M*: these are set by thermal or feedback scales (exponential knees), with no packing reading.
- Flares: the 2D-log and 3D-linear readings fit equally well. They stay graded suggestive/motivated until flare footprint areas discriminate (alpha_A 2 vs 7/3; observed 2.1 ± 0.3).

A recipe that falls out of these cases, to apply before fitting:
1. Identify the support and its dimension d_s.
2. Write the content scaling k ∝ L^(D_k) from the physics.
3. Predict zeta_k = d_s/D_k.
4. For a cascade, add the measured rate exponent.
5. For thresholds or level sets, include the level-hit probability L^H.

Readings that pass this pre-registration are graded derived: craters, fractures, lakes (approximately), rivers, halos, Dohnanyi. Those that need a free H, gamma or SHMR slope to fit (islands, landslides, galaxy masses) are motivated at best, and wildfires remain numerology.

Verification notes. Web fetch was blocked (arXiv, Copernicus and others), so all values were checked against abstracts and search-engine summaries. The fault-length a-values are inferred from D via a = D + 1, so that case is marked unverified. Moster 2013's beta ≈ 1.38, the Apollonian packing exponent and the knee details are from memory and were not used as evidence.

checks.system: Earthquakes, global shallow seismicity (Gutenberg-Richter): seismic moment and rupture length
checks.corrected_alpha_uncertainty: Recomputed in this task from repo data/raw/usgs_2010_2024.csv (Aki-Utsu MLE with a 0.05 correction for 0.1-unit magnitude bins). b = 1.03 ± 0.01 (M>=5.5, n=7174); 1.00 ± 0.02 (M>=6.0); 1.02 ± 0.05 (M>=6.7); 1.09 ± 0.07 (M>=7.0); 1.32 ± 0.15 (M>=7.5, n=74, inside the corner-moment taper). These give beta = 0.66-0.69 and alpha_M0 = 1.66-1.69. The repo's own estimator gives 0.998. Kagan's catalogue values (0.60-0.68, per the repo compilation) widen alpha_M0 to 1.60-1.69, and it is 1.50 if Kagan's beta = 1/2 holds. Regional b of 0.7-1.2 is systematic, not noise: it tracks faulting style and differential stress (Schorlemmer et al. 2005; Scholz 2015, both in repo references).
checks.algebra_note: The conversions are correct: beta = 2b/3, alpha = 1 + beta, zeta_L = 2b, alpha_L = 3, and above the crossover zeta_A = 4b/3. Three problems. (1) Decomposition 3 under the L-model (fixed width, so A ∝ L) is decomposition 1 continued past the crossover, not an independent alternative. (2) Box counting gives a number of available slots, which is a capacity, but G-R counts events per unit time. The area reading needs an extra assumption: each L-sized patch ruptures at a rate independent of L. With constant stress drop and constant loading, recurrence time scales as slip/v ∝ L. That makes the rate per ln L ∝ L^-3, i.e. equal moment rate per log class and b = 1.5. The slot-count argument therefore does not by itself give b = 1. (3) The 1D W-model branch (b = 1.5) can also be reached by keeping N(>L) ∝ L^-2 with the L-model M0 ∝ L^2. Two different resources predict the same large-event b.
checks.best_reading: The event flux is log-orthopolic in a 2D territory L^2, meaning equal ruptured fault area per unit time per ln L. The content is M0 ∝ L^3 under constant stress drop, which gives zeta_M0 = 2/3 and b = 1. Below about Mw 6.7, 'territory L^2' and 'rupture area' are the same quantity. Above width saturation they diverge. Rupture-area orthopolity (with the Hanks-Bakun M0 ∝ A^2) predicts b = 0.75. A length-indexed territory (N(>L) ∝ L^-2 continues, with M0 ∝ L^2) predicts b = 1.5; as I recall, Pacheco, Scholz & Sykes 1992 interpreted a b-value increase at the crossover this way, and Kagan disputed it. Repo data show b of 1.0-1.1 up to M7, rising to 1.3 ± 0.15 above M7.5. That argues against rupture area and cannot separate the length-territory reading from the corner taper.
checks.numerology_risk: High. At least three readings give b = 1 exactly: log-orthopolic in area L^2, linear-orthopolic in volume L^3 (FD-SOC), and Aki/King's fault geometry with D = 2. Aki's D = 2b was obtained by inverting the observed b, so the geometric motivation is partly post hoc. A non-geometric mechanism (critical branching, beta = 1/2) fits within Kagan's bias argument. The reading predicts a universal b = 1, but b varies from 0.7 to 1.2 with stress regime. The width-saturation test fails for the rupture-area version. I downgraded the grade from 'motivated' to 'suggestive'.
checks.source: Repo data/raw/usgs_2010_2024.csv (recomputed here); results/resource_choice.json; docs/zeta-compilation.md rows 47-48 (Kagan 2002 GJI 148:520; Kagan 1999; arXiv 0908.1207; Schorlemmer et al. 2005 Nature 437:539); docs/references.md (Hanks & Bakun 2002 BSSA 92:1841; Scholz 2015 GRL 42:1399). The Hanks-Bakun coefficients and the Pacheco et al. 1992 result are from the checker's recollection. No new web verification: the harness web-search budget was exhausted, and direct fetches failed (DNS and proxy 403 on arXiv, PMC).

checks.system: Fault and joint networks: trace lengths in 2D, disc sizes in 3D
checks.corrected_alpha_uncertainty: As I recall, Bour et al. 2002 (Hornelen) give D ≈ 1.8 and a ≈ 2.8, i.e. a = D + 1, which agrees with the catalogue. Published density exponents span roughly 1-4 (Bonnet et al. 2001). 2D traces fall around 2.6-3.0 and 3D around 3-3.6 (convention unchecked). Not web-verified in this task.
checks.algebra_note: zeta = a - 1 = D, d_log = 1.8 and d_lin = 2.8 are correct. There are two internal problems. (1) The moment decomposition predicts a_3D = 3 + n = 4 for n = 1, the same as the territory reading, yet one is flagged as matching and the other not. (2) The stereology test (a_3D = a_2D + 1, scanline = a_2D - 1) is a geometric identity for isotropic disc populations. It holds for any size distribution and any mechanism, so it cannot test the territory reading. The real tests are a_3D = 4 in the dense regime, and a = D + 1 with D measured from fracture-centre positions independently of lengths.
checks.best_reading: Capacity reading. Each fracture holds an exclusion or stress-shadow territory ∝ l^D. In the dense regime fractures stop at larger ones, so each log-length class fills the same share of the D-dimensional domain, giving n(l) ∝ l^-(D+1). Davy et al. (2010, UFM) derive this for the dense regime. Bour et al. 2002 found a = D + 1 with D taken from centre positions, which is a semi-independent check.
checks.numerology_risk: Low within the dense regime, where D is measured separately from lengths. High for the catalogue's representative value. Published a values cover almost the whole possible range, the 2.8 comes from one well-studied site, and with D free the formula a = D + 1 can absorb almost anything. The dilute regime (growth-controlled) and the 3D shortfall (3-3.6 against 4) restrict 'derived' to dense networks.
checks.source: Catalogue citations: Bour et al. 2002 JGR 107(B6); Bonnet et al. 2001 Rev. Geophys. 39; Davy et al. 2010 JGR. Checked against the checker's recollection only; the web was unavailable in this task.

checks.system: Impact craters in saturation equilibrium
checks.corrected_alpha_uncertainty: 2.83-3.0: Hartmann's empirical saturation slope is -1.83, Gault's is -2. This matches the checker's recollection. Equilibrium forms only where the production slope is steeper than -2. Many surfaces (large craters, young terrains) are in production, not equilibrium, and the production function is wavy (local slopes about -1 to below -3).
checks.algebra_note: alpha = zeta + 1 = 3, d_log = 2 and d_lin = 3 are correct. Testable consequence (3), the transect giving D^-1, is stereology. For any 2D population of discs, the number crossing a line with diameter >= D scales as D^(1-zeta), whatever the mechanism, so it does not test the reading. Consequences (1) (production steeper than -2) and (2) (non-area erasure footprints) are genuine tests.
checks.best_reading: Equal crater-covered surface area per ln D: a 2D territory kept in steady state by area-based (cookie-cutter or degradation-footprint ∝ D^2) erasure. Gault 1970 is analytic and Richardson 2009 is a model, and both use this mechanism.
checks.numerology_risk: Low. The exponent is fixed in advance by 2D geometry, and the only rival (linear-orthopolic in D^3) has no mechanism. One residual: Hartmann's -1.83 departs by 0.17 from -2. That would require an erasure footprint growing slightly slower than D^2, or incomplete equilibrium, and it is not explained.
checks.source: Catalogue citations (Gault 1970; Hartmann 1984; Richardson 2009; Minton et al. 2019; Xiao & Werner 2015). Checker's recollection only; the web was unavailable in this task.

checks.system: Asteroid-belt collisional cascade (Dohnanyi)
checks.corrected_alpha_uncertainty: The theory is exact at s = 0. (21+s)/(6+s) gives about 3.6-3.7 in the strength regime (s ≈ -0.3 to -0.5) and about 3.05 in the gravity regime (s ≈ 1.2-1.5). I checked this algebra; it agrees with zeta_m = 5/(6+s) in research-program.md. The observed slopes were not verified. The D > 100 km population is widely held to be primordial (Bottke et al. 2005; 'asteroids were born big', Morbidelli et al. 2009; from recollection), so a 3.5-like slope there is not evidence for the cascade. Debris-disk mm indices give q ≈ 3.36 (MacGregor et al. 2016, from recollection), shallower than the strength-regime prediction.
checks.algebra_note: alpha_m = (alpha_D + 2)/3 = 11/6 and zeta_m = 5/6 are correct. The rate D^2 × D^-2.5 = D^-0.5 is correct, but it is a fixed point of the population's own slope, not an independently measured rate. The only independent inputs are s and the scaling of cross-section and velocity. The 'stock mass alone' decomposition is refuted (it predicts 4), so 'suggestive' is the wrong grade for it.
checks.best_reading: Log-orthopolic in mass flux: m × disruption rate ∝ D^2.5. This is the transport identity B = F/v with log-speed ∝ m^-1/6. It is derived by Dohnanyi 1969, Tanaka et al. 1996 and O'Brien & Greenberg 2003.
checks.numerology_risk: Low for the theory, which is pre-registered by mass conservation and self-similar collisions. The observational support is weak: the observed slopes vary from 2.3 to more than 4 by size range, and the large-body range is not collisionally relaxed.
checks.source: Repo docs/zeta-compilation.md row 52 and docs/research-program.md section 3; catalogue citations (Dohnanyi 1969; O'Brien & Greenberg 2003). Recollection for the main-belt and debris-disk slopes; the web was unavailable in this task.

checks.system: Interstellar dust grains (MRN)
checks.corrected_alpha_uncertainty: As I recall, MRN found acceptable fits for indices of about 3.3-3.6. Later dust models (Weingartner & Draine 2001; Zubko et al. 2004) are not pure power laws. The index is degenerate with composition and the size cutoffs, because it is constrained mainly by extinction.
checks.algebra_note: Correct as in Dohnanyi: d_log = 2.5 and d_lin = 3.5.
checks.best_reading: A steady grain-shattering cascade with constant mass flux (mass × collision rate ∝ a^2.5), as in Dohnanyi.
checks.numerology_risk: Moderate to high. 3.5 is the generic number for any steady, self-similar fragmentation cascade, so matching it does not single out ISM shattering. ISM dust is not shown to be in a steady cascade, since accretion, coagulation and sputtering compete. The empirical exponent itself is weakly determined. The area-volume geometric mean is pure numerology, as the catalogue says. I downgraded the grade from 'motivated' to 'suggestive'.
checks.source: Catalogue citations (MRN 1977; Jones, Tielens & Hollenbach 1996). Checker's recollection; the web was unavailable in this task.

checks.system: Global lakes (surface areas)
checks.corrected_alpha_uncertainty: 2.13-2.14 for two datasets above 0.46 km^2 (repo compilation, verified in an earlier task). No confidence interval was reported. The value depends strongly on the cutoff: the original analysis gave 1.97 above 8.5 km^2.
checks.algebra_note: Hyperscaling is correct: tau = 1 + 2/(91/48) = 187/91 and zeta = 96/91. The 3D analogue 1 + 3/2.52 ≈ 2.19 is correct. There is a cross-entry contradiction. The islands entry says B → 1 as H → 0 'consistent with lakes at 1.05-1.14', but this entry correctly notes that hull areas cannot exceed zeta = 1. Both cannot hold.
checks.best_reading: Log-orthopolic in gyration territory L^2. Water area is a fractal cluster mass, A ∝ L^(91/48), so tau = 1 + d/D_f (percolation hyperscaling, Cael & Seekell 2016).
checks.numerology_risk: Moderate. Three simple readings lie within about 0.15 of the data: log-orthopolic in water area (tau = 2, off by 0.14), territory/percolation (2.055, off by 0.085), and the hull bound (≤ 2). There is no CI to separate them. Whether lakes (depressions filled to their spill points) are critical percolation clusters is an assumption. The decisive test, a gyration-radius distribution N(>L) ∝ L^-2, has not been done. I downgraded the grade from 'derived' to 'motivated' because the established theory does not match within the stated precision.
checks.source: Repo docs/zeta-compilation.md row 32 (Cael & Seekell 2016 Sci. Rep. 6:29633; Corrigendum 2017 Sci. Rep. 7:42155; Cael, Biggs & Seekell 2022). The web was unavailable in this task.

checks.system: Islands (Korcak law)
checks.corrected_alpha_uncertainty: 1.5-1.75 by region (Mandelbrot's figures as quoted in the repo compilation). Korcak himself claimed B = 1/2. The value from the 131k-island compilation was not retrieved.
checks.algebra_note: B = 1 - H/2 is consistent with level-set loop counting: the number of loops larger than L ∝ L^-(2-H) (Isichenko; Kondev & Henley), and coastline D = 2 - H. The heuristic dA/dz ∝ A/relief ∝ L^(2-H) does give equal dA/dz per log class. The single-loop coastline alternative, D = (3-H)/2, gives 0.625 at H = 0.5, which is correct. The claim of consistency with lakes contradicts the hull bound (see the lakes entry).
checks.best_reading: Count = (2D slots ∝ L^-2) × (probability that the water level falls within an L-patch's relief ∝ L^H), so q ∝ L^(2-H) = A^(1-H/2), read as area per unit relief.
checks.numerology_risk: High unless H is measured first. H anywhere in [0, 1] maps onto B in [0.5, 1], which covers every reported value, so with H fitted afterwards the reading cannot fail. Real topography is neither Gaussian nor monofractal, and continents impose a cutoff. Oline et al. reportedly find that H estimates disagree (not verified here). The 'area per unit relief' label is post hoc; the slot × level-hit mechanism is the established part. I downgraded the grade from 'motivated' to 'suggestive'.
checks.source: Repo docs/zeta-compilation.md row 33 (Korcak 1938; Mandelbrot via arXiv 1303.1610; arXiv 2512.16659). Recollection for Isichenko 1992 and Kondev & Henley 1995. The web was unavailable in this task.

checks.system: Landslides (event inventories)
checks.corrected_alpha_uncertainty: 2.0-3.0 across inventories, mostly 2.3-2.5; 2.40 for the inverse-gamma tail of Malamud et al. 2004 (repo compilation). Volume-area gamma: 1.1-1.3 for soil and 1.3-1.6 for bedrock (Larsen et al. 2010), 1.45 (Guzzetti et al. 2009); both from recollection and consistent with the catalogue. The Brunetti et al. 2009 volume exponents (1.0-1.9) were not verified and come from mixed, non-event inventories that include rockfalls.
checks.algebra_note: alpha_A = 1 + gamma for zeta_V = 1, and alpha_V = 1 + (alpha_A - 1)/gamma, are correct. The condition gamma = alpha_A - 1 is exactly the criterion that separates erosion budgets dominated by large landslides from those dominated by small ones (the Larsen et al. argument, analogous to Hudson's alpha = 2). Volume orthopolity therefore places landslides on that knife edge.
checks.best_reading: Log-orthopolic in mobilized volume V = A × depth, with depth ∝ A^(gamma - 1).
checks.numerology_risk: High. The gamma range 1.1-1.6 maps onto alpha_A = 2.1-2.6, most of the observed range. The 3D-territory reading (count ∝ L^-3) gives 2.5, which is identical to gamma = 1.5. Where volumes are estimated from areas through V ∝ A^gamma, zeta_V = zeta_A/gamma automatically, so testing on such data is circular. A real test needs measured volumes in complete event inventories, with soil and bedrock separated.
checks.source: Repo docs/zeta-compilation.md row 55 (Malamud et al. 2004 ESPL 29:687); catalogue citations for Larsen 2010, Guzzetti 2009 and Brunetti 2009, checked against recollection only. The web was unavailable in this task.

checks.system: Wildfires (USA, Australia)
checks.corrected_alpha_uncertainty: 1.3-1.8 by ecoregion (Malamud et al. 2005; my recollection of the upper end is about 1.8). 2.2 ± 0.3 at xmin ≈ 6,300 acres (Clauset et al. 2009). Truncated lognormal fits are often preferred (Corral & Gonzalez 2019).
checks.algebra_note: Size-biased sampling, alpha_fire = tau_cluster - 1 = 1.055 for percolation, is correct. Perimeter orthopolity, alpha = 1 + D_P/2, is correct.
checks.best_reading: No natural reading. The nearest motivated mechanism, size-biased ignition of fuel clusters (percolation or forest-fire model, 1.06-1.19), underpredicts every observed value.
checks.numerology_risk: High. The spread from 1.3 to 2.2 lets perimeter (1.5-1.7), SOC (1.19), 2D territory (2.0) and others each fit some region or cutoff. Fire sizes depend on weather, suppression and fuel management, which change over time, so no fixed resource is expected. This is an informative failure.
checks.source: Repo docs/zeta-compilation.md row 54 (Malamud et al. 1998, 2005; Clauset et al. 2009; Corral & Gonzalez 2019). The web was unavailable in this task.

checks.system: River networks: drainage area and Hack's law
checks.corrected_alpha_uncertainty: 1.43-1.45 (0.45 in the 1992 abstract; 0.43 per La Barbera & Roth 1994; repo compilation). Hack's h is 0.5-0.6.
checks.algebra_note: tau = 2 - h (Maritan et al. 1996) is correct, as are the Scheidegger value h = 2/3 → beta = 1/3 and the energy exponent 0.45/0.5 = 0.90. Caveat: drainage areas are nested (the repo compilation flags this). The 'shared total' (basin area) is re-tiled at every threshold, so summing over classes gives basin area × ln(range). This is a per-class capacity identity, the same structure as the territory rule, not one fixed total divided among classes.
checks.best_reading: Drained width W = A/l(A) ∝ A^(1-h). Channel sites with area >= a tile the basin at spacing W(a), so N(>=a) ∝ basin area/W(a).
checks.numerology_risk: Low. h is measured somewhat independently, although from the same DEM networks. The relation beta = 1 - h holds across network types (optimal channel networks against Scheidegger) and was predicted before fitting.
checks.source: Repo docs/zeta-compilation.md row 34 (Rodriguez-Iturbe et al. 1992 WRR 28; Maritan et al. 1996, cond-mat/9610004); catalogue citations (Rigon 1996; La Barbera & Roth 1994). The web was unavailable in this task.

checks.system: Solar flares (energy, fluence, peak flux)
checks.corrected_alpha_uncertainty: 1.5-2.1 depending on waveband and variable, so a single 1.66 ± 0.2 is misleading. Hard X-ray nonthermal electron energy: 1.53 ± 0.02 (Crosby et al. 1993). Hard X-ray peak: 1.73-1.8. GOES soft X-ray fluence: 2.03 ± 0.09 (Veronig et al. 2002). The repo's own GOES 2022-2024 MLE gives 1.90 [1.82, 1.99] after background subtraction, 2.13 [2.03, 2.22] raw, and 2.27 for peak irradiance (results/resource_choice.json). The 1.66 is a mean over 61 heterogeneous datasets and does not represent thermal soft X-ray energy.
checks.algebra_note: Each reading's algebra is correct. The FD-SOC set (5/3, 9/5, 2, 7/3) follows from D_3 = 2.5, D_2 = 1.5 and diffusive T ∝ L^2. But the catalogue's 'energy itself (alpha = 2), does not match' decomposition does match the GOES fluence data.
checks.best_reading: No single reading fits. For hard X-ray, log-orthopolic in footprint area L^2 and linear-orthopolic in volume L^3 (FD-SOC) both give 5/3 for E ∝ L^3. For soft X-ray fluence, alpha ≈ 2 is log-orthopolic in the measured fluence itself (zeta = 1). The best-supported reading is FD-SOC for nonthermal energy, and it holds only for that waveband.
checks.numerology_risk: High. Three readings each fit some dataset. FD-SOC's joint predictions are checked against means with ±0.2-0.3 spread, and individual well-measured catalogues (GOES) deviate. The footprint-area test (2.0 against 2.33; observed 2.1 ± 0.3) does not discriminate. I downgraded the FD-SOC grade from 'motivated' to 'suggestive'.
checks.source: Repo results/resource_choice.json (GOES 2022-2024); docs/zeta-compilation.md rows 49-50 (Veronig et al. 2002 A&A 382:1070; Crosby et al. 1993; Aschwanden & Scholkmann 2025 arXiv 2505.00748); docs/references.md (Hudson 1991). The web was unavailable in this task.

checks.system: Stellar IMF above the turnover (Salpeter)
checks.corrected_alpha_uncertainty: Kroupa 2001: 2.3 ± 0.3 (0.5-1 Msun) and 2.3 ± 0.7 (>1 Msun) (repo compilation). The Padoan-Nordlund slope 3/(4-beta) is 1.33 for beta = 1.74, which I recall as the value their abstract quotes, or 1.36 for beta = 1.8.
checks.algebra_note: The algebra is correct. m ∝ rho_0 L^3 M_A^-2 with v ∝ L^((beta-1)/2) gives L^(4-beta), and count per ln L ∝ L^-3 gives Gamma = 3/(4-beta). The Burgers value 1.5, the Kolmogorov value 1.29 and the sheet case 2/(4-beta) ≈ 0.91 are all correct.
checks.best_reading: A 3D territory of self-similar turbulent structures (count ∝ L^-3), with core mass ∝ L^(4-beta) from MHD shock compression (Padoan & Nordlund 2002). The orthopolic reading is literally PN's self-similarity assumption.
checks.numerology_risk: Moderate. Other mechanisms give similar numbers: Hennebelle-Chabrier about 1.33, and competitive accretion about 1.5 (Bondi-type gives 1). Mapping the core mass function to the IMF assumes constant efficiency. A near-universal IMF while measured beta varies between clouds would be a tension; this is a useful test.
checks.source: Repo docs/zeta-compilation.md row 29 (Salpeter 1955; Kroupa 2001); catalogue citation Padoan & Nordlund 2002 ApJ 576:870, checked against recollection. The web was unavailable in this task.

checks.system: Dark-matter halo mass function, low-mass end
checks.corrected_alpha_uncertainty: The 1.87-1.93 is the Aquarius subhalo mass function, which is shaped by tidal stripping, while the Press-Schechter formula describes field halos. The catalogue conflates the two. For field halos at dwarf scales, n_eff ≈ -2.5 to -2.8 gives a PS alpha of 1.92-1.97. Sheth-Tormen (mass per d nu ∝ nu^-0.6 at low nu) gives 2 - 0.4(n+3)/6 ≈ 1.93-1.99. The slope tends to 2 as n_eff → -3.
checks.algebra_note: alpha = 2 - (n+3)/6, mass per ln M ∝ M^((n+3)/6) and d_log = 1 - (n+3)/6 are correct. The flat-in-nu (linear-orthopolic in peak height) statement is exact only for PS's constant barrier. Ellipsoidal (ST) and simulation fits are not flat in nu at low nu.
checks.best_reading: Field halos: Lagrangian-volume (mass) log-orthopolity tilted by the spectral slope. In PS, equal mass per unit peak height nu, giving alpha = 2 - (n+3)/6.
checks.numerology_risk: Low for field halos: the tilt is fixed in advance by the linear power spectrum, and scale-free simulations test it. Not derived for subhalos, whose slope depends on accretion history and stripping.
checks.source: Repo docs/zeta-compilation.md row 31 (Springel et al. 2008 MNRAS 391:1685; arXiv 0705.1599). The Sheth-Tormen low-nu behaviour is from the checker's derivation from the standard ST form. The web was unavailable in this task.

checks.system: Galaxy stellar mass function, faint end (GAMA)
checks.corrected_alpha_uncertainty: ±0.15 systematic (Baldry et al. 2012 -1.47; Wright et al. 2017 -1.50 ± 0.01 ± 0.15; repo compilation). The faint-end slope varies from about -1.3 to -1.6 with sample depth and environment, and steepens with redshift.
checks.algebra_note: alpha = -alpha_S and zeta = 0.47 are correct. The energy-driven value 0.9/(5/3) = 0.54, the momentum-driven value 0.9/(4/3) = 0.68, the SHMR range 0.47-0.56, and the Local Group value 0.9/3.1 ≈ 0.29 all check. The 'resource' (halo mass^0.9 = M*^0.54) is a change of variable from the halo case, not a new resource.
checks.best_reading: Halo near-orthopolity (zeta_h ≈ 0.9) viewed through M* ∝ M_h^(5/3) from energy-driven feedback (Dekel & Silk 1986; Dekel & Woo 2003), giving zeta_* ≈ 0.54.
checks.numerology_risk: Moderate. Energy-driven (0.54) and momentum-driven (0.68) feedback both lie within about 1.5 sigma of 0.47-0.50 given the ±0.15 systematic. SHMR slopes from abundance matching are circular, because they use the GSMF itself. Feedback prescriptions in galaxy-formation models are tuned to the faint end.
checks.source: Repo docs/zeta-compilation.md row 30 (Baldry et al. 2012 MNRAS 421:621; Wright et al. 2017 arXiv 1705.04074). Dekel & Woo 2003 is a catalogue citation. The web was unavailable in this task.

checks.system: Galactic cosmic rays below the knee
checks.corrected_alpha_uncertainty: 2.7 is the all-particle index. Protons have about 2.85 at 45-200 GV (AMS-02), harden by about 0.1-0.13 above about 300 GV, and soften near 10-20 TeV (DAMPE); helium is about 2.78. These are the checker's recollection. The real uncertainty is therefore about ±0.1, and the index depends on energy, not ±0.05. AMS-02 B/C: delta = 0.333 ± 0.014 ± 0.005 above 65 GV, and secondaries harden above about 200 GV.
checks.algebra_note: Leaky box: alpha = alpha_source + delta. DSA: d_log = 3/(r-1). Both are correct. With protons at 2.85 and delta = 1/3, the required source index is about 2.5, not 2.37.
checks.best_reading: Leaky box N = Q × tau_esc. The standing stock is log-orthopolic in E^(1+delta) times the source tilt. The structure is derived, but no resource reading predicts the source index. DSA at r = 4 gives 2, and r ≈ 3.0-3.2 is fitted after the fact.
checks.numerology_risk: Moderate to high. delta (1/3 Kolmogorov, 1/2 Kraichnan, about 0.6 in older fits) and the source index (2.0-2.5) are both adjustable, and many pairs sum to 2.7. Only delta is measured independently.
checks.source: Catalogue citations (AMS-02 PRL 117:231102, 2016). AMS-02 proton and DAMPE spectral features are from recollection. The web was unavailable in this task.

verification.missing_cases:
Verification status: no new web verification was possible in this task. The harness web-search budget (200 per turn, shared by all agents) was already used up, and direct fetches failed (DNS failure, and proxy 403 on arXiv and PMC). Checks rely on the repo's data and compilation, which I recomputed where possible (USGS b-values), and on my own recollection, flagged per case. Searching can resume if the user sends a follow-up message or raises CLAUDE_CODE_MAX_WEB_SEARCHES_PER_SESSION. All values below are from recollection and unverified.

Omitted power laws:
