(1) Euclidean source counts, N(>S) ∝ S^-3/2. This is the cleanest pre-registered territory case: uniformly spread sources fill a 3D territory r^3 and have flux S ∝ r^-2, so zeta_S = 3/2 (d_s/D_k). Its known failures (evolving radio sources; the BATSE GRB faint-end flattening) show the rule breaking when the sources evolve or the geometry is not Euclidean.

(2) Omori-Utsu aftershock decay, rate ∝ t^-p with p ≈ 0.9-1.5. Near p = 1 this is equal aftershocks per ln t: log-orthopolic in time, not size. Aftershock productivity ∝ 10^(alpha M) with alpha ≈ 0.8-1 ≈ b implies productivity ∝ M0^(2/3), i.e. ∝ rupture area. This independently supports the area reading of G-R and is a better test than b itself.

(3) Rock fragmentation and comminution: N(>r) ∝ r^-D with D ≈ 2.5-2.6 for many materials (Turcotte 1986; Sammis et al. 1987 derive 2.58 from the rule that same-size neighbours cannot both break). This is a 3D packing that does not fill space, a counterexample to the territory rule, which predicts D = 3. Its zeta_m = D/3 ≈ 0.84 coincides with Dohnanyi's 5/6.

(4) Giant molecular cloud and clump mass spectra: dN/dM ∝ M^-1.5 to M^-1.8 in the inner Milky Way, steeper (about 2-2.5) in the outer Galaxy and M33. With Larson's M ∝ R^2, a 3D territory predicts alpha = 2.5 and a 2D disc territory predicts 2.0. Inner-Galaxy values fail both, in the same medium where the IMF reading is claimed. This is a strong counterexample to the program's pattern 1.

(5) Kuiper-belt object sizes: steep q ≈ 4-5 above about 100 km, breaking to about 2-3 below. These are primordial (accretion or streaming instability), with no territory or flux reading.

(6) Debris-disk grain index from mm spectral slopes, q ≈ 3.36 ± 0.02. This directly tests the Dohnanyi strength reading, which predicts 3.6-3.7, and it comes out shallower.

(7) Planetary-ring particles, q ≈ 2.7-3.1 (Saturn): q = 3 would be log-orthopolic in cross-section, i.e. optical depth shared equally per log size. A possible positive case.

(8) Photospheric magnetic-flux features, N(Phi) ∝ Phi^-1.85 over five decades (Parnell et al. 2009), against sunspot areas, which are lognormal (Bogdan 1988), a no-power-law counterexample.

(9) Topography and gravity spectra: Earth topography P(k) ∝ k^-2 (H ≈ 0.5); Kaula's rule (gravity degree variance ∝ l^-3). These are where an independent H for the islands reading must come from. Variance per log scale is not flat.

(10) Volcanic eruption volumes: frequency falls by roughly 3-10x per VEI step, zeta ≈ 0.5-0.7. Volcanic swarm b-values of 1.5-3 are the natural test of the 'volumetric seismicity, b = 1.5' prediction, but they are usually attributed to pore pressure and heterogeneity.

(11) Galaxy correlation function, xi ∝ r^-1.8 (correlation dimension about 1.2 at small scales, approaching 3 above about 100 Mpc). This shows the territory dimension itself depends on scale.

(12) The task asked for scaling laws, and the catalogue gave none. Kepler T^2 ∝ a^3, inverse-square flux, Stefan-Boltzmann, stellar mass-luminosity L ∝ M^3-4, Tully-Fisher L ∝ V^4, Kennicutt-Schmidt Sigma_SFR ∝ Sigma_gas^1.4, Larson sigma ∝ R^0.5, fault displacement-length (n ≈ 1), and Horton/Tokunaga ratios are all missing.

(13) Ultra-high-energy cosmic rays (E^-3.2, then an ankle at about E^-2.6, then the GZK cutoff); solar energetic particle fluences (alpha about 1.1-1.5, top-heavy); tsunami run-ups and flood peaks.

Cross-cutting issues for the domain_patterns:

(a) Several proposed 'tests' are stereological identities that hold for any mechanism: crater transect D^-1, fracture a_3D = a_2D + 1, scanline. They cannot test a resource reading.

(b) Slot counting gives capacities. Event catalogues (earthquakes, flares) are rates, so a territory reading also needs a per-slot rate independent of size. With recurrence ∝ slip ∝ L, slot counting gives b = 1.5, not 1.

(c) b varies systematically with stress (0.7-1.2), which the geometric reading does not predict.

(d) The islands and lakes entries contradict each other (hull bound against 'consistent with lakes').

(e) The fracture-moment and territory decompositions predict the same a_3D = 4 but are flagged differently.

(f) The halo entry mixes field-halo theory with subhalo data.

(g) Flare exponents depend on waveband: GOES soft X-ray fluence is about 2.0 (zeta = 1), so the 'energy itself' reading fits there.

(h) Asteroids larger than 100 km are primordial, not cascade-relaxed.

(i) The territory rule zeta_k = d_s/D_k has two choices, d_s and D_k. It counts as pre-registered only when D_k comes from a measured scaling (Hanks-Bakun, Larson, percolation D_f) and d_s from geometry. Case (4) shows it can fail even then, which makes it a genuinely falsifiable rule.

cases.system: Point-source radiation intensity; Newtonian gravity and Coulomb fields (Gauss's law); d-dimensional generalization
cases.law_or_distribution: I(r) = P/(4 pi r^2); g(r) = GM/r^2; E(r) = q/(4 pi eps0 r^2); in d spatial dimensions field or intensity ∝ r^-(d-1)
cases.variable_k: distance r from the source (m)
cases.reported_exponent: -2. Coulomb: deviation delta in r^-(2+delta) bounded at (2.7 +/- 3.1)e-16 (Williams, Faller & Hill 1971). Gravity: inverse square holds at 95% CL down to 56 um, so any large extra dimension R <= 44 um (Kapner et al. 2007). Later Eot-Wash bounds reach ~42 um (2013).
cases.alpha_uncertainty: |delta| < ~3e-16 (Coulomb); no gravitational-strength Yukawa deviation for lambda >= 56 um
cases.conversion: Sharing law y ∝ x^a with a = -2. Mapping for laws with a<0, where y is a per-unit share of a conserved total: treat y as the density, so alpha_equiv = -a = 2, d_lin = -a = 2 (units sharing the total ∝ r^2), d_log = -a - 1 = 1.
cases.orthopolic_reading: Conserved total: the power P, or the field flux (q/eps0, 4 pi G M), crossing every closed surface around the source. This is a FLUX, conserved by energy conservation in a lossless medium or by Gauss's law. Classes are concentric spheres. The units sharing the total are unit-area cells, numbering ∝ r^(d-1), each holding I ∝ P/r^(d-1). Every sphere holds the same total, so the law is discretely orthopolic across spheres. It is also linear-orthopolic in the radiation energy STOCK: energy per shell dr = P/c, independent of r, which is the transport identity B = F/v with constant F = P and v = c. In the author's mapping (density ∝ r^-2, so resource ∝ r^2) the orthopolic resource is the sphere's area, d_lin = 2 = d-1. The log reading (d_log = 1) has no physical referent, because energy per d ln r grows ∝ r.

decompositions.resource: area of the enclosing sphere (number of unit-area slots)
decompositions.composition: d_lin = d - 1 (dimension of the sphere S^(d-1)) with the total flux conserved
decompositions.predicted_exponent: -(d-1): -2 in 3D, -1 for a line source or in 2D
decompositions.independent_motivation: Argued before looking at the exponent: energy conservation in a lossless, non-scattering medium, or Gauss's law for flux lines that neither begin nor end in empty space, requires the same total through every enclosing surface. Isotropy spreads it uniformly. A sphere of radius r in d dimensions has area ∝ r^(d-1).
decompositions.theory_agreement: Derived: the divergence theorem gives exactly this resource reading, with an identical mechanism.
decompositions.testable_consequence: (a) Line source (cylindrical spreading, effectively d=2): I ∝ 1/r, i.e. 3 dB per doubling of distance instead of 6 dB. (b) If gravity spreads into n compact extra dimensions, the slot count becomes r^(2+n) for r << R and the force steepens to r^-(2+n). Torsion balances exclude this above ~50 um. (c) In an absorbing medium the flux is not conserved, so the reading predicts an extra exp(-kappa r), i.e. transport-identity condition (i) failing. (d) A photon mass would add a Yukawa factor, which Coulomb tests bound at delta < 3e-16.

decompositions.resource: radiation energy stock per radial shell dr
decompositions.composition: B = F/v: constant flux P divided by constant propagation speed c gives energy per dr = P/c, flat in r
decompositions.independent_motivation: At stationarity, the energy between r and r+dr equals the flux times the transit time dr/c.
decompositions.theory_agreement: Exact for radiation in vacuum.
decompositions.testable_consequence: Where the propagation speed varies with r (a graded medium, or group velocity in a dispersive medium), the stock per shell must vary as 1/v(r) while the flux, and so the ray-tube intensity law, stays fixed. The stock and flux readings then separate.

cases.source: Kapner et al. (2007) PRL 98:021101, arXiv hep-ph/0611184 (abstract and summaries); Williams, Faller & Hill (1971) PRL 26:721 (value via secondary teaching sources); Gauss's law (textbook).

cases.system: Thermal (blackbody) radiation: Rayleigh-Jeans and Wien tails of Planck's law, Stefan-Boltzmann law, photon number density
cases.law_or_distribution: u_nu = (8 pi nu^2/c^3) h nu/(exp(h nu/kT) - 1). RJ tail: u_nu ≈ 8 pi nu^2 kT/c^3. Wien tail: ∝ nu^3 exp(-h nu/kT). Totals: u = a T^4 (emitted flux sigma T^4), n_gamma ∝ T^3. In d dimensions: u ∝ T^(d+1), n_gamma ∝ T^d.
cases.variable_k: temperature T (K) for the aggregate laws; frequency nu (Hz) for the spectral tails
cases.reported_exponent: u ∝ T^4 (Stefan 1879 empirical, Boltzmann 1884 derived); n_gamma ∝ T^3; RJ spectral slope +2 in nu; the Wien tail is exponential, not a power law. 1D analogue: a single ballistic channel carries heat ∝ T^2, i.e. thermal conductance quantum g0 = pi^2 kB^2 T/(3h), measured by Schwab et al. (2000).
cases.alpha_uncertainty: exact in theory
cases.conversion: Aggregate law y ∝ x^a, a = 4. Mapping for laws with a>0, where y = (number of active slots) x (resource per slot): the implied resource exponent is a, so d_lin = d_log = 4. This is measure-free, since no abundance density is involved. For the RJ spectral tail read as a density in nu: slots per d nu ∝ nu^(d-1) = nu^2 and slots per d ln nu ∝ nu^d = nu^3.
cases.orthopolic_reading: Classical equipartition is the archetype of discrete orthopolity: every field mode (slot) holds the same mean energy kT whatever its frequency. Objects are the cavity's standing-wave modes, whose count per d nu grows as nu^(d-1). That count is a CAPACITY, the number of k-space cells in a shell. The RJ nu^2 is therefore pure slot geometry (d-1) times an equal per-slot resource. Quantization caps which slots participate: a mode holds kT only if h nu ≲ kT. Above that its occupation is the Boltzmann factor (Wien tail), the maximum-entropy exponential for discrete classes at fixed mean cost, and no orthopolic reading works. The total u(T) is a final resource: active slots ∝ (kT/h c)^d times energy per active slot ∝ kT.

decompositions.resource: energy density u(T) = active mode count x energy per mode
decompositions.composition: u ∝ N_active x eps_slot ∝ T^d x T^1 = T^(d+1); d = 3 from the k-space volume up to the thermal cutoff (linear dispersion), +1 from equipartition
decompositions.predicted_exponent: T^(d+1): T^4 in 3D, T^3 in 2D, T^2 in 1D; T^(1+d/s) for dispersion omega ∝ k^s
decompositions.independent_motivation: Mode counting in a box (Rayleigh, Jeans) and equipartition predate Planck. Each mode occupies a fixed k-space cell (2 pi/L)^d, so the number of modes inside the thermal radius k_T ∝ T is ∝ T^d. The cutoff h nu ~ kT follows from quantization.
decompositions.theory_agreement: Derived: integrating Planck's law gives a_d T^(d+1) with exactly this slots x per-slot structure.
decompositions.testable_consequence: 1D blackbody: a single-mode channel (transmission line or phonon waveguide) carries heat ∝ T^2. This was measured as the thermal conductance quantum pi^2 kB^2 T/(3h) in suspended SiN phonon waveguides (Schwab et al. 2000) and later for one electronic channel (Jezouin et al. 2013). The mean energy per photon u/n_gamma ≈ 2.70 kT must be linear in T in every dimension.

decompositions.resource: momentum flux shared equally among the d spatial directions (radiation pressure p = u/d)
decompositions.composition: Thermodynamic identity (dU/dV)_T = T (dp/dT)_V - p with p = u/d gives (d+1) u = T du/dT, so u ∝ T^(d+1)
decompositions.independent_motivation: Isotropic radiation divides its momentum flux equally among the d axes, an equal-share statement fixed by isotropy alone, without mode counting.
decompositions.theory_agreement: Derived: Boltzmann's 1884 route. Here the d enters as the number of directions sharing the momentum flux.
decompositions.testable_consequence: Any isotropic gas of massless quanta (phonons with a single sound speed, neutrinos) must obey the same T^(d+1) through p = u/d. A gas with p = w u (w ≠ 1/d) gives u ∝ T^(1+1/w).

decompositions.resource: equal energy kT per slot continued to all frequencies (classical equipartition)
decompositions.composition: slots ∝ nu^2 x kT for all nu
decompositions.predicted_exponent: u_nu ∝ nu^2 at all nu (ultraviolet catastrophe)
decompositions.independent_motivation: Classical equipartition applied to every mode.
decompositions.theory_agreement: Refuted by Planck 1900: Bose-Einstein occupation, whose tail is the Boltzmann exponential (the maximum-entropy result of concept.md section 4, not orthopolity).
decompositions.testable_consequence: The breakdown frequency scales linearly with T (Wien displacement, nu_peak ≈ 2.82 kT/h). This marks where the per-slot budget kT falls below the per-slot cost h nu. Gapped excitations (superconductors, Schottky levels) show the same exponential freezing.

cases.source: Planck and Stefan-Boltzmann laws (textbook); d-dimensional T^(d+1): arXiv quant-ph/0510002 and quant-ph/0506131 (search summaries); Schwab, Henriksen, Worlock & Roukes (2000) Nature 404:974-977 (abstract); Jezouin et al. (2013) Science (cited in summary).

cases.system: Low-temperature heat capacity from gapless excitations: phonons (Debye), magnons (Bloch), 2D lattices, graphene flexural phonons, conduction electrons
cases.law_or_distribution: C ∝ T^3 (3D acoustic phonons, Debye 1912). Generally C ∝ T^(d/s) for excitations with omega ∝ k^s in d dimensions: 3D ferromagnet magnons T^(3/2); 2D lattice phonons T^2; graphene flexural (ZA) phonons T^1. Metals: electronic C = gamma T in any d.
cases.variable_k: temperature T (K), well below the Debye/exchange temperature
cases.reported_exponent: 3 (Debye, standard); 3/2 for ferromagnets (Bloch; magnetization deficit also T^(3/2)); ~2 for graphite at intermediate T, crossing to T^3 at the lowest T from interlayer coupling (Klemens 1953); ~1 from flexural phonons in graphene/expanded graphite, mixed with defect terms; electrons 1.
cases.alpha_uncertainty: exact asymptotically; real materials show crossovers
cases.conversion: Aggregate law, a = 3 = d/s with d = 3, s = 1; d_lin = d_log = 3 under the aggregate mapping.
cases.orthopolic_reading: Heat capacity counts thermally active slots. Each mode with hbar omega ≲ kT holds kT by equipartition and contributes kB to C. Much stiffer modes are frozen. The per-slot resource (kB of heat capacity) is equal across active slots, i.e. discrete orthopolity across modes. The exponent is the CAPACITY exponent: the k-space volume of active modes, (k_T)^d with k_T ∝ T^(1/s). Energy is U ∝ T^(1+d/s), the same structure as Stefan-Boltzmann, so C = dU/dT ∝ T^(d/s).

decompositions.resource: number of thermally active modes (k-space volume inside the thermal shell)
decompositions.composition: d/s: d from the k-space volume, 1/s from inverting the dispersion omega ∝ k^s at hbar omega = kT
decompositions.predicted_exponent: T^3 (3D phonons); T^(3/2) (3D ferromagnet magnons, s=2); T^3 (3D antiferromagnet magnons, s=1); T^2 (2D phonons); T^1 (2D flexural, s=2)
decompositions.independent_motivation: Phonons and magnons are bosonic oscillators. The number of oscillators below a frequency follows from the dispersion relation (measured by neutron scattering) and the dimension, independently of any thermal data. Equipartition gives kB per active oscillator.
decompositions.theory_agreement: Derived: Debye model and Bloch spin-wave theory; the mechanism is exactly slot counting x kB.
decompositions.testable_consequence: Every slot-counting observable of the same excitations must share d/s. For ferromagnets the magnon number, hence the magnetization deficit (Bloch's law), has the same exponent as C. Graphite must cross over from T^2 to T^3 below the temperature where interlayer coupling resolves the third dimension. In 2D isotropic ferromagnetic films the reading predicts a T-linear magnon count with an infrared log divergence. The observed T^(3/2) in 2D films is anomalous and has been attributed to dipolar/elliptical-precession dispersion (arXiv cond-mat/0210674): the slot count needs the true dispersion.

decompositions.resource: conduction-electron states within kT of the Fermi surface
decompositions.composition: Active slots ∝ T^1 in any d: a shell of thickness kT in energy on a fixed Fermi surface, with Pauli blocking freezing the interior
decompositions.independent_motivation: Fermion occupation can change only within ~kT of E_F.
decompositions.theory_agreement: Derived (Sommerfeld).
decompositions.testable_consequence: A counterexample to 'the exponent is a spatial dimension': the active region is one-dimensional in energy. Opening a gap Delta (superconductor) freezes the slots and gives C ∝ exp(-Delta/kT), as in the Wien tail.

cases.source: Debye and Bloch laws (textbook); Klemens (1953) Aust. J. Phys. 6:405 (T^2 in graphite, abstract); graphene ZA quadratic dispersion (Lindsay, Broido & Mingo; summaries); arXiv cond-mat/0210674 (Bloch law in 2D). The general T^(d/s) rule is a standard derivation, confirmed case by case by these sources.

cases.system: Two-body Newtonian orbits (planets, satellites, binaries); galactic rotation curves
cases.law_or_distribution: T^2 = 4 pi^2 a^3/(G M); equivalently T^2 G rho_bar(<a) = 3 pi for circular orbits, with rho_bar the mean density enclosed
cases.variable_k: semimajor axis a (m); orbital period T (s)
cases.reported_exponent: T^2 ∝ a^3 (T ∝ a^(3/2)), precise in the Solar System. Flat galactic rotation curves (v ≈ const) correspond to T ∝ r.
cases.alpha_uncertainty: exact within Newtonian gravity
cases.conversion: Aggregate law y = T^2 ∝ a^3, a = 3; d_lin = d_log = 3 under the aggregate mapping (3/2 in T itself).
cases.orthopolic_reading: Two exact readings. (A) Kepler's second law is itself orthopolic: angular-momentum conservation makes the areal velocity h/2 constant, so time is allocated equally to equal swept areas (linear-orthopolic in area). The period is total area ∝ a^2 times time per unit area ∝ 1/h ∝ a^(-1/2). (B) Dilution: the central mass is spread over the orbital volume, rho_bar = 3M/(4 pi a^3), and T^2 = 3 pi/(G rho_bar). The 3 is the volume dimension over which M is averaged; the square comes from second-order dynamics. (A) is a flux reading (area per time), (B) a capacity/dilution reading.

decompositions.resource: orbital volume per unit central mass (inverse mean enclosed density)
decompositions.composition: T^2 ∝ a^d/M: the d-volume, with T ∝ (G rho_bar)^(-1/2), i.e. exponent d/z with z = 2 from Newton's second law
decompositions.predicted_exponent: T^2 ∝ a^d (gravity ∝ r^-(d-1)): a^3 in 3D, a^2 in 2D
decompositions.independent_motivation: Gauss's law for gravity makes only the enclosed mass matter. Circular-orbit balance gives v^2/a = GM/a^(d-1). The free-fall time is ∝ (G rho)^(-1/2) by dimensional analysis. None of this uses orbital data.
decompositions.theory_agreement: Derived (Newton); T^2 = 3 pi/(G rho_bar) is exact for circular orbits.
decompositions.testable_consequence: (i) With extended mass M(<r) ∝ r (isothermal halo), rho_bar ∝ r^-2, so T ∝ r and v is constant: the observed flat rotation curves, from which halos are inferred. (ii) Inside a uniform sphere rho_bar is constant, so T is independent of radius: the harmonic period, e.g. ~84 min for any chord through a uniform Earth. (iii) In 2D gravity (force ∝ 1/r), T ∝ a.

decompositions.resource: swept area per unit areal velocity (time allocated equally per area)
decompositions.composition: T = pi a^2 sqrt(1-e^2)/(h/2), with h ∝ sqrt(G M a (1-e^2)): 2 (planar area) - 1/2 (areal velocity) = 3/2
decompositions.independent_motivation: Equal areas in equal times follows from angular-momentum conservation alone, independently of the third law.
decompositions.theory_agreement: Derived.
decompositions.testable_consequence: In d dimensions the planar area stays ∝ a^2 while h ∝ a^((4-d)/2), giving T ∝ a^(d/2), consistent with the dilution reading. For non-central forces L is not conserved, so the equal-time-per-area allocation fails, while an averaged dilution reading can survive.

cases.source: Kepler's third law: textbook (MIT 8.223 lecture 8, UMD ASTR320 notes, via search). The d-dimensional generalization and the T^2 G rho_bar = 3 pi identity are my own derivations from Gauss's law; no source stating them was found.

cases.system: 3D homogeneous isotropic turbulence, inertial range (velocity spectrum)
cases.law_or_distribution: E(k) = C_K eps^(2/3) k^(-5/3) (Kolmogorov 1941, Obukhov 1941)
cases.variable_k: wavenumber k (rad/m); E(k) = kinetic energy per unit mass per unit wavenumber (m^3 s^-2)
cases.reported_exponent: -5/3 over several decades in a tidal channel at Re ~ 1e8, R_lambda up to ~3000, with 1D Kolmogorov constant ≈ 0.5 (Grant, Stewart & Moilliet 1962). Intermittency adds mu/9 with mu ≈ 0.25 +/- 0.05, giving ≈ 1.69-1.70; She-Leveque zeta_2 = 0.696 gives 1.696.
cases.alpha_uncertainty: theory 5/3; measured 1.67-1.71 depending on Re and fit range; intermittency ≈ +0.03
cases.conversion: Spectrum read as a density in k: alpha = 5/3, d_log = alpha - 1 = 2/3 (energy per ln k ∝ k^(-2/3)), d_lin = 5/3.
cases.orthopolic_reading: Orthopolic in a FLUX, not a stock. The energy flux eps through every log-wavenumber is the same, because energy is conserved in the inertial range (no forcing, no dissipation). Transport identity: energy per ln k is B = F/v with F = eps and log-speed v = 1/tau(k) ∝ eps^(1/3) k^(2/3), the eddy turnover rate. So B ∝ eps^(2/3) k^(-2/3), and the stock exponent d_log = 2/3 is exactly the exponent of the cascade rate. Per-object version: eddies of size l are slots in a space-filling packing, numbering ∝ l^-3 per unit volume per ln l, and each carries flux eps l^3 ∝ its volume, so flux per ln l is flat.

decompositions.resource: energy flux eps through scale (stock x turnover rate)
decompositions.composition: stock per ln k = flux/rate: 0 (flat flux) + 2/3 (turnover rate ∝ k^(2/3)) = 2/3 = d_log. Dimensionally kE = eps^(2/3) l^(2/3).
decompositions.independent_motivation: The nonlinear term conserves energy and transfers it locally in scale (Richardson's cascade). The only rate at scale l built from eps alone is eps^(1/3) l^(-2/3).
decompositions.theory_agreement: Derived: K41 is precisely the constant-flux reading.
decompositions.testable_consequence: (a) The 2D inverse energy cascade must also give k^(-5/3); observed by Paret & Tabeling (1997) with Kolmogorov constant 5.5-7. (b) A passive scalar in the same range with constant variance flux must give k^(-5/3) (Obukhov-Corrsin). (c) The exact flux statement <du^3> = -(4/5) eps r should hold without intermittency correction, while the stock (spectrum) may carry one, as observed.

decompositions.resource: active-eddy volume (beta-model: flux carried on a fractal set of dimension D < 3)
decompositions.composition: slots per ln l ∝ l^(-D) instead of l^(-3): spectral exponent 5/3 + (3-D)/3 = 5/3 + mu/3
decompositions.independent_motivation: Dissipation is spatially intermittent, so the flux is carried by a shrinking fraction of space at small scales.
decompositions.theory_agreement: Frisch, Sulem & Nelkin (1978) beta-model. Its zeta_p is linear in p, while measured zeta_p are concave. Lognormal (mu/9) and She-Leveque models fit better.
decompositions.testable_consequence: The beta-model predicts zeta_p linear in p; data show concavity, especially at p > 6. The 'reduced slot count' reading overshoots the spectral correction.

cases.source: Grant, Stewart & Moilliet (1962) JFM 12:241-268 (abstract and secondary accounts); Paret & Tabeling (1997) PRL 79:4162 (abstract); Frisch, Sulem & Nelkin (1978) JFM 87:719 (abstract via summaries); mu ≈ 0.25 +/- 0.05 (Sreenivasan & Kailasnath 1993; Praskovsky & Oncley) via secondary summary.

cases.system: 2D turbulence (soap films, thin stratified layers, mesoscale atmosphere), direct enstrophy cascade range
cases.law_or_distribution: E(k) = C' eta^(2/3) k^-3 [ln(k/k_f)]^(-1/3) (Kraichnan 1967, log correction 1971); inverse energy range E ∝ eps^(2/3) k^(-5/3)
cases.variable_k: wavenumber k (rad/m)
cases.reported_exponent: Theory -3 with log correction, confirmed numerically by Pasquero & Falkovich (2002). Many forced simulations give -3.3 to -3.6 (Maltrud & Vallis). Linear drag steepens the spectrum (Nam, Ott, Antonsen & Guzdar 2000). Decaying soap-film turbulence gives good k^-3.
cases.alpha_uncertainty: -3 (theory) to about -4 (drag, non-locality); commonly -3.3 to -3.6 in forced runs
cases.conversion: Density in k: alpha = 3, d_log = 2, d_lin = 3.
cases.orthopolic_reading: The author's k^-3 example, realized physically. Enstrophy Z = ∫k^2 E dk is conserved in 2D and cascades forward with constant flux eta. Its cascade rate is scale-independent (strain from the large scales, ∝ eta^(1/3)). So by B = F/v the enstrophy STOCK per ln k, k^3 E(k), is flat, as is the flux. Read as an energy density, k^-3 is log-orthopolic in a resource ∝ k^2 per unit energy. That k^2 is the squared-gradient weight converting energy into enstrophy, not a geometric area, and certainly not a 3D 'volume' k^3.

decompositions.resource: enstrophy (k^2 x energy) per ln k; stock and flux both flat
decompositions.composition: d_log = 2 (gradient-squared weight k^2) + 0 (scale-independent cascade rate); alpha = 2 + 0 + 1 (Jacobian)
decompositions.independent_motivation: 2D inviscid flow conserves both energy and enstrophy, and Fjortoft's argument sends enstrophy to small scales. The straining that transfers it comes from the large-scale vorticity, so its rate does not depend on k.
decompositions.theory_agreement: Derived (Kraichnan-Leith-Batchelor). The log correction arises because the transfer is non-local, a marginal case where the rate integral diverges logarithmically.
decompositions.testable_consequence: (a) Drag removes enstrophy at every scale (flux not conserved), so the spectrum must steepen by an amount set by the drag and the distribution of finite-time Lyapunov exponents; confirmed (Nam et al. 2000). (b) Because the rate is scale-independent, pair separation in this range should be exponential in time, not Richardson t^3. (c) A passive scalar in this range should show a Batchelor-like k^-1. (d) The inverse range must show k^-5/3 (flux reading); observed by Paret & Tabeling 1997.

decompositions.resource: a 'volume' k^3 under the linear measure
decompositions.composition: d_lin = 3 read as a 3D volume
decompositions.independent_motivation: None: the flow is 2D, so a 3D volume has no referent.
decompositions.theory_agreement: No theory supports it.
decompositions.testable_consequence: It would predict k^-3 in 3D turbulence as well, which is false (3D gives k^-5/3).

cases.source: Kraichnan (1967) Phys. Fluids 10:1417; Kraichnan (1971) JFM 47:525 (log correction, via secondary); Pasquero & Falkovich (2002) PRE 65:056305 (abstract); Nam, Ott, Antonsen & Guzdar (2000) PRL 84:5134 (abstract); Maltrud & Vallis slopes via secondary summary; Boffetta & Ecke (2012) Annu. Rev. Fluid Mech. 44:427.

cases.system: Passive scalar (temperature, salinity, dye) at high Prandtl/Schmidt number, viscous-convective range
cases.law_or_distribution: E_theta(k) = q chi (nu/eps)^(1/2) k^-1 between the Kolmogorov and Batchelor wavenumbers (Batchelor 1959)
cases.variable_k: wavenumber k (rad/m), 1/eta_K < k < 1/eta_B
cases.reported_exponent: -1. Supported by ocean microstructure (Grant, Hughes, Vogel & Moilliet 1968; Oakey & Elliott 1982), laboratory work (Williams & Paulson 1977) and numerics. Kraichnan's (1968) fluctuating-strain model keeps k^-1 and changes only the constant and the roll-off. A version has been proved for a model flow (Bedrossian, Blumenthal & Punshon-Smith).
cases.alpha_uncertainty: -1 within the viscous-convective range; the range is short in most data
cases.conversion: Density in k: alpha = 1, d_log = 0 (scalar variance per ln k flat), d_lin = 1.
cases.orthopolic_reading: Log-orthopolic in the scalar-variance STOCK itself, because both transport-identity conditions hold. The variance flux chi is conserved through the range (diffusion acts only beyond the Batchelor scale). The log-speed at which variance moves to small scales is the strain rate gamma ≈ (eps/nu)^(1/2), independent of k, because the sub-Kolmogorov velocity field is smooth. So B = chi/gamma is flat. This is the cleanest physical analogue of the Gibrat condition: the transfer does not care about scale.

decompositions.resource: scalar variance per ln k (stock = flux/strain rate)
decompositions.composition: d_log = 0 (conserved flux chi) + 0 (scale-independent strain rate)
decompositions.independent_motivation: Below the Kolmogorov scale the velocity is locally a uniform strain, so scalar filaments are thinned at the same exponential rate at every scale, and scalar variance is conserved except by diffusion. Both facts are argued from the flow, not from scalar spectra.
decompositions.theory_agreement: Derived: Batchelor 1959; Kraichnan 1968 confirms k^-1 with fluctuating strain.
decompositions.testable_consequence: (a) The spectral level must scale as chi (nu/eps)^(1/2). Inverting this is the standard way to estimate eps from temperature microstructure. (b) Where the rate scales as k^(2/3) (inertial-convective range) the same flux gives k^(-5/3) (Obukhov-Corrsin); at low Prandtl number the inertial-diffusive range gives k^(-17/3). (c) In the 2D enstrophy range, also with a scale-independent strain, a passive scalar should again give k^-1.

cases.source: Batchelor (1959) JFM 5:113; Grant, Hughes, Vogel & Moilliet (1968) JFM 34:423; Williams & Paulson (1977); a 1990 JFM paper confirming k^-1 (doi 10.1017/S0022112090000684). All via abstracts and secondary summaries.

cases.system: Relative dispersion of fluid-particle pairs in the inertial range of turbulence
cases.law_or_distribution: <r^2(t)> = g eps t^3 (Richardson 1926; equivalently relative diffusivity K(r) ∝ eps^(1/3) r^(4/3))
cases.variable_k: time t since release (s); separation r (m)
cases.reported_exponent: Theory 3. DNS give Richardson constant g ≈ 0.5-0.55 (Boffetta & Sokolov 2002). Lab evidence is weak: Ott & Mann (2000) found a t^3 range shorter than half a decade, using a virtual time origin. Bodenschatz-group experiments up to R_lambda = 815 see Batchelor's ballistic t^2 rather than t^3. Jullien, Paret & Tabeling (1999) studied 2D inverse-cascade dispersion. The law remains contested (arXiv 2307.01746).
cases.alpha_uncertainty: 3 in theory and DNS; experimental t^3 ranges under one decade
cases.conversion: Aggregate law y = <r^2> ∝ t^3, a = 3; d_lin = d_log = 3 under the aggregate mapping.
cases.orthopolic_reading: Time is the allocated resource. Under the K41 flux reading, the time a pair spends per log of separation is the eddy turnover time tau(r) ∝ eps^(-1/3) r^(2/3), so residence per ln r ∝ r^(2/3), r ∝ t^(3/2) and r^2 ∝ t^3. Equivalently, the pair's relative kinetic energy grows linearly in time at the constant rate eps (linear-orthopolic in time: equal energy per dt), and separation is ballistic at that velocity: r^2 ∝ (eps t) t^2.

decompositions.resource: relative kinetic energy delivered at constant rate eps, converted ballistically into separation
decompositions.composition: 3 = 1 (dv^2 ∝ eps t, flux constant in time) + 2 (r ∝ dv t)
decompositions.independent_motivation: The cascade delivers energy to each scale at rate eps, and a pair at separation r is pulled apart by eddies of size r.
decompositions.theory_agreement: Derived from K41 dimensional analysis (Obukhov 1941, Batchelor 1950); equivalent to Richardson's 4/3 law. Matches DNS; lab confirmation is weak.
decompositions.testable_consequence: (a) The 2D inverse energy cascade must also give t^3. (b) In the 2D enstrophy range, and below the Kolmogorov scale (scale-independent rate), separation must be exponential. (c) Before t_0 = (r0^2/eps)^(1/3), dispersion is ballistic t^2 (Batchelor), which is what high-Re experiments with large r0 see.

decompositions.resource: residence time per log separation (dynamic exponent z, with tau ∝ r^z)
decompositions.composition: <r^2> ∝ t^(2/z): diffusion z = 2 gives t^1, ballistic z = 1 gives t^2, K41 z = 2/3 gives t^3. For a spectrum k^-(1+2H), dv ∝ r^H, z = 1-H, so r^2 ∝ t^(2/(1-H)).
decompositions.independent_motivation: Any scale-local process in which the time to double a separation r is ∝ r^z.
decompositions.theory_agreement: Derived (scaling theory of relative dispersion). Intermittency makes z multivalued, which is one reason the experiments disagree.
decompositions.testable_consequence: A velocity field with k^-2 (H = 1/2, Burgers-like) should give r^2 ∝ t^4. Smooth fields (H → 1, k^-3) give exponential separation, linking this case to Kraichnan and Batchelor.

cases.source: Richardson (1926); Salazar & Collins (2009) Annu. Rev. Fluid Mech. 41:405-432; secondary summaries of Ott & Mann (2000) JFM 422:207 and the Bodenschatz-group results (arXiv 1410.0982, nlin/0102023, 2307.01746). Jullien, Paret & Tabeling (1999) PRL 82:2872: citation verified; whether they report a t^3 law was not confirmed from the text.

cases.system: Resistance (flicker) fluctuations in metals and semiconductors (1/f); integrated white noise and Brownian motion (1/f^2); fractional processes (1/f^beta)
cases.law_or_distribution: S(f) ∝ f^-beta. Pink beta ≈ 1 (Hooge: S_V/V^2 = alpha_H/(N f)); brown beta = 2; fBm beta = 2H + 1.
cases.variable_k: frequency f (Hz); equivalently relaxation time tau = 1/(2 pi f)
cases.reported_exponent: beta close to 1 in most solids, with no saturation down to ~1e-6 to 1e-7 Hz. Deviations from 1 track temperature as in the Dutta-Dimon-Horn relation. Brownian beta = 2 exactly.
cases.alpha_uncertainty: beta ≈ 1, device-dependent departures of order 0.1-0.3 (no compiled range retrieved)
cases.conversion: Spectrum as a density in f: alpha = beta = 1, d_log = 0 (equal power per octave), d_lin = 1. Brown: alpha = 2, d_log = 1, d_lin = 2.
cases.orthopolic_reading: Pink noise is log-orthopolic in variance: equal power per octave. In the Dutta-Horn mechanism the signal is a sum of independent two-state fluctuators (Lorentzians), each contributing the same variance, with tau = tau0 exp(E/kT). Activation energies spread uniformly (linear-orthopolic in E) make ln tau uniform (log-orthopolic count across timescales), and the sum is 1/f. Brown noise is white noise passed through an integrator. White noise is equipartition: equal variance per Hz (linear-orthopolic, d_lin = 0), as in Johnson-Nyquist 4kTR, the 1D blackbody. The integrator's power gain (2 pi f)^-2 adds 2, a legitimate additive composition because a deterministic transfer function multiplies the spectrum. Equivalently, the variance of increments grows linearly with lag, so time itself is the resource behind d_log = 1.

decompositions.resource: fluctuator variance per log relaxation time
decompositions.composition: Uniform activation-energy density (linear-orthopolic in E) mapped through Arrhenius tau = tau0 exp(E/kT) into log-uniform tau: d_log = 0
decompositions.predicted_exponent: beta = 1 where D(E) is flat across the window; departures fixed by the slope of D(E)
decompositions.independent_motivation: Thermally activated defects in disordered solids have broad barrier distributions, measurable independently (e.g. from annealing). Arrhenius kinetics turns energy into log-time.
decompositions.theory_agreement: Dutta, Dimon & Horn (1979); Dutta & Horn (1981) RMP 53:497. The mechanism agrees, conditional on a smooth D(E).
decompositions.testable_consequence: DDH relation: the local slope must change with temperature in step with the noise magnitude, beta(omega,T) = 1 - [d ln S/d ln T - 1]/ln(omega tau0), with ln(omega tau0) < 0. Reported as consistent in Al and Al-Cu films. The same log-uniform-timescale mechanism predicts 1/t relaxation in the time domain (compare Omori).

decompositions.resource: white-noise power per Hz (equipartition) x integrator gain
decompositions.composition: d_lin = 0 (equal power per Hz) + 2 (|1/(i 2 pi f)|^2); for fBm, d_log = 2H from Var[increment] ∝ lag^(2H)
decompositions.predicted_exponent: beta = 2 for Brownian motion; 2H + 1 for fBm
decompositions.independent_motivation: Brownian position is the time integral of an uncorrelated force or velocity. Independent increments make variance additive in time.
decompositions.theory_agreement: Derived (Langevin, Wiener-Khinchin).
decompositions.testable_consequence: A Brownian particle in a harmonic trap must cross from f^-2 to flat below the corner frequency (Lorentzian), the standard optical-tweezers calibration. A second integration gives f^-4.

decompositions.resource: total relative noise power shared among N carriers (Hooge)
decompositions.composition: S_V/V^2 = alpha_H/(N f): magnitude ∝ 1/N, shape 1/f
decompositions.predicted_exponent: noise magnitude ∝ 1/volume at fixed carrier density
decompositions.independent_motivation: Independent fluctuations of N carriers add in variance.
decompositions.theory_agreement: Empirical; no accepted derivation of alpha_H.
decompositions.testable_consequence: Scaling with sample volume. Reported violations, with noise scaling as inverse linear size, would falsify the per-carrier sharing.

cases.source: Dutta & Horn (1981) RMP 53:497 (via citations and summaries); Dutta, Dimon & Horn (1979) PRL 43:646 (not retrieved); exponent near 1 down to 1e-6 to 1e-7 Hz: arXiv 1211.4167 (summary); Al/Al-Cu DDH test: MRS proceedings abstract (Biery, Smith & Ficalora).

cases.system: Critical percolation clusters (lattice percolation at p_c)
cases.law_or_distribution: n_s ∝ s^-tau at p = p_c, with hyperscaling tau = 1 + d/D_f
cases.variable_k: cluster size s (number of sites)
cases.reported_exponent: 2D: tau = 187/91 ≈ 2.0549 (exact; D_f = 91/48). 3D: tau ≈ 2.186-2.190 (Monte Carlo 2.186 +/- 0.002 with D_f ≈ 2.53; 2.190(2); Ziff-Stell consistent set 116/53 ≈ 2.1887). Mean field (d >= 6): tau = 5/2.
cases.alpha_uncertainty: exact in 2D; about +/-0.002 in 3D
cases.conversion: Density: d_log = tau - 1 = 96/91 ≈ 1.055 (2D), ≈ 1.19 (3D), 3/2 (mean field); d_lin = tau.
cases.orthopolic_reading: Space is the allocated resource. Per log interval of linear size R, critical clusters pack space: about one cluster of size ~R per volume R^d, so the number per unit volume per ln R ∝ R^-d. Each cluster requires its span volume R^d ∝ s^(d/D_f). The system is therefore log-orthopolic in span volume: every log scale receives the same share of space. Converting to mass gives n_s ∝ s^-(1 + d/D_f). This is a CAPACITY reading (slots of size R ∝ R^-d), and its final resource is a ratio of the embedding dimension to the fractal dimension.

decompositions.resource: span volume R^d ∝ s^(d/D_f) (space-filling slots per log scale)
decompositions.composition: d_log = d/D_f: embedding dimension divided by fractal dimension
decompositions.independent_motivation: At criticality the correlation length is the only scale, and clusters of each size fill space at their own scale without systematic gaps. D_f is measured independently from cluster mass-radius relations.
decompositions.theory_agreement: Derived: hyperscaling tau = 1 + d/D_f (Stauffer & Aharony), with the same packing mechanism.
decompositions.testable_consequence: (a) Above the upper critical dimension d_c = 6, hyperscaling fails: tau stays 5/2 while d/D_f = d/4 > 3/2, and the number of spanning clusters grows as L^(d-6). The slot reading must fail exactly there, and it does. (b) Any space-filling critical cluster ensemble should obey tau - 1 = d/D_f. The repo's lake row is a live test: percolation predicts 96/91 ≈ 1.055, observed 1.14.

decompositions.resource: per-site cluster membership at mean field (critical branching tree)
decompositions.composition: s n_s ∝ s^(-3/2): Zipf in chemical length (martingale; see the avalanche case) with s ∝ l^2 gives 1/2; +1 converting per-site to per-cluster counts, so tau - 1 = 3/2
decompositions.independent_motivation: Bethe-lattice percolation is a critical Galton-Watson process.
decompositions.theory_agreement: Derived (Fisher & Essam 1961).
decompositions.testable_consequence: The two readings coincide only at d = 6. Agreement exactly at the upper critical dimension is a non-trivial consistency check.

cases.source: Hyperscaling and 2D values: arXiv 1101.0807 and 1709.00887 (summaries); 3D: Monte Carlo tau = 2.186 +/- 0.002 with D_f ≈ 2.53 (search summary), tau = 2.190(2) (arXiv cond-mat/0106354 table), Ziff-Stell 116/53 cited in Lorenz & Ziff (1998) J. Phys. A 31:8147 (arXiv cond-mat/9710044 introduction); repo docs/zeta-compilation.md (lakes).

cases.system: Unbiased random walk or Brownian motion: first return (first passage) to the origin
cases.law_or_distribution: 1D: f(t) ∝ t^(-3/2), survival S(t) ∝ t^(-1/2). d >= 3 (transient, defective distribution): f(t) ∝ t^(-d/2). d = 2: f(t) ~ 1/(t ln^2 t).
cases.variable_k: return time t (steps)
cases.reported_exponent: 1D: 3/2 exactly (e.g. Newman 2005). Universal for symmetric continuous jump laws, including Levy flights: Sparre Andersen gives S_n = C(2n,n) 2^(-2n) ~ (pi n)^(-1/2). d >= 3: d/2, by my own renewal argument; not verified from a source.
cases.alpha_uncertainty: exact
cases.conversion: Density: zeta = 1/2, alpha = 3/2, d_log = 1/2, d_lin = 3/2.
cases.orthopolic_reading: Two different final resources give 3/2. In 1D, position is a martingale (fair game): the probability of reaching distance L before returning is ∝ 1/L, so excursions are Zipf (zeta = 1) in their span. The conserved expected displacement is shared equally across log levels. Span and duration are deterministically linked (t ∝ L^2), so zeta_t = zeta_L x 1/2 = 1/2: exponents compose MULTIPLICATIVELY under a change of coordinate. For d >= 3, the return probability at time t is the inverse of the number of sites within reach, ∝ t^(-d/2). That is linear-orthopolic in explored volume (a capacity reading), and in 3D it also gives 3/2.

decompositions.resource: excursion span L (martingale: P(reach L) ∝ 1/L)
decompositions.composition: zeta_t = zeta_L x (d ln L/d ln t) = 1 x 1/2 = 1/2, so alpha = 3/2
decompositions.independent_motivation: Optional stopping of a martingale gives P(hit L before 0 | start at 1) = 1/L. Finite-variance steps give diffusive scaling L ∝ t^(1/2).
decompositions.theory_agreement: Correct for finite-variance walks, but it is not the universal mechanism. Sparre Andersen shows survival ∝ n^(-1/2) also for Levy flights, where L ∝ t^(1/mu). The span reading then requires zeta_L = mu/2 (the ladder-height tail), not 1. The true invariant is combinatorial (symmetry and exchangeability of the steps).
decompositions.testable_consequence: For Levy flights of index mu < 2, the naive 'zeta_L = 1 x diffusion' decomposition predicts zeta_t = 1/mu, while Sparre Andersen requires 1/2. The decomposition survives only if the span distribution changes to zeta_L = mu/2, which can be checked in simulation.

decompositions.resource: explored volume (number of sites within diffusive reach)
decompositions.composition: f(t) ∝ P(at origin at t) ∝ 1/V(t), V ∝ t^(d/2), so the exponent is d/2
decompositions.predicted_exponent: t^(-3/2) in 3D, t^-2 in 4D, t^(-5/2) in 5D; logarithmic at d = 2 (marginal)
decompositions.independent_motivation: Local central limit theorem: the probability spreads uniformly over a diffusion volume of radius ∝ t^(1/2).
decompositions.theory_agreement: Derived for transient walks by renewal theory (f_n ~ u_n/U^2); my own derivation, not verified from a source.
decompositions.testable_consequence: The 4D first-return density should be ∝ t^-2. The 1D and 3D exponents coincide numerically (3/2) for different reasons, a warning that one exponent can carry two final resources.

cases.source: Newman (2005) Contemp. Phys. 46:323, arXiv cond-mat/0412004; arXiv 1509.04800 (elementary derivation of 1D first-return times); Sparre Andersen universality: Majumdar et al., arXiv 0912.2586 (summary); Polya recurrence (textbook). The d >= 3 tail is my own derivation.

cases.system: Critical branching processes and mean-field avalanches: neuronal avalanches, mean-field depinning and Barkhausen noise, mean-field sandpiles
cases.variable_k: avalanche size s (activations); duration T (generations or time bins)
cases.reported_exponent: Mean field: tau_s = 3/2 and tau_T = 2, exact for a critical Galton-Watson process with finite variance. Kolmogorov: P(Z_n > 0) ~ 2/(sigma^2 n). Yaglom: Z_n/n conditioned on survival tends to an exponential. Neuronal avalanches in cortical cultures: 1.5 +/- 0.1 (size) and 2.0 +/- 0.1 (lifetime), sensitive to time-bin width (Beggs & Plenz 2003).
cases.alpha_uncertainty: exact in theory; +/-0.1 in neuronal data
cases.conversion: Size density: zeta_s = 1/2, d_log = 1/2, d_lin = 3/2. Duration: alpha_T = 2, zeta_T = 1, d_log(T) = 1.
cases.orthopolic_reading: An exact orthopolic identity holds at every generation. At criticality E[Z_t] = 1 for all t, a conserved expected population (a martingale). Written as P(alive at t) x E[Z_t | alive] = 1, it is q_bar(t) n(t) = C, with q_bar ∝ t (Yaglom) and n = P(alive) ∝ 1/t (Kolmogorov): the conserved population is held by ever fewer surviving lineages, each holding more. Durations are therefore Zipf (zeta_T = 1, log-orthopolic in duration, with the carried population as resource). Size integrates the population over the lifetime, s ∝ T x T = T^2 (a deterministic composition), so zeta_s = zeta_T/2 = 1/2 and alpha_s = 3/2.

decompositions.resource: expected population (martingale) shared among surviving lineages
decompositions.composition: zeta_T = 1 from q_bar ∝ t x n ∝ 1/t; s ∝ T^(1+1) = T^2; hence zeta_s = 1/2
decompositions.independent_motivation: Criticality means each unit replaces itself on average (branching ratio 1), a conservation law for the expected population. It is measurable independently of avalanche statistics; Beggs & Plenz report a branching ratio close to 1.
decompositions.theory_agreement: Derived: Kolmogorov (1938) and Yaglom (1947), with the same mechanism.
decompositions.testable_consequence: (a) The crackling-noise relation must hold jointly: (alpha_T - 1)/(alpha_s - 1) = exponent of <s|T> = 2. (b) A subcritical branching ratio m < 1 breaks the conservation (E[Z_t] = m^t) and must produce an exponential cutoff at T ~ 1/|ln m|. (c) The mean avalanche shape at fixed T is a parabola in mean field. (d) Short-range systems (2D/3D depinning, the Barkhausen class with tau ≈ 1.27) fall outside this reading.

decompositions.resource: a 'length' ∝ s^(1/2) under the log measure
decompositions.composition: alpha = 1 + 1/2 read as log-orthopolic in an avalanche radius
decompositions.independent_motivation: None: mean-field avalanches have no spatial structure. The 1/2 is the time-to-size map s ∝ T^2.
decompositions.theory_agreement: No theory.
decompositions.testable_consequence: It would predict a 3/2 that changes with spatial dimension through the avalanche geometry, while mean-field 3/2 is dimension-independent above d_c.

cases.source: Beggs & Plenz (2003) J. Neurosci. 23:11167-11177 (PMC6741045; values via secondary reviews); Kolmogorov (1938) and Yaglom (1947) via arXiv 2305.11801 and math/0404083 (summaries); mean-field S ∝ T^2 and alpha_T = 2 via arXiv cond-mat/0102091 and 1312.7156 (summaries).

cases.system: Earthquake aftershock sequences
cases.law_or_distribution: n(t) = K/(c + t)^p (modified Omori, or Omori-Utsu, law)
cases.variable_k: time since the mainshock t (days)
cases.reported_exponent: p usually 0.9-1.5; reasonable range 0.6-2.5 over more than 200 sequences (Utsu, Ogata & Matsu'ura 1995). Southern California, 39 sequences: mean 1.11 +/- 0.25, range about 0.7-1.8, uncorrelated with b or mainshock magnitude, and higher where heat flow is high (Kisslinger & Jones 1991).
cases.alpha_uncertainty: +/-0.25 (standard deviation across sequences); full range 0.6-2.5
cases.conversion: The rate is a count density in time: alpha = p, d_log = p - 1 ≈ 0.1 (≈ 0 for p = 1), d_lin = p.
cases.orthopolic_reading: p = 1 means equal numbers of aftershocks per log time: each decade after the mainshock holds the same count, so the sequence is log-orthopolic in event count. In Dieterich's rate-and-state reading, a stress step shifts the log slip speed of a population of nucleating patches. That spreads their failure times uniformly in ln t between c and t_a = A sigma/tau_dot. This is the same 'Arrhenius bridge' as 1/f noise: an exponential map of a uniformly distributed variable gives log-uniform timescales. The resource is a count, nucleation sites per log time-to-failure (d = 0), not a stock of energy.

decompositions.resource: nucleation sites per log time-to-failure (Dieterich)
decompositions.composition: Uniform initial state/stress (linear) mapped through the exponential rate-state nucleation law into log-uniform failure times: d_log = 0, so p = 1
decompositions.predicted_exponent: p = 1 for c < t < t_a, then a return to the background rate
decompositions.independent_motivation: Rate- and state-dependent friction laws are measured in laboratory sliding experiments, independently of seismicity.
decompositions.theory_agreement: Derived for a constant stressing rate (Dieterich 1994), where p is asymptotically 1. Values p ≠ 1 need extra mechanisms (secondary triggering cascades such as ETAS, stress relaxation).
decompositions.testable_consequence: Aftershock duration t_a = A sigma/tau_dot should scale with mainshock recurrence time, i.e. inversely with loading rate; data support this. The reading also predicts that Omori decay and 1/f-type spectra share one mechanism (log-uniform timescales).

decompositions.resource: stress feeding aftershocks, lost to temperature-controlled relaxation
decompositions.composition: Non-conservation (transport-identity condition (i) failing): p - 1 grows with the relaxation rate
decompositions.independent_motivation: Creep relaxes the stress that drives aftershocks, faster in hotter crust.
decompositions.theory_agreement: Kisslinger & Jones (1991), empirical, with viscoelastic interpretations. The correlation is disputed because heat-flow uncertainties were not propagated.
decompositions.testable_consequence: Across regions p should correlate with heat flow (reported: high p in the Salton Trough), not with b or mainshock magnitude.

cases.source: Utsu, Ogata & Matsu'ura (1995) J. Phys. Earth 43:1-33 (abstract; the 0.6-2.5 range via a 2022 Frontiers in Earth Science paper); Kisslinger & Jones (1991) JGR 96:11947 (via secondary summaries); Dieterich (1994) JGR 99:2601-2618 (abstract and later summaries).

cases.system: Wind-generated ocean surface gravity waves; capillary-wave turbulence
cases.law_or_distribution: S(omega) = alpha_T u_* g omega^-4 (Toba 1973; Zakharov-Filonenko constant energy flux); S(omega) = beta g^2 omega^-5 (Phillips 1958 saturation); capillary weak turbulence S(omega) ∝ P^(1/2) omega^(-17/6), E(k) ∝ k^(-7/4)
cases.variable_k: angular frequency omega (rad/s) of surface elevation; wavenumber k via omega^2 = g k (gravity) or omega^2 = (sigma/rho) k^3 (capillary)
cases.reported_exponent: omega^-4 from the spectral peak to about 2.5x the mean frequency, with level ∝ u_*, and omega^-5 above that (Forristall 1981, Gulf of Mexico and Baltimore Canyon). omega^-4 is also reported by Toba 1973, Kahma 1981, Donelan et al. 1985, and Battjes et al. 1987 (reanalysing JONSWAP). The capillary range on mercury agrees fairly with -17/6, but the spectral level's scaling with energy flux disagrees with weak-turbulence theory in both regimes (Falcon, Laroche & Fauve 2007).
cases.alpha_uncertainty: 4 near the peak (Toba/ZF); 5 at high frequency (Phillips); in small tanks the gravity-range exponent depends on forcing
cases.conversion: Frequency spectrum as a density in omega: alpha = 4, d_log = 3, d_lin = 4. In wavenumber (omega ∝ k^(1/2)): omega^-4 corresponds to F(k) ∝ k^(-5/2) (d_log(k) = 3/2) and omega^-5 to F(k) ∝ k^-3 (d_log(k) = 2).
cases.orthopolic_reading: One system shows two orthopolic readings in adjacent ranges. (1) Phillips's saturation range is a CAPACITY: breaking caps wave slope at every scale, so slope variance (k^2 x elevation variance) per ln k is constant and F(k) ∝ k^-3. This is the author's 'log-orthopolic in k^2' again, with k^2 the squared-gradient weight, as in Kraichnan's enstrophy. (2) The Toba/Zakharov-Filonenko range is a FLUX: energy flux P through scales is constant. Four-wave interactions make the transfer rate ∝ (stock)^2, so B = F/v with v ∝ B^2 gives B ∝ P^(1/3) and omega^-4. Capillary waves interact in triads, so v ∝ B gives B ∝ P^(1/2) and omega^(-17/6). The dispersion laws themselves decompose cleanly (capillary 3 = 2 for curvature + 1 for the mass within depth 1/k), but they share no conserved total, so they are compositions without orthopolity.

decompositions.resource: slope variance per ln k, saturated by breaking
decompositions.composition: d_log(k) = 2 (gradient-squared weight) + 0 (saturation is scale-free), so F(k) ∝ k^-3. With k ∝ omega^2, d_log(omega) = 2 x 2 = 4, so S ∝ g^2 omega^-5.
decompositions.predicted_exponent: omega^-5, with a level independent of wind
decompositions.independent_motivation: Breaking limits crest slope and acceleration at every scale (limiting steepness), leaving g as the only dimensional parameter.
decompositions.theory_agreement: Phillips 1958 (dimensional saturation argument). Phillips 1985 abandoned wind-independence for the range below.
decompositions.testable_consequence: The spectral level should be independent of u_* in the omega^-5 range and ∝ u_* in the omega^-4 range; Forristall found ∝ u_* in the f^-4 range. A slope-saturation range should give k^-3 in wavenumber for any dispersion law.

decompositions.resource: energy flux through scales via four-wave resonances
decompositions.composition: B = P/v with v ∝ B^2 x (power of omega), so B ∝ P^(1/3) omega^-3 and S ∝ omega^-4
decompositions.independent_motivation: Weak nonlinearity: four-wave resonant transfer conserves energy and wave action, and the kinetic equation has constant-flux (Kolmogorov-Zakharov) solutions.
decompositions.theory_agreement: Derived: Zakharov & Filonenko's exact KZ solution. It remains debated whether the observed omega^-4 reflects this cascade or a local input-dissipation balance (Phillips 1985).
decompositions.testable_consequence: (a) The inverse wave-action cascade should give omega^(-11/3) (Zakharov-Zaslavskii) below the forcing. (b) The level should scale as P^(1/3). In the capillary analogue the exponent matched but the flux scaling failed (Falcon et al. 2007), so the exponent alone does not confirm the flux reading.

decompositions.resource: capillary energy flux via three-wave resonances
decompositions.composition: v ∝ B, so B ∝ P^(1/2); dimensionally E(k) ∝ P^(1/2) (sigma/rho)^(1/4) k^(-7/4), and with omega ∝ k^(3/2), S_eta ∝ omega^(-17/6)
decompositions.independent_motivation: The capillary dispersion law permits three-wave resonances.
decompositions.theory_agreement: Zakharov & Filonenko 1967. The exponent is confirmed; the flux dependence is not.
decompositions.testable_consequence: Level ∝ P^(1/2) failed in the mercury experiments (Falcon et al. 2007). The resource reading is only half confirmed.

cases.source: Phillips (1958) JFM 4:426 (abstract); Phillips (1985) JFM 156:505 (abstract); Toba 1973 and Zakharov-Filonenko via arXiv 1801.09096 and 1502.02628 (summaries); Forristall (1981) JGR 86(C9):8075-8084 (abstract); Falcon, Laroche & Fauve (2007) PRL 98:094503, arXiv cond-mat/0610297 (abstract).

catalogue.domain_patterns:
How I mapped laws that are not distributions. Sharing laws, y ∝ x^a with a < 0, where y is a per-unit share of a conserved total (inverse-square): I treat y as the density, so d_lin = -a and d_log = -a - 1, and grade only the reading that has a physical referent. Aggregate laws, a > 0 (Stefan-Boltzmann, Debye, Kepler's T^2, Richardson's r^2): y = (number of active slots) x (resource per slot), and I report d_lin = d_log = a, because no abundance density and hence no choice of reference measure is involved. Spectra are treated as densities in k, omega or f.

Verification. WebFetch could not reach arxiv.org, wikipedia.org or the university servers I tried (DNS failure), so every value was checked from search-result abstracts and secondary summaries, never full text. The d-dimensional generalizations of Kepler and of random-walk return are my own derivations and are flagged as such.

REGULARITIES

1. A final resource is built in three ways, and each composes differently.
- Deterministic products ADD exponents. Stefan-Boltzmann d+1 = d (slots) + 1 (energy per slot). Richardson 3 = 1 (energy gained linearly in time) + 2 (ballistic conversion). Brown noise 2 = 0 (white, equal power per Hz) + 2 (integrator gain). Kraichnan and Phillips k^-3 = 2 (squared-gradient weight) + 0 (scale-free rate) + 1 (Jacobian).
- Ratios d/z of a slot dimension to a scaling exponent. Debye T^(d/s) (dispersion), percolation tau - 1 = d/D_f (fractal dimension), random-walk return t^(-d/2) (diffusion, z = 2), Kepler T ∝ a^(d/2) (second-order dynamics), Richardson r^2 ∝ t^(2/z) with z = 2/3. The numerator is almost always the embedding dimension, i.e. a capacity: the number of boxes of size L scales as L^-d. The denominator is the exponent that converts the measured variable into a length.
- Changes of coordinate MULTIPLY survival exponents. A conserved expectation (martingale) gives Zipf (zeta = 1) in the variable that carries it: the span of a fair random walk, or the duration of a critical branching process. A deterministic map such as t ∝ L^2 or s ∝ T^2 then multiplies zeta by 1/2. This is where the ubiquitous 3/2 density exponent comes from: random walks, mean-field and neuronal avalanches, Bethe-lattice percolation counted per site.

2. Stock, flux and capacity are separated by the transport identity B = F/v.
- With a conserved flux and a scale-independent log-speed, the stock is log-flat: Batchelor k^-1, Kraichnan enstrophy, 1/f from log-uniform rates, Omori p = 1.
- With a log-speed ∝ k^z, the stock exponent equals z: K41 d_log = 2/3 is the exponent of the eddy-turnover rate.
- Flat stocks go with exponential separation of particle pairs (Batchelor range, enstrophy range), and power-law stocks with power-law separation (Richardson). This is a cross-check between spectra and particle-tracking data.
- Capacity readings are equal-per-slot statements, and their exponent counts slots: inverse-square area, Rayleigh-Jeans mode count, Debye active modes, percolation packing, Phillips slope saturation.

3. The author's k^-3 example occurs physically twice, and both times as log-orthopolic in k^2, not linear-orthopolic in k^3: Kraichnan (enstrophy = k^2 x energy) and Phillips (slope variance = k^2 x elevation variance). In both, k^2 is a squared gradient, not an area. More generally, for any spectrum d_log equals zeta_2 = 2H, the second-order structure-function exponent, so the resource per log scale is the increment variance. That reading saturates at d_log = 2 for smooth fields: spectra steeper than k^-3 still have zeta_2 = 2.

4. An "Arrhenius bridge": linear-orthopolic allocation in an energy-like variable becomes log-orthopolic in time through an exponential map. One mechanism gives two observables: f^-1 in Dutta-Horn noise and t^-1 in Dieterich's Omori decay.

5. Marginal cases produce logarithms, where the slot exponent meets the dynamical one: Kraichnan's ln^(-1/3) correction, the 2D random walk, the 2D gravitational potential ln r.

6. The same number can carry different resources: 3/2 arises from the 1D span martingale and from the 3D explored volume. Conversely, the same system can carry different exponents in adjacent ranges: ocean waves omega^-4 (flux) and omega^-5 (capacity); 2D turbulence k^-5/3 and k^-3.

COUNTEREXAMPLES AND LIMITS (informative)
- Wien tail and gapped excitations: when the per-slot cost exceeds the per-slot budget, occupation is exponential (maximum entropy) and no orthopolic reading exists. Orthopolity across slots holds only in the classical, gapless regime.
- Electrons in metals: C ∝ T in every dimension, because the active slots form a shell around the Fermi surface. The exponent need not be a spatial dimension.
- Bloch's T^(3/2) observed in 2D films contradicts the naive slot count; the true dispersion is needed.
- Hyperscaling fails above d = 6: the percolation slot reading breaks exactly where clusters stop packing space.
- Sparre Andersen: the 1D first-passage exponent 1/2 is universal even for Levy flights, so 'span x diffusion' is not the real reason for it.
- K41 intermittency: the flux reading gives the mean-field 5/3, and the beta-model's 'fewer active slots' correction (mu/3) overshoots the measured ≈ mu/9.
- Kraichnan's enstrophy range is usually steeper, about -3.3 to -4, because drag breaks flux conservation. This is a predicted failure mode, not an anomaly.
- Richardson's t^3 is barely seen in the laboratory.
- Omori p ranges 0.6-2.5, and only p ≈ 1 has a reading.
- Wave turbulence matches the exponent but not the predicted flux scaling (Falcon et al. 2007): an exponent alone underdetermines the resource. Prefactors and flux dependences must be tested too.
- Dispersion laws (capillary omega^2 = (sigma/rho) k^3, where 3 = 2 for curvature + 1 for the mass within depth 1/k) are compositions without a shared conserved total, so they are not orthopolic.

OVERALL. In this domain most readings grade 'derived', because the established theories already are resource-allocation arguments: Gauss flux, equipartition per mode, constant cascade flux, hyperscaling packing, martingale conservation. Here orthopolity works mainly as a unifying vocabulary (slots x per-slot resource; flux/rate; coordinate change) rather than as a source of new exponents. Its value lies in the cross-system tests it suggests: dimension dependence, flux scaling, drag-induced steepening, the hyperscaling limit, and Lagrangian-Eulerian consistency. Choosing the resource after seeing the data does produce numerology, for example reading Kraichnan's spectrum as linear-orthopolic in k^3 or mean-field avalanches as log-orthopolic in sqrt(s). In each such case the physically motivated alternative wins on a testable consequence.

checks.system: Point-source radiation intensity; Newtonian gravity and Coulomb fields (Gauss's law); d-dimensional generalization
checks.corrected_alpha_uncertainty: exponent exactly -2 in the law; Coulomb |delta| < ~3e-16 (Williams-Faller-Hill, usually quoted as (2.7 +/- 3.1)e-16); gravity: Kapner et al. 2007 inverse square holds down to 56 um, R <= 44 um (verified). CORRECTION: I found no 2013 Eot-Wash bound at ~42 um. The next Eot-Wash result is Lee, Adelberger, Cook, Fleischer & Heckel (2020, arXiv 2002.11761): separations down to 52 um, gravitational-strength Yukawa range < 38.6 um at 95% CL (verified).
checks.algebra_note: The sign is inconsistent. The alpha_density field says -2, while the conversion uses alpha_equiv = -a = +2 with d_lin = 2 and d_log = 1. Under the convention dN/dk ∝ k^-alpha, with I treated as the density, alpha = +2, and then d_lin = 2 and d_log = 1 are consistent. This is a role swap. Physically, I is the per-cell share (q_bar ∝ r^-(d-1)) and the number of cells per sphere (∝ r^(d-1)) is the abundance. q_bar*n = P is then discretely orthopolic across spheres, and also linear in r: energy per shell = u*4 pi r^2 dr = P dr/c (checked). Because q_bar*n = C is symmetric, calling the area 'the resource' is only the dual description. General lesson for sharing laws: the exponent the program reads off identifies the NUMBER OF SHARERS (a capacity), not the shared quantity.
checks.best_reading: The conserved flux (P, or the Gauss flux q/eps0, 4 pi G M) is shared equally among the area cells of every enclosing sphere. The cell count ∝ r^(d-1) is a capacity, and the per-cell share is ∝ r^-(d-1). The system is discretely orthopolic across spheres and linear-orthopolic in the radiation energy stock (P/c per dr). Measure: discrete per sphere, or linear in r.
checks.numerology_risk: Low. The divergence theorem fixes the resource before any data are seen. The only alternative simple reading (log, d_log = 1) has no physical referent. The d-dependence is tested independently: line sources give 1/r, and extra-dimension searches look for r^-(2+n).
checks.source: Kapner et al. (2007) PRL 98:021101, arXiv hep-ph/0611184 (abstract; 56 um and 44 um verified in this session). Lee et al. (2020), arXiv 2002.11761, and UW news release (52 um and 38.6 um verified in this session). Williams, Faller & Hill (1971) PRL 26:721 (secondary sources and the PDG listing; the digits 2.7 vs 2.76 are not pinned down). Gauss's law (textbook).

checks.system: Thermal (blackbody) radiation: Rayleigh-Jeans and Wien tails, Stefan-Boltzmann law, photon number density
checks.corrected_alpha_uncertainty: exact. Note that 4 is a law exponent, not a density exponent.
checks.algebra_note: The slots x per-slot algebra (T^d x T = T^(d+1)) is correct. So is Boltzmann's route: (dU/dV)_T = T(dp/dT)_V - p with p = u/d gives (d+1)u = T du/dT, and p = w u gives T^(1+1/w). The mean photon energy u/n = (pi^4/15)/(2 zeta(3)) kT = 2.701 kT was recomputed. Caveat: setting 'd_log = d_lin = 4' is a convention. It breaks d_log = alpha - 1 and is not an orthopolic resource exponent, because no abundance density over T exists. The genuinely orthopolic statement is across modes at fixed T: equal kT per active mode, a per-slot exponent of 0 (discrete). T^4 is a capacity exponent (d) times a share exponent (1). Report those two separately rather than d_log = d_lin = 4. The refuted classical-equipartition-at-all-nu decomposition (matches = false) should be graded 'none', not 'suggestive'.
checks.best_reading: The number of active slots (the k-space volume inside the thermal radius k_T ∝ T, ∝ T^d, a capacity) times an equal energy kT per active slot. Equivalently, the isotropic momentum flux is shared equally among the d axes (p = u/d). Discrete measure across modes.
checks.numerology_risk: Low. The two derivations agree; they do not compete. The dimension dependence has been tested independently: a 1D single channel carries heat ∝ T^2, which is the thermal conductance quantum. Readings such as '4 = 2x2' have no referent and fit nothing else.
checks.source: Planck and Stefan-Boltzmann (textbook). Schwab et al. (2000) Nature 404:974 and the d-dimensional T^(d+1) results were cited by the catalogue; I could not re-verify them this session (shared web-search budget exhausted). I re-derived the algebra myself.

checks.system: Low-temperature heat capacity: Debye phonons, Bloch magnons, 2D lattices, graphene flexural phonons, conduction electrons
checks.corrected_alpha_uncertainty: exact asymptotically. The graphite T^2 attribution is questionable (see numerology_risk).
checks.algebra_note: C ∝ T^(d/s) and U ∝ T^(1+d/s) are correct, with the same aggregate-law caveat as for the blackbody (d_log = 3 is not alpha - 1). A more general and more accurate form: C ∝ T^(1+gamma), where the density of states near the active edge is g(E) ∝ E^gamma. For anisotropic dispersion the slot exponent is the sum over directions of 1/s_i. Bosons with omega ∝ k^s have gamma = d/s - 1. A Fermi surface has gamma = 0, giving C ∝ T. Dirac electrons in graphene have gamma = 1, giving C ∝ T^2. The slot exponent is the DOS exponent plus 1, not necessarily a spatial dimension.
checks.best_reading: The number of thermally active modes (the DOS integrated up to kT, a capacity) times one kB of heat capacity per active mode (discrete equipartition across active slots). Frozen modes (hbar omega >> kT, or gapped) drop out exponentially.
checks.numerology_risk: Low for 3D phonons and magnons, whose dispersions are measured independently by neutron scattering. Moderate for graphite's T^2, which has at least two decompositions giving 2. One is an isotropic 2D linear phonon gas (d=2, s=1; Klemens's layer model). The other is interlayer-coupled flexural modes, omega^2 = c_z^2 k_z^2 + kappa k_par^4, giving 1 + 1/2 + 1/2 = 2 (the Komatsu bending-mode theory; from memory, not verified). Only the measured dispersion decides, so the exponent alone underdetermines the slot geometry. The electron T-law in every d shows that a matching integer need not be a dimension.
checks.source: Debye, Bloch and Sommerfeld laws (textbook). The catalogue's Klemens (1953) and graphene ZA citations were not re-verified this session (search budget exhausted). The Komatsu bending-mode alternative is from memory.

checks.system: Two-body Newtonian orbits (Kepler's third law); galactic rotation curves
checks.corrected_alpha_uncertainty: exact in Newtonian gravity (T^2 ∝ a^3; 3/2 in T). This is a law exponent, not a density exponent.
checks.algebra_note: Checked in d dimensions. v^2/a = GM/a^(d-1) gives T ∝ a^(d/2), and the swept-area route gives h ∝ a^((4-d)/2), so T ∝ a^2/h = a^(d/2). The two agree. T^2 = 3 pi/(G rho_bar) is exact for circular orbits. The surface-orbit and uniform-sphere chord period of 84.3 min was recomputed. Aggregate-law convention as before (d_log = 3 is not alpha - 1).
checks.best_reading: Dilution: T^2 = 3 pi/(G rho_bar(<a)). T^2 is set by the orbital volume per unit enclosed mass, with exponent d/z (volume dimension over the order of the dynamics). Caveat: no resource is allocated ACROSS orbits, since the planets share nothing. The only genuine equal-allocation statement is Kepler II (equal time per swept area, exact from angular-momentum conservation), and it carries no exponent (d = 0 within one orbit). The orthopolic vocabulary relabels Newton here; it adds no new prediction.
checks.numerology_risk: Low to moderate. The labels '3 = volume' and '3/2 = area 2 minus 1/2 from h' are one Newtonian derivation, not competitors. However, the d-dimensional prediction cannot be tested, and flat rotation curves are used to INFER M(r), so they are circular rather than an independent test. The one non-circular consequence is the harmonic period inside a uniform body.
checks.source: Kepler's laws and Newtonian gravity (textbook). The d-dimensional algebra was re-derived here. No web verification was needed.

checks.system: 3D homogeneous isotropic turbulence, inertial range (Kolmogorov 1941)
checks.corrected_alpha_uncertainty: theory 5/3. Intermittency raises it by about 0.03 (lognormal 5/3 + mu/9 = 1.694 with mu = 0.25; She-Leveque 1 + zeta_2 = 1.696, recomputed). The beta-model's 5/3 + mu/3 = 1.75 overshoots (recomputed).
checks.algebra_note: alpha = 5/3, d_log = 2/3 (energy per ln k ∝ k^(-2/3)) and d_lin = 5/3 are correct. B = F/v with v ∝ eps^(1/3) k^(2/3) gives B ∝ eps^(2/3) k^(-2/3), which is correct. The per-eddy count is ∝ l^-3 per ln l, and the flux per eddy is ∝ eps l^3, so the flux per ln l is flat, which is consistent.
checks.best_reading: Constant energy flux eps through each log-wavenumber. The stock per ln k equals the flux divided by the eddy turnover rate, so d_log = 2/3 is exactly the exponent of the turnover rate. Log measure; this is a flux reading, not a stock reading.
checks.numerology_risk: Low. Energy conservation and locality fix the flux reading before any spectrum is seen. d_lin = 5/3 has no referent. The 4/5 law is an exact flux statement that holds without intermittency correction, so the stock and flux readings make separable predictions.
checks.source: Grant, Stewart & Moilliet (1962) JFM 12:241-268 (abstract verified this session: k^-5/3 over several decades, Re ~1e8; R_lambda ~3000 and a constant of ~0.5 come only from secondary sources). Paret & Tabeling (1997) PRL 79:4162 (abstract verified: 2D inverse-cascade k^-5/3 with constant 5.5-7). Intermittency corrections were recomputed from the stated models.

checks.system: 2D turbulence, direct enstrophy cascade (Kraichnan-Leith-Batchelor)
checks.corrected_alpha_uncertainty: theory -3 with an ln^(-1/3) correction. Forced runs and drag steepen it to about -3.3 to -4. These numbers come from the catalogue; I could not re-verify them this session.
checks.algebra_note: Enstrophy per ln k = k * k^2 * E(k) ∝ k^0 is correct. alpha = 3, d_log = 2 and d_lin = 3 are consistent. The rule d_log = zeta_2 = 2H, saturating at 2 for smooth fields, is correct.
checks.best_reading: Constant enstrophy flux eta with a scale-independent (non-local, large-scale) strain rate. Both the enstrophy stock per ln k and the flux are flat. Read as an energy density, the 'resource' k^2 is the squared-gradient weight that converts energy into enstrophy. Log measure.
checks.numerology_risk: Low for the enstrophy reading, because the second conservation law is known independently of any spectrum. Two post-hoc temptations exist. One is the catalogue's 'linear-orthopolic in a k^3 volume', which is numerology. The other is that in 2D the number of Fourier modes per ln k (∝ k^2) coincides with the enstrophy weight. The 3D case separates them: the gradient weight stays k^2 while the mode count becomes k^3. Observed slopes of -3.3 to -4 support the reading only through a derived drag correction (Nam et al.). The exponent alone does not.
checks.source: Kraichnan (1967, 1971), Pasquero & Falkovich (2002), Nam et al. (2000) and Boffetta & Ecke (2012), as cited by the catalogue. These were not re-verified this session because the shared web-search budget ran out. The theory is standard.

checks.system: Passive scalar at high Prandtl/Schmidt number, viscous-convective range (Batchelor k^-1)
checks.corrected_alpha_uncertainty: exact in theory; the observed range is short
checks.algebra_note: alpha = 1, d_log = 0 and d_lin = 1 are correct. B = chi/gamma with gamma = (eps/nu)^(1/2) independent of k gives a flat spectrum. The k^(-5/3) (Obukhov-Corrsin) and k^(-17/3) (inertial-diffusive) alternatives are stated correctly.
checks.best_reading: Scalar variance per ln k = conserved variance flux chi / scale-independent strain rate. Log-orthopolic in the stock itself, because both transport-identity conditions hold.
checks.numerology_risk: Low. Both conditions (conserved flux, scale-free rate) are argued from the sub-Kolmogorov flow, not from scalar data. Because the range is short, the exponent is weakly constrained. The prefactor test (level ∝ chi (nu/eps)^(1/2)) carries most of the evidential weight and is used routinely.
checks.source: Batchelor (1959) and Kraichnan (1968), textbook. The catalogue's ocean and laboratory citations were not re-verified this session (search budget exhausted).

checks.system: Richardson pair dispersion in the inertial range
checks.corrected_alpha_uncertainty: 3 in theory and DNS (Richardson constant g ≈ 0.5-0.55). Laboratory t^3 ranges are under a decade and remain contested. This is a law exponent.
checks.algebra_note: r^2 ∝ t^(2/(1-H)) is correct: H = 1/3 gives 3 and H = 1/2 gives 4. The composition 3 = 1 + 2 (dv^2 ∝ eps t, r ∝ dv t) is correct. The aggregate-law convention (d_log = 3) is not a density conversion.
checks.best_reading: Residence time per log separation equals the eddy turnover time tau(r) ∝ eps^(-1/3) r^(2/3). Equivalently, relative kinetic energy is supplied at the constant rate eps (linear in time) and converted ballistically into separation. Time is the allocated resource.
checks.numerology_risk: Low. The two decompositions are one K41 scaling argument, not competing fits. The weakness is empirical, not numerological: the t^3 range is barely resolved in the laboratory, and ballistic t^2 dominates at finite r0.
checks.source: Richardson (1926) and Salazar & Collins (2009), as cited by the catalogue. Not re-verified this session (search budget exhausted). The algebra was re-derived.

checks.system: 1/f (flicker) noise; Brownian 1/f^2; fBm 1/f^(2H+1)
checks.corrected_alpha_uncertainty: beta ≈ 1, typically 0.8-1.4 depending on device and temperature (Dutta-Horn range, from memory). Brownian beta = 2 exactly.
checks.algebra_note: These are correct: d_log = 0 for beta = 1; Brownian alpha = 2 = 0 (white) + 2 (integrator gain); fBm alpha = 2H+1, d_log = 2H; the Arrhenius map p(ln tau) = kT p(E); and the DDH slope formula. Log-uniform tau gives relaxation ∝ -ln t, i.e. a 1/t relaxation RATE, which is the stated Omori analogy.
checks.best_reading: Equal fluctuator variance per log relaxation time. It arises from an exponential map of a uniformly distributed linear variable: the barrier energy (Dutta-Horn, Arrhenius) or the tunnelling depth (McWhorter). The underlying linear-orthopolic resource is therefore the barrier or depth, and the log-orthopolic one is time.
checks.numerology_risk: Moderate. d_log = 0 merely restates beta = 1 (flat per octave by definition), so all the content lies in the mechanism. At least two mechanisms give log-uniform tau from DIFFERENT linear variables (energy vs depth), so the exponent cannot identify the resource. The DDH temperature relation is the discriminating test. Hooge's per-carrier sharing concerns magnitude, not shape, and is only suggestive.
checks.source: Dutta & Horn (1981) RMP 53:497 (standard). The low-frequency limit of 1e-6 to 1e-7 Hz and the Al/Al-Cu DDH test were not re-verified this session (search budget exhausted).

checks.system: Critical percolation cluster sizes
checks.corrected_alpha_uncertainty: 2D exact 187/91 (confirmed). The 3D value needs CORRECTING. The catalogue's 'Monte Carlo 2.186 +/- 0.002 with D_f ≈ 2.53' is outdated. Modern estimates give D_f ≈ 2.5229 (η ≈ -0.046), so tau = 1 + 3/D_f ≈ 2.1891, about +/-0.0001 (recomputed). Ziff-Stell 116/53 = 2.18868 sits about 0.0004 below this. The Wang et al. (2013) paper exists, but its digits are from memory and were not confirmed this session.
checks.algebra_note: 1 + 2/(91/48) = 187/91 = 2.05495 and d_log = 96/91 = 1.0549 are correct. 3/2.52293 = 1.1891 (recomputed). For mean field, d_log = 3/2 and tau = 5/2. The Bethe-tree route is correct: s n_s ∝ s^(-3/2), with Kolmogorov survival in chemical length and s ∝ l^2.
checks.best_reading: Log-orthopolic in span volume R^d ∝ s^(d/D_f). Space-filling packing gives about one cluster per correlation volume per log scale (hyperscaling, tau - 1 = d/D_f). This is a capacity reading, and it fails above d_c = 6, where it should.
checks.numerology_risk: Low for hyperscaling itself, since D_f is measured independently. Two caveats. (i) The reading moves the irrational content into D_f, which has no resource reading in 3D. (ii) The catalogue's 'live test' against lakes is mis-specified. Lake surface area could be compared with cluster mass (zeta = 96/91 ≈ 1.055) or with hull-enclosed area. For the latter, Cardy & Ziff (2003) give exactly N(>A) = C*Omega/A with C = 1/(8 sqrt(3) pi) ≈ 0.02297, i.e. zeta = 1 (verified this session). Real lakes contain few islands, so the hull reading is arguably closer, and the observed 1.14 fits neither. Two percolation readings 0.055 apart are both off from the data, so the area must be specified before the test means anything.
checks.source: Hyperscaling and the 2D exact values (standard). Cardy & Ziff, arXiv cond-mat/0205404, and Ziff, arXiv cond-mat/0510633 (verified this session). Wang, Zhou, Zhang, Garoni & Deng (2013) PRE 87:052107 (existence verified; digits from memory). Repo docs/zeta-compilation.md (lakes, Cael & Seekell 2016).

checks.system: Random walk / Brownian first return to the origin
