checks.corrected_alpha_uncertainty: exact (1D). The d >= 3 result t^(-d/2) is correct by the standard renewal identity f_n ~ (1-F)^2 u_n for transient walks (from memory). 2D gives 1/(t ln^2 t).
checks.algebra_note: zeta = 1/2, alpha = 3/2, d_log = 1/2 and d_lin = 3/2 are correct. Survival exponents multiply under a deterministic coordinate change (zeta_t = zeta_L * 1/2), which is correct. Note: the explored-volume reading FAILS in d = 1. There 1/V(t) gives the occupation probability u_n ∝ t^(-1/2), not f_n ∝ t^(-3/2), so the volume reading applies only to transient walks.
checks.best_reading: For a 1D finite-variance walk: optional stopping of the position martingale gives P(reach L before return) = 1/L, i.e. equal expected displacement per log span class. Diffusive scaling then gives zeta_t = 1/2. For d >= 3: the return probability is the inverse of the explored volume ∝ t^(d/2) (linear, capacity).
checks.numerology_risk: High for the number 3/2 taken alone. At least three unrelated readings produce it: the 1D span martingale times diffusion, the 3D explored volume, and mean-field branching read as 1 + 1/2. The universal reason for the 1D value is Sparre Andersen's combinatorial symmetry, which also holds for Levy flights; it is not the span resource. Only the dimension series (1D 3/2, 2D log, 3D 3/2, 4D 2) separates the readings.
checks.source: Newman (2005) and the Sparre Andersen theorem (standard; as cited by the catalogue). Not re-verified this session (search budget exhausted). The renewal argument for d >= 3 is from memory.

checks.system: Critical branching processes and mean-field avalanches (neuronal avalanches, mean-field depinning)
checks.corrected_alpha_uncertainty: exact in theory (tau_s = 3/2, tau_T = 2). Neuronal data give 1.5 +/- 0.1 and 2.0 +/- 0.1, and the values depend on the time-bin width.
checks.algebra_note: Correct. P(alive at t) x E[Z_t | alive] = 1 gives zeta_T = 1. With <s|T> ∝ T^2 and a scaling form P(s|T) = T^-2 g(s/T^2), zeta_s = 1/2. The crackling relation gives (2-1)/(1.5-1) = 2. Precision: the exact orthopolic identity holds across GENERATIONS (a linear measure in time: the conserved expected population is held by the ∝ 1/t surviving lineages). It does not hold across avalanches. Zipf in duration follows from Kolmogorov's survival law.
checks.best_reading: The expected population (a martingale at branching ratio 1) is conserved per generation and shared among the surviving lineages (Kolmogorov and Yaglom). Durations are Zipf, and size integrates the population over the lifetime (s ∝ T^2).
checks.numerology_risk: Low for the mathematical model. Moderate to high for the neuronal data: the exponents depend on bin width, subsampling biases the inferred branching ratio, and non-critical mechanisms reproduce similar exponents. The '1 + 1/2 length' reading is numerology, as the catalogue says, and the same 3/2 also arises from random walks.
checks.source: Kolmogorov (1938) and Yaglom (1947) (standard). Beggs & Plenz (2003) J. Neurosci. 23:11167 (values as cited by the catalogue; not re-verified this session because the search budget was exhausted).

checks.system: Earthquake aftershock decay (Omori-Utsu)
checks.corrected_alpha_uncertainty: Kisslinger & Jones (1991): mean 1.11 +/- 0.25 over 39 southern-California sequences, range about 0.7-1.8 (verified). Utsu et al. (1995) abstract: 'usually p = 0.9-1.5' (verified). The catalogue's wider range of 0.6-2.5 could not be confirmed this session.
checks.algebra_note: alpha = p, d_log = p - 1 ≈ 0.1 and d_lin = p are correct.
checks.best_reading: Dieterich rate-and-state nucleation. An exponential time-to-failure map of a uniformly distributed initial state or stress gives log-uniform failure times. The result is an equal number of nucleation sites per log time (d_log = 0, a count), so p = 1 for c < t < t_a.
checks.numerology_risk: Moderate to high. d_log = 0 is the generic scale-free value. Several distinct mechanisms give p ≈ 1: rate-state nucleation, static fatigue or stress corrosion, viscoelastic relaxation, and ETAS cascades (which renormalize the bare p). The exponent therefore does not pick out the resource. The spread of p from 0.7 to 1.8 has only ad hoc readings. The heat-flow correlation (verified as reported, with no correlation to b or mainshock magnitude) is the best independent test, and it is disputed.
checks.source: Kisslinger & Jones (1991) JGR 96:11947 (earthref abstract, verified this session). Utsu, Ogata & Matsu'ura (1995) J. Phys. Earth 43:1-33 (CiNii abstract, verified this session; the 0.6-2.5 range is not confirmed). Dieterich (1994) (standard).

checks.system: Wind-wave spectra (Toba/Zakharov-Filonenko omega^-4, Phillips omega^-5) and capillary wave turbulence
checks.corrected_alpha_uncertainty: omega^-4 near the peak and omega^-5 above roughly 2-3 times the peak (field data). In tanks the gravity-range exponent depends on the forcing (Falcon et al. 2007, verified).
checks.algebra_note: These are correct (re-derived): omega^-4 → k^(-5/2), omega^-5 → k^-3, d_log(omega) = 2 d_log(k) under k ∝ omega^2, and the kinetic-equation stock scalings P^(1/3) (four-wave) and P^(1/2) (three-wave). The capillary chain skips one step: E(k) ∝ k^(-7/4) gives an elevation spectrum F_eta ∝ E/k^2 ∝ k^(-15/4), which gives S_eta ∝ omega^(-17/6). The final result is right.
checks.best_reading: Energy flux through scales via four-wave resonances (the Kolmogorov-Zakharov solution). The stock per ln omega is set by flux divided by a stock-dependent rate, giving omega^-4 with level ∝ P^(1/3). Log measure. The saturated omega^-5 range is a separate capacity reading: slope variance per ln k capped by breaking.
checks.numerology_risk: Moderate. Phillips (1985) obtains the same omega^-4 AND the same level ∝ u_* from a local balance of wind input, transfer and breaking. With P ∝ u_*^3, KZ's P^(1/3) ∝ u_* as well, so neither the exponent nor the level scaling discriminates the cascade reading. In the capillary analogue the exponent matched but the predicted flux scaling failed in both regimes (Falcon et al. 2007, verified). The exponent therefore underdetermines the resource. The omega^-5 saturation reading is motivated.
checks.source: Falcon, Laroche & Fauve (2007) PRL 98:094503, arXiv cond-mat/0610297 (abstract verified this session). Phillips (1958, 1985), Toba (1973), Zakharov-Filonenko and Forristall (1981) are as cited by the catalogue and were not re-verified this session (search budget exhausted). The algebra was re-derived.

verification.missing_cases:
Verification limits: the web-search budget shared by this run ran out after about ten queries, and WebFetch could not resolve arxiv, ar5iv or frontiersin. Values marked verified above were confirmed this session; everything else is from standard knowledge or memory, as flagged. Omitted cases, with counterexamples to the program first.

(1) Critical-point exponents. 3D Ising has nu ≈ 0.630, beta ≈ 0.326, eta ≈ 0.036, all irrational. They are renormalization-group eigenvalues with no resource reading. The hyperscaling relation 2 - alpha = d nu does have a derived capacity reading: one kT of singular free energy per correlation volume xi^d, the critical analogue of equipartition. It fails above d_c = 4, exactly as the percolation packing fails above 6. Like percolation's d/D_f, it relocates the unexplained number rather than explaining it.

(2) The Flory exponent nu = 3/(d+2) for self-avoiding polymers. A resource-balance argument (elastic versus excluded-volume free energy) gives the exact 3/4 in 2D and 0.6 against 0.588 in 3D, but de Gennes showed this comes from a cancellation of errors. A balance reading can match an exponent for the wrong reason.

(3) Multipole and dispersion laws. Dipole fields go as r^-3, London/van der Waals as r^-6, Casimir-Polder as r^-7, Casimir pressure as d^-4, and Rayleigh scattering as lambda^-4. The total flux through a sphere around a dipole is zero, so the Gauss sharing reading gives nothing. The exponents come from differentiation (+1 per multipole order) and from squaring in perturbation theory (x2), not from a shared conserved total. The Lennard-Jones r^-12 is a pure computational convention, the limiting case of an exponent with no physical content.

(4) Non-derived or irrational exponents: DLA D_f ≈ 1.71, the 2D Manna/BTW sandpile tau ≈ 1.27, the 3D percolation D_f, the Salpeter IMF 2.35, Glen's ice flow law n ≈ 3 and power-law creep n = 3-8, the empirical Blasius f ∝ Re^(-1/4) and the 1/7 velocity profile, and the galaxy correlation function r^-1.8, which is only approximately a power law.

Cases that fit the program well:

(5) Cosmic rays. Diffusive shock acceleration at a strong shock gives dN/dE ∝ E^-2, i.e. (r+2)/(r-1) with compression ratio r = 4. That is equal energy per ln E, log-orthopolic in energy, and derived. Energy-dependent escape (residence ∝ E^-delta) steepens the spectrum to about 2.7. This is exactly the transport identity: stock = flux x residence time. The B/C ratio measures delta independently (about 1/3, which ties to the Kolmogorov turbulence spectrum, from memory), making it a clean 'final resource' composition: source + 0 + delta.

(6) The primordial curvature spectrum, n_s ≈ 0.965 (Planck 2018, from memory). Harrison-Zel'dovich means equal power per ln k (d_log = 0), derived from a nearly constant H per e-fold of inflation. The measured n_s - 1 ≈ -0.035 measures the slow-roll departure.

(7) The Sedov-Taylor blast wave, R ∝ (E t^2/rho)^(1/5), followed by the momentum-conserving snowplow, R ∝ t^(1/4). A conserved total is shared over the swept mass, and the exponent changes when the conserved quantity switches from energy to momentum. This is the same 'one system, two readings' pattern as the wave and turbulence spectra. Diffusion and the porous-medium equation (R ∝ t^(1/(d(m-1)+2))) are the same sharing in time.

(8) The Fermi energy and BEC T_c, both ∝ n^(2/d): k-space slot counting.

(9) Gutenberg-Richter, b ≈ 1 (zeta_M0 ≈ 0.6-0.67). The catalogue includes aftershock decay but omits the frequency-size law. Aki's D = 2b reads b = 1 as packing of a 2D fault plane (zeta_L = 2), a capacity reading. Rupture-width saturation in large events, with an observed change in the frequency-size slope, is the natural test. The repo has already found b = 1 far from log-equipartition of energy.

(10) Dohnanyi constant-mass-flux fragmentation, Larson's constant column density, and Aschwanden's scale-free-probability conjecture (N(L) ∝ L^-d, i.e. space-filling packing identical to the percolation reading). These are already in the repo but missing from this physics catalogue.

Pattern from the checks: in every case the strongest discriminator was a dimension series, a prefactor, or a flux scaling. A matching exponent alone never sufficed. The number 3/2 alone carries at least three unrelated resources.

cases.system: Whole-organism metabolic rate across species (mammals mainly; also birds, ectotherms, plants)
cases.law_or_distribution: B = B0 M^b with b about 3/4 (Kleiber's law); mass-specific rate B/M ∝ M^-1/4
cases.variable_k: body mass M (kg); y = metabolic power B (W)
cases.reported_exponent: Kleiber 1932: 0.74. Savage et al. 2004, mammal BMR (52 studies, 626 measurements): 0.737 ± 0.026; field metabolic rate 0.749 ± 0.054. White & Seymour 2003 (619 species, corrected for body temperature, digestive state and phylogeny): 2/3; 0.686 in their herbivore-exclusion analysis. Kolokotrones et al. 2010: the log-log relation is convex, so the local slope rises from about 2/3 in small mammals to above 3/4 in large ones. Range across studies: 0.67-0.76.
cases.alpha_uncertainty: ±0.03 within a study; 0.67-0.76 across studies. Curvature means no single exponent holds.
cases.conversion: Scaling law, so there is no density conversion: a = b = 0.74. For laws I set d_log = d_lin = the implied resource exponent. Here the number of equally supplied terminal units sharing B scales as M^0.75, and tissue mass per unit as M^0.25.
cases.orthopolic_reading: Conserved total: the organism's metabolic power B, a flux. Units sharing it: terminal supply units (capillaries or 'service volumes'). West, Brown and Enquist (WBE) and Banavar et al. take these to be size-invariant, so each unit receives the same power. B is then proportional to the number of units, which scales as M^3/4: the units are discretely orthopolic in power. Tissue mass served per unit grows as M^1/4, which is the mass-specific rate M^-1/4 read inversely. This is a flux reading, not a stock reading.

decompositions.resource: Number of supplied sites in a D-dimensional body, fed by a space-filling supply network
decompositions.composition: sites ∝ L^D. Minimum network (blood) volume ∝ L^D × L = L^(D+1), because each unit of supply travels about L. With mass ∝ network volume, B ∝ sites ∝ M^(D/(D+1)). The final resource is D spatial dimensions plus 1 transport dimension; D = 3 gives 3/(3+1).
decompositions.predicted_exponent: 3/4 for D = 3; 2/3 for D = 2; 1/2 for D = 1
decompositions.independent_motivation: Every cell must be reached from a single pump, and supplying N sites spread over a region of size L costs about N×L. This is a geometric argument that does not use metabolic data.
decompositions.theory_agreement: Banavar, Maritan & Rinaldo 1999 (Nature 399:130): the minimum-cost network scales as C ∝ N^(1+1/D); inverting gives D/(D+1). WBE 1997/1999 get 3/4 from fractal networks with invariant terminal units (the 'fourth dimension'). Both mechanisms count supplied units, so they agree with this reading. Kolokotrones et al. 2010 report that WBE fails to reproduce the observed curvature. The reading matches Kleiber and Savage et al., not White & Seymour.
decompositions.testable_consequence: Organisms or colonies supplied within a plane should scale as 2/3, and filamentous ones as 1/2. Blood volume must scale as M^1. The reading does not predict the curvature seen in mammals.

decompositions.resource: Heat-exchange surface (Rubner surface law)
decompositions.composition: Skin area ∝ L^2 and M ∝ L^3, so q ∝ M^(2/3)
decompositions.independent_motivation: An endotherm at constant body temperature must lose its heat through its surface.
decompositions.theory_agreement: Rubner's surface law; Banavar et al. 2010 also get 2/3 when flow velocity is constant. It matches White & Seymour's corrected BMR and the small-mammal end of the Kolokotrones curve. Savage et al.'s interval excludes it.
decompositions.testable_consequence: Ectotherms have no heat-loss constraint, so they should not show 2/3. If the curvature is a crossover from surface-limited to network-limited metabolism, the local slope should change at the mass where heat loss stops binding.

decompositions.resource: Flux = service capacity × flow velocity
decompositions.composition: B ∝ (capacity ∝ M^2/3) × (velocity ∝ M^1/12), giving 2/3 + 1/12 = 3/4
decompositions.predicted_exponent: 3/4 if velocity scales as M^1/12; 2/3 if velocity is constant
decompositions.independent_motivation: Any flux is a cross-section times a speed. Velocity can rise with the linear size of the terminal service volume.
decompositions.theory_agreement: Banavar et al. 2010 (PNAS 107:15816) state this decomposition exactly, for both radial-explosion and branched networks. M^1/12 is the maximum allowed velocity exponent, not one measured independently.
decompositions.testable_consequence: Terminal blood velocity should scale as about M^0.083 across mammals. Species or tissues with size-invariant velocity should scale as 2/3.

cases.source: Savage et al. 2004 (Funct Ecol, 'The predominance of quarter-power scaling in biology'; values from a comparison table); White & Seymour 2003 PNAS 100:4046; Kolokotrones et al. 2010 Nature 464:753; Banavar, Maritan & Rinaldo 1999 Nature 399:130; Banavar et al. 2010 PNAS 107:15816; West, Brown & Enquist 1999 Science 284:1677. All from abstracts and search summaries (full-text fetch was blocked by the network).

cases.system: Resting heart rate and maximum lifespan across mammal species
cases.law_or_distribution: f_H ∝ M^-1/4 and lifespan T ∝ M^+1/4, so heartbeats per lifetime f_H·T is roughly constant (about 10^9)
cases.variable_k: body mass M (kg)
cases.reported_exponent: Heart rate: -0.25 (Holt et al. 1968; Stahl, whose data were never published; Brody's data give -0.27, which Savage et al. binned to -0.25). Maximum lifespan: about +0.15 to +0.25. An AnAge all-species fit gives t_max ∝ M^0.146 (n = 1,701, r² = 0.34). Levine 1997: 7.3 ± 5.6 × 10^8 heartbeats per lifetime across mammals, roughly constant within an order of magnitude.
cases.alpha_uncertainty: Heart rate about ±0.02. The lifespan exponent ranges from 0.15 to 0.25 depending on taxon and phylogenetic control.
cases.conversion: Scaling laws; a = -0.25 for heart rate. Implied resource exponent (d_log = d_lin): lifetime metabolic energy per individual ∝ (B/M)·T·M ∝ M^(-1/4 + 1/4 + 1) = M^1, i.e. equal lifetime energy per gram.
cases.orthopolic_reading: Conserved total: a lifetime budget. There are two candidate units. (i) Each life gets the same number of cardiac cycles, a dimensionless count, discrete across species. (ii) Each gram of tissue processes the same lifetime energy (Rubner's constant), so lifetime energy per individual ∝ M. Both are deterministic compositions of a rate (∝ M^-1/4) and a duration (∝ M^+1/4). Both are time-integrated flux budgets (event totals), not stocks.

decompositions.resource: Lifetime energy throughput per gram of tissue
decompositions.composition: Mass-specific power (∝ M^-1/4, from Kleiber) × lifespan (∝ M^+1/4) gives M^0 per gram and M^1 per individual. Exponents add because this is a deterministic product.
decompositions.predicted_exponent: 0 per gram. Lifespan must scale as +1/4 when mass-specific rate scales as -1/4.
decompositions.independent_motivation: Rate of living: if damage accrues per unit energy processed per unit tissue, tissue fails after a fixed processed energy, so lifespan ∝ 1/(mass-specific rate).
decompositions.theory_agreement: This is the rate-of-living theory (Rubner 1908; Pearl 1928). Speakman 2005 (J Exp Biol 208:1717) found the link is an artefact of body size and phylogeny. After controlling for both, mammal species with higher metabolism have larger lifetime expenditure per gram; Furness & Speakman 2008 found the same in more than 300 bird species. Birds have higher lifetime energy per gram than mammals of the same size. The mechanism is contradicted even though the allometric exponents roughly cancel.
decompositions.testable_consequence: Birds and mammals of equal mass should have equal lifetime energy per gram; observed values for birds are higher, so the reading fails across classes. Within a species, larger dog breeds live shorter lives despite lower mass-specific rates (from memory, not verified here), which the reading does not predict.

decompositions.resource: Number of physiological cycles (heartbeats) per life
decompositions.composition: f_H ∝ M^-1/4 × T ∝ M^+1/4 gives M^0. Both would be set by one physiological clock ∝ M^1/4 (network transit time).
decompositions.independent_motivation: If all biological durations scale with one physiological time, any ratio of two durations is size-invariant. The heartbeat count is then a dimensionless invariant rather than a budget being spent.
decompositions.theory_agreement: WBE derive transit times ∝ M^1/4 for network-supplied organisms, but they do not derive lifespan. Levine 1997 treats heart rate as a marker of metabolic rate, which reduces this reading to the first. The invariant holds only within an order of magnitude (CV about 77%).
decompositions.testable_consequence: If lifespan follows physiological time, its exponent must equal the heart-period exponent in every clade. Heartbeats per life should then be size-invariant within birds as well, at a different constant.

cases.source: Levine 1997 J Am Coll Cardiol 30:1104 (PubMed 9316546, abstract); Holt et al. 1968 and Brody/Savage values via arXiv 0802.1513; de Magalhães AnAge fit via senescence.info; Speakman 2005 J Exp Biol 208:1717 and Furness & Speakman 2008 via abstracts.

cases.system: Population density across species: mammalian primary consumers (Damuth's rule) and maximum stand density of plants (self-thinning)
cases.law_or_distribution: Animals: D ∝ M^-3/4. Plants: Yoda's mean mass w ∝ N^-3/2, i.e. N ∝ w^-2/3, versus Enquist, Brown & West's N_max ∝ M^-3/4, i.e. w ∝ N^-4/3.
cases.variable_k: mean adult body or plant mass M (kg); y = individuals per unit area
cases.reported_exponent: Damuth 1981: slope -0.75 for 307 mammalian primary-consumer species. Single-community slopes range from -0.56 to -0.95, none significantly different from -0.75. A later meta-analysis gives a pooled mammal slope of about -0.755 but rejects homogeneity. Carbone & Gittleman 2002 (25 carnivores): carnivore number per unit prey biomass ∝ M^-1, and per unit prey productivity ∝ M^-0.75 (about 90 kg of carnivore per 10,000 kg of prey). Plants: Yoda gives a = -2/3 and EBW 1998 give -3/4. Empirical thinning slopes scatter around both: Chinese fir sits near -3/2 and differs from -4/3; Li, Han & Wu 2006 (1,266 plots) find the exponent varies with community.
cases.alpha_uncertainty: Animals: ±0.05 globally, -0.56 to -0.95 within communities. Plants: -0.67 to -0.75, with stands outside both.
cases.conversion: Discretely orthopolic: the count in class j (a species or a stand) ∝ 1/q̄_j. With D ∝ M^-a the resource exponent is d = a = 0.75. Yoda's w ∝ N^-3/2 converts to N ∝ w^-2/3, so d = 2/3.
cases.orthopolic_reading: Conserved total: the supply rate of the limiting resource per unit area (primary production for herbivores; light or water flux for plants). This is a flux. Units: species populations (animals) or stands at maximum density (plants). Each gets an equal share, so individuals per area = share / per-individual use. Biomass per area ∝ M^1/4 rises with size, so the stock is not orthopolic; the energy flux is (energetic equivalence). The plant alternative is a capacity: slots of ground area.

decompositions.resource: Individual metabolic rate (energy flux)
decompositions.composition: q ∝ M^3/4 (Kleiber, itself 3/(3+1)), and D × q = constant
decompositions.independent_motivation: Each species draws on a supply whose rate per area does not depend on the consumer's size. Individuals pack until their summed use equals that species' share.
decompositions.theory_agreement: Damuth 1981 established it empirically. Enquist, Brown & West 1998 (Nature 395:163) derive it for plants from xylem flux ∝ M^3/4 and size-invariant supply per area. The mechanism is the reading itself, but why each species gets an equal share is not derived.
decompositions.testable_consequence: Normalizing by the supply that actually reaches each species should restore -3/4. Carbone & Gittleman's carnivores pass this test: -1 per unit prey biomass, but -0.75 per unit prey productivity. Ectotherm slopes should track their own metabolic exponents and body temperatures.

decompositions.resource: Ground area occupied (crown projection), a capacity
decompositions.composition: Isometric plant: area ∝ L^2 and mass ∝ L^3, so q ∝ M^2/3. The number of slots of size L in a fixed area ∝ L^-2.
decompositions.independent_motivation: Plants cannot overlap at ground level, so a stand at maximum density is a packing problem.
decompositions.theory_agreement: This is Yoda et al. 1963's geometric model. It matches some stands (Chinese fir) but not the EBW compilation, and not animals.
decompositions.testable_consequence: Packing along one dimension (hedgerows, riparian strips) predicts N ∝ M^-1/3, i.e. w ∝ N^-3. The flux and capacity readings differ by only 1/12 in the exponent; separating them needs more than 4 decades of mass and many stands. A stand whose limiting resource is a flux (water in drylands) should give -3/4; one limited by space should give -2/3.

cases.source: Damuth 1981 Nature 290:699 (via secondary summaries; community-slope range from the paper as quoted); Carbone & Gittleman 2002 Science 295:2273 (abstract-style summary); Enquist, Brown & West 1998 Nature 395:163; Yoda et al. 1963; Li, Han & Wu 2006 J Integr Plant Biol; Chinese fir self-thinning study (J Resour Ecol 2019).

cases.system: Pelagic marine and aquatic communities, bacteria to whales (the Sheldon spectrum)
cases.law_or_distribution: Abundance density n(m) ∝ m^-2. Equivalently, the normalized biomass size spectrum (NBSS) has slope -1 and biomass per log-mass interval is constant.
cases.variable_k: individual body mass m (g wet weight or carbon)
cases.reported_exponent: Sheldon et al. 1972: roughly equal particle concentration per logarithmic size class (measured from about 1 to 100 µm). Hatton et al. 2021: about 1 Gt wet weight per order of magnitude over most of 23 decades. The repo's re-expression gives an abundance-per-log-mass slope of -1.04 (95% CI -1.05 to -1.02, upper 200 m). GLOSSAQUA (repo): median NBSS slope -1.015 (study-block 95% CI -1.100 to -0.990). Theory: Andersen & Beyer 2006 derive n ∝ m^-2.05; Platt & Denman 1978 give NBSS -1.22 for heterotroph parameters.
cases.alpha_uncertainty: 2.0-2.1 across syntheses. Individual spectra are widely dispersed (SD about 0.3).
cases.conversion: An NBSS slope β gives α = 1 - β; an abundance-per-log-mass slope s gives α = 1 - s. Then d_log = α - 1 and d_lin = α.
cases.orthopolic_reading: Conserved total: standing biomass, a stock. Units: log-mass classes (decades). The spectrum is log-orthopolic in biomass: each decade holds about 1 Gt. The underlying transfer is an energy flux up through sizes. By the transport identity, biomass per log mass B = F/v, where F is the flux through ln m and v is the log-growth speed.

decompositions.resource: Biomass (stock), as energy flux × residence time
decompositions.composition: Per log class, energy flux F ∝ m^(ln TE / ln PPMR), where TE is trophic transfer efficiency and PPMR the predator-prey mass ratio. TE = 0.1 and PPMR = 10^4 give m^-1/4 (trophic loss). Log-growth speed v ∝ m^(n-1) = m^-1/4 (Kleiber). So B = F/v ∝ m^0, and the log-orthopolic resource is mass: d = 1 = 3/4 (individual metabolic flux) + 1/4 (trophic dilution of supply). In general, biomass per log mass ∝ m^((1-n) + ln TE / ln PPMR).
decompositions.predicted_exponent: α = 2 when ln TE / ln PPMR = n - 1 = -1/4; in general α = 2 - [(1-n) + ln TE / ln PPMR]
decompositions.independent_motivation: Energy enters at the bottom and moves up as larger organisms eat smaller ones. Each transfer loses a fraction (TE) and spans a factor PPMR in mass, and larger individuals turn over more slowly (Kleiber). All three inputs are measured independently of the spectrum (stable isotopes, gut contents, respirometry).
decompositions.theory_agreement: Brown & Gillooly 2003 (PNAS 100:1467): with 10% efficiency and a 10^4 mass step, abundance ∝ M^-1, biomass ∝ M^0 and energy use ∝ M^-1/4 (my derivation from their stated inputs). Jennings & Mackinson 2003 formalize this; Andersen & Beyer 2006 derive -2.05 from individual-level processes. The mechanism agrees with the composition exactly.
decompositions.testable_consequence: Lower transfer efficiency (nutrient-stressed systems) or smaller PPMR should steepen the spectrum by the formula. Jennings & Mackinson report N ∝ M^-1.2 for a North Sea web. Fishing truncates and steepens the top.

decompositions.resource: Individual metabolic rate (energy flux): energetic equivalence across size classes
decompositions.composition: q ∝ m^3/4, with equal energy use per log-mass class
decompositions.independent_motivation: Size classes would share a single energy source equally, as in Damuth's rule.
decompositions.theory_agreement: Brown & Gillooly 2003: this holds only when all classes draw on one source, i.e. within one trophic level. Across trophic levels the transfer loss steepens the slope to -1.
decompositions.testable_consequence: Rejected for whole spectra (observed 2.0-2.05). Within a single trophic level, such as phytoplankton alone, the slope per log mass should be -3/4 (α = 1.75).

cases.source: Sheldon, Prakash & Sutcliffe 1972 L&O 17:327; Hatton, Heneghan, Bar-On & Galbraith 2021 Sci Adv 7:eabh3732; repo results/independent.json (ocean_top200) and GLOSSAQUA summary in docs/evidence.md; Brown & Gillooly 2003 PNAS 100:1467 (summary); Jennings & Mackinson 2003 Ecol Lett; Andersen & Beyer 2006 Am Nat 168:54 (abstract); Platt & Denman 1978 (reprint snippet).

cases.system: Trees in forest stands (worldwide plots; tropical ForestGEO plots)
cases.law_or_distribution: dN/dD ∝ D^-2 for stem diameter D (Enquist & Niklas 2001); f(r) ∝ r^-2 (West, Enquist & Brown 2009)
cases.variable_k: stem diameter D (cm)
cases.reported_exponent: Enquist & Niklas 2001: individuals per area ∝ D^-2, which they also state as the -3/4 power of aboveground biomass. A macroecological analysis finds fitted exponents clustered near -2, varying with successional stage. Coomes et al. 2003: power laws fit small stems only, with exponents significantly different from -2 and changing over time; large stems are better fit by an exponential. Muller-Landau et al. 2006 (14 tropical plots): data are uniformly inconsistent with the metabolic predictions, and a demographic-equilibrium model fits better. Simini et al.: the power law holds only below about 30-40 cm.
cases.alpha_uncertainty: About 1.5-2.5 for small and medium stems; steeper or exponential for large stems.
cases.conversion: α is in D. With M ∝ D^(8/3), dN/dM ∝ M^-11/8 (ζ_M = 0.375). d_log = α - 1 = 1 (resource ∝ D); d_lin = α = 2 (resource ∝ D^2).
cases.orthopolic_reading: Conserved total: the stand's water and energy flux, or its basal area. Units: linear diameter classes (e.g. 1-cm bins). The stand is linear-orthopolic in metabolic rate ∝ D^2 (basal area, sapwood flux): each diameter increment carries the same total flux. That equality is with respect to dD, which depends on the coordinate: per log mass, metabolic flux rises as M^3/8, so the same forest is top-heavy in flux per log size.

decompositions.resource: Metabolic rate / xylem flux ∝ D^2 (equivalently basal area)
decompositions.composition: B ∝ M^3/4 and M ∝ D^8/3, so B ∝ D^2. The exponent 2 = (3/4)(8/3): changing the coordinate multiplies exponents.
decompositions.independent_motivation: Trees in a stand compete for the same light and water supply, so energetic equivalence across size classes applies, as in Damuth's rule.
decompositions.theory_agreement: Enquist & Niklas 2001 and West, Enquist & Brown 2009 derive f(r) ∝ r^-2 from space filling and the analogy that a forest is like a tree. The mechanism agrees only in part. The derivation is geometric and demographic, and energetic equivalence holds only per linear diameter bin, which the theory does not motivate. Muller-Landau et al. find growth and mortality do not scale as required. A 2008 Ecology Letters paper notes that D^-2 corresponds to mass density M^-11/8, not M^-3/4.
decompositions.testable_consequence: In height (h ∝ D^2/3) the reading predicts dN/dh ∝ h^-5/2. Measured sap flux should scale as D^2 wherever the D^-2 law holds. Disturbance should break it (it does: Coomes et al.).

decompositions.resource: Cross-sectional area per branching level (Leonardo's rule; forest as one tree)
decompositions.composition: If stems are distributed like the branches of an area-preserving tree, counts per geometric size class ∝ r^-2. That is log-orthopolic in area (d_log = 2), with density ∝ r^-3.
decompositions.independent_motivation: WBE's analogy: canopy space is filled the way a crown is, and area-preserving branching conserves total cross-section across levels.
decompositions.theory_agreement: WEB 2009 tabulate the continuous f(r) ∝ r^-2; reading the branch analogy as per-level counts gives α = 3. The disagreement lies in binning, not in the physics.
decompositions.testable_consequence: Counting stems per logarithmic diameter class, the area reading predicts counts ∝ D^-2 and the flux reading ∝ D^-1. The central data tendency (density ≈ D^-2) rejects the area reading for small and medium stems.

decompositions.resource: An unidentified quantity ∝ D per stem (log measure)
decompositions.composition: A log-orthopolic resource with d = 1 in D, i.e. ∝ M^3/8
decompositions.independent_motivation: None. Crown radius and height both scale as D^2/3 in WBE, so no standard tree trait scales as D^1.
decompositions.theory_agreement: No theory proposes this.
decompositions.testable_consequence: None until a physical quantity ∝ D is named. This is the no-natural-reading branch of the same exponent.

cases.source: Enquist & Niklas 2001 Nature 410:655 (abstract; corrigendum Nature 425:741); West, Enquist & Brown 2009 PNAS 106:7040 (table via PMC snippet); Coomes et al. 2003 Ecol Lett 6:980 (abstract); Muller-Landau et al. 2006 Ecol Lett 9:575/589 (abstracts); Simini et al. arXiv 1005.1265; repo docs/zeta-compilation.md.

cases.system: Species richness vs area (islands and mainland samples; many taxa)
cases.law_or_distribution: S = c A^z
cases.variable_k: area A (km²)
cases.reported_exponent: Canonical z ≈ 0.25 (Preston 1962 gives about 0.26; from memory). Drakare et al. 2006 meta-analysis (about 700 SARs): variance-weighted mean z ≈ 0.27, unweighted 0.30 (from a secondary summary). In that analysis islands have lower z than mainland, and nested designs are steeper than independent ones (terrestrial about 0.37 vs 0.28, from a secondary calculation). z rises with the body size of the taxon; microbial SARs are very shallow. Triantis et al. 2012: the power model ranks first of 20 models across 601 island datasets.
cases.alpha_uncertainty: About 0.1-0.4 across systems and sampling designs
cases.conversion: Scaling law, a = z. Under random placement of individuals with a Pareto abundance tail P(N_i ≥ n) ∝ n^-ζ, z = ζ (Irie & Tokita 2006 give the general SAR-to-SAD map). So the species-abundance density exponent is α_SAD = 1 + z, d_log = z = 0.27 and d_lin = 1.27.
cases.orthopolic_reading: Conserved total: area (a capacity), or the individuals it holds (∝ A). Units: species. Species are not shares of a fixed total: area per species grows as A^(1-z) = A^0.73. The candidate orthopolic reading is a capacity, the number of niche slots an area can host.

decompositions.resource: Niche-space slots (capacity)
decompositions.composition: S ∝ (extent of niche space)^D_niche, with D_niche ≈ 3/2 from the species-length frequency distribution. Length ∝ M_max^1/3, and the largest vertebrate mass M_max ∝ A^1/2. So z = (3/2)(1/3)(1/2) = 1/4.
decompositions.independent_motivation: Packing boxes into a D-dimensional niche space gives a count ∝ extent^D. The extent along the size axis is set by the largest body the area supports, which is measured independently (Burness et al. 2001).
decompositions.theory_agreement: Southwood, May & Sugihara 2006 (PNAS 103:6931) propose exactly this link between three independently measured power laws. The step from L_max to S is heuristic, and I could not verify its details.
decompositions.testable_consequence: Taxa whose maximum size does not scale with area (microbes, small invertebrates) should have shallow z, consistent with Drakare et al.'s positive correlation of z with body size. Ectotherms with a different M_max–A exponent should shift z in proportion.

decompositions.resource: Individuals (q = n per species), log-orthopolic across species
decompositions.composition: If species abundances were log-orthopolic in individuals (ζ = 1), random placement would give z = 1
decompositions.independent_motivation: Individuals are the additive resource of a community, and an area holds N ∝ A of them.
decompositions.theory_agreement: Irie & Tokita 2006 give z as a function of the SAD exponent. Real SADs are lognormal or log-series in the body, and García Martín & Goldenfeld 2006 need conspecific clustering to recover power-law SARs.
decompositions.testable_consequence: Rejected: z = 0.27 would require a top-heavy SAD tail (ζ ≈ 0.27), which is not observed.

decompositions.resource: Unidentified quantity ∝ abundance^0.27 per species
decompositions.composition: The only log-orthopolic per-species resource consistent with z under random placement
decompositions.independent_motivation: None.
decompositions.theory_agreement: None.
decompositions.testable_consequence: None: this reading is fitted after the fact.

cases.source: Drakare, Lennon & Hillebrand 2006 Ecol Lett 9:215 (values via D. Tyre's summary and Wikipedia); Triantis, Guilhaumon & Whittaker 2012 J Biogeogr 39:215; Southwood, May & Sugihara 2006 PNAS 103:6931 (abstract); Irie & Tokita 2006 arXiv q-bio/0609012; García Martín & Goldenfeld 2006 PNAS.

cases.system: Species per genus (angiosperm families, Willis & Yule 1922; mammals)
cases.law_or_distribution: Fraction of genera with n species ∝ n^-α
cases.variable_k: n, number of species in a genus
cases.reported_exponent: Willis & Yule (e.g. Leguminosae): Yule's fit ρ = s/g = 2.457 gives a tail exponent 1 + 1/ρ = 1.41 for the infinite-time model, and about 1.5 with finite age (from a Reed–Hughes-related note). Yule observed faster decay above about 30 species. Mammals (Clauset et al. 2009): α = 2.4 ± 0.2 with x_min = 4, from memory and not verified.
cases.alpha_uncertainty: 1.4-1.5 for plants; about 2.4 for mammals (unverified)
cases.conversion: Density exponent read directly; d_log = α - 1 and d_lin = α.
cases.orthopolic_reading: Conserved total: species, a count, but additive. Units: genera, sized by species per genus. Log-orthopolic in species would mean equal numbers of species in each log-size class of genera (α = 2). α ≈ 1.45 puts most species in the largest genera (top-heavy); mammals at 2.4 would be bottom-heavy. The 'resource' is a taxonomic count, not a quantity anything holds or exchanges.

decompositions.resource: Species (q = n), log measure
decompositions.composition: Proportional (Gibrat) growth of genera by speciation, with conserved flux
decompositions.independent_motivation: Every species can split, so genera grow in proportion to their size. That is Gibrat's condition for flat resource per log size.
decompositions.theory_agreement: The repo's transport identity: flat B requires Gibrat growth and no net entry relative to growth.
decompositions.testable_consequence: Rejected for both plants (1.45) and mammals (2.4), which fall on opposite sides of 2.

decompositions.resource: Rate ratio g/s (Yule process)
decompositions.composition: Genus size grows as e^(st), and genera originate at rate g per genus, so genus ages are distributed as e^(-gt). Genera per unit ln n ∝ n^(-g/s), and species per unit ln n ∝ n^(1 - g/s). So d_log = g/s.
decompositions.predicted_exponent: α = 1 + g/s; flat in species only if g = s
decompositions.independent_motivation: Rates of species origin and genus origin are separate evolutionary parameters.
decompositions.theory_agreement: Yule 1925 derives exactly this. The Simon/Newman variant, with one new genus per m speciation events, gives α = 2 + 1/m > 2 and is needed for mammals. Which model applies is chosen after seeing α.
decompositions.testable_consequence: Estimate s and g independently from dated phylogenies and taxonomic revision rates, then predict α = 1 + g/s. Taxonomic splitting raises g and should steepen α.

cases.source: Willis & Yule 1922; Yule 1925 (model via arXiv physics/0601192 and a Reed–Hughes note giving ρ = 2.457, D_s ≈ 1.4–1.5); Newman 2005 / Wikipedia (γ = 2 + 1/m); Clauset, Shalizi & Newman 2009 SIAM Rev 51:661 (mammal value from memory).

cases.system: Paralogous gene-family sizes in complete genomes (bacteria, archaea, yeast, viruses)
cases.law_or_distribution: Number of families of size n ∝ n^-α
cases.variable_k: n, genes per family
cases.reported_exponent: Huynen & van Nimwegen 1998: power laws with exponents between -2 and -4, flatter (smaller α) in genomes with more genes. Later studies consistently find -2 to -3 (review arXiv 1102.2331). Karev et al. 2002 birth–death–innovation fit: asymptotic power 1.9 (as cited by the review).
cases.alpha_uncertainty: 2-4; lower in larger genomes
cases.conversion: Density exponent; d_log = α - 1 and d_lin = α.
cases.orthopolic_reading: Conserved total: genes (coding sequence), each costing replication and expression. Units: families. Duplication adds genes in proportion to family size (Gibrat), and innovation founds new families (entry). Log-orthopolic in genes (α = 2) means equal numbers of genes in each log-size class of families. This is a stock.

decompositions.resource: Genes (q = n), log measure, as the limit of no innovation
decompositions.composition: Duplication–innovation: N(≥S) ∝ S^(-1/(1-r)), so ζ = 1/(1-r) and α = 1 + 1/(1-r) ≥ 2, with equality as the innovation probability r → 0
decompositions.predicted_exponent: α ≥ 2 always, approaching 2 when new families are rare relative to duplication
decompositions.independent_motivation: Duplication probability per family scales with family size, and genes are the additive resource.
decompositions.theory_agreement: Qian et al. 2001's model as analysed by Durrett & Schweinsberg 2005; Karev et al. 2002 BDIM. This is the repo's 'orthopolity as the long-residence limit' (ζ - 1 ≈ entry/growth), and the mechanism agrees. Every reported α is at least 2, so the bound holds, unlike species per genus in plants.
decompositions.testable_consequence: α should approach 2 where new families originate rarely relative to duplication, and rise with innovation, for example in small bacterial genomes rich in horizontal gene transfer. The observed flattening with genome size is consistent.

decompositions.resource: Genes with an entry (innovation) penalty
decompositions.composition: d_log = 1/(1-r) = 1 + r/(1-r): genes plus an entry correction
decompositions.predicted_exponent: α = 2.5 needs r = 1/3; α = 4 needs r = 2/3
decompositions.independent_motivation: Family founding is a separate process from duplication and can be measured separately.
decompositions.theory_agreement: Karev et al. BDIM. Huynen & van Nimwegen argue that duplications and deletions within a family must be coherent.
decompositions.testable_consequence: Measure r directly, as the fraction of genes in newly founded (singleton/ORFan) families per unit time, and predict α. As fitted here, α = 4 would need two-thirds innovation, which seems implausibly high.

cases.source: Huynen & van Nimwegen 1998 Mol Biol Evol 15:583 (abstract); review 'The pattern and process of gene family evolution' arXiv 1102.2331; Durrett & Schweinsberg 2005 (arXiv math/0406216); Karev et al. 2002 BMC Evol Biol 2:18.

cases.system: Functional gene-category sizes vs genome size (bacteria)
cases.law_or_distribution: n_c ∝ N^x_c: transcription regulators x ≈ 2, metabolic genes x ≈ 1, core processes x < 1
cases.variable_k: N, total number of genes in the genome
cases.reported_exponent: van Nimwegen 2003 and the 2004 revisit: the transcription-regulation exponent is close to 2, with a 99% posterior interval of 1.72-1.95. Molina & van Nimwegen 2008: metabolic categories scale approximately linearly; DNA replication and cell division have exponents below 1.
cases.alpha_uncertainty: 1.72-1.95 (99%) for regulators; metabolism ≈ 1; core processes < 1
cases.conversion: Scaling law, a = x. Implied resource exponent (d_log = d_lin): the total regulatory requirement ∝ N^1.85. Per gene that is N^0.85, so genes per regulator ∝ N^-0.85.
cases.orthopolic_reading: Conserved total: the genome's gene count N. Units: regulators, each controlling a task or regulon. Regulators multiply faster than genes, so each regulator's share of genes shrinks as N^-0.85, like an inverse-square law with genome size as the radius. Categories form a ladder of exponents 0, 1 and 2: fixed core needs, additive needs, and pairwise or combinatorial needs.

decompositions.resource: Gene pairs (combinatorial interactions)
decompositions.composition: Need ∝ N(N-1)/2 ∝ N^2, so d = 1 + 1 (each gene × its potential partners)
decompositions.independent_motivation: Regulation resolves conditional interactions among genes, and possible interactions grow as pairs.
decompositions.theory_agreement: van Nimwegen names pair counting as the natural candidate but argues it is implausible given how transcription factors act.
decompositions.testable_consequence: Regulators per gene should rise linearly with N. The 99% interval excludes exactly 2.

decompositions.resource: Tasks under tool reuse (toolbox model)
decompositions.composition: Each new task needs ∝ 1/N new enzymes because existing enzymes are reused, so tasks T ∝ ∫N dN ∝ N^2 and regulators ∝ tasks. d = 1 (genes) + 1 (reuse discount ∝ N).
decompositions.predicted_exponent: 2 asymptotically; the finite-network value depends on topology
decompositions.independent_motivation: Horizontal transfer brings co-regulated pathways, and a larger enzyme toolbox needs fewer new tools per task.
decompositions.theory_agreement: Maslov, Krishna, Pang & Sneppen 2009 (PNAS 106:9743) derive quadratic scaling from this mechanism and match E. coli pathway branch lengths; Pang & Maslov 2011 extend it to general topologies. The reading is theirs. The observed 1.72-1.95 lies just below the asymptote, and I did not verify whether finite-size corrections reach it.
decompositions.testable_consequence: The number of new enzymes per acquired pathway should fall as 1/N across genomes, and pathway branch lengths should shorten with genome size.

cases.source: van Nimwegen 2003 Trends Genet 19:479 (arXiv physics/0307001); van Nimwegen 2004 arXiv q-bio/0405022 (abstract with 1.72–1.95); Molina & van Nimwegen 2008 Biology Direct (PMC2615428); Maslov et al. 2009 PNAS 106:9743 (abstract).

cases.system: Neuronal avalanches in cortical slices and cultures (multielectrode arrays)
cases.law_or_distribution: P(s) ∝ s^-3/2; P(T) ∝ T^-2; mean size ⟨s⟩ ∝ T^γ with γ = 2 (mean field)
cases.variable_k: avalanche size s (active electrodes or summed LFP events); duration T (time bins)
cases.reported_exponent: Beggs & Plenz 2003: size exponent -3/2 with branching parameter about 1 (critical); duration exponent -2 suggested more tentatively. Friedman et al. 2012: approximate power laws in size and duration, collapse of avalanche shapes, and the crackling relation (α_T - 1)/(α_s - 1) = 1/(σνz) satisfied. Apparent exponents shift with time bin and subsampling. Spike-based avalanches give about 2.1 (repo compilation, secondary).
cases.alpha_uncertainty: ±0.1; depends on time bin and subsampling
cases.conversion: Density in s: d_log = 0.5, d_lin = 1.5. In duration T, α_T = 2, so d_log(T) = 1.
cases.orthopolic_reading: Conserved total: expected activity. At the critical branching ratio σ = 1, the expected number of active units E[Z_t] is constant in avalanche age t (a martingale). Fewer, larger survivors carry it: P(T > t) ∝ 1/t and activity per survivor ∝ t. So activity is shared equally across age classes, and the total time spent in avalanches is equal per log-duration class: the avalanches are log-orthopolic in time. In the size coordinate T ∝ s^1/2, so the resource is s^1/2. This is a flux or time-budget reading, not a stock.

decompositions.resource: Avalanche duration (time), carried by conserved expected activity
decompositions.composition: Log-orthopolic in T (α_T = 2) composed with s ∝ T^γ, γ = 2, gives α_s = 1 + (α_T - 1)/γ = 3/2. The resource in s is s^(1/γ) = s^1/2.
decompositions.independent_motivation: In a critical network each active unit triggers on average one other, so expected activity is conserved from step to step. Conservation through age is the transport identity, with activity as the flux and surviving avalanches as its carriers.
decompositions.theory_agreement: Harris 1963 and Kolmogorov: a critical Galton–Watson process has survival ∝ 1/t and total progeny ∝ s^-3/2. Beggs & Plenz and Friedman et al. support mean-field critical branching, so the mechanism agrees.
decompositions.testable_consequence: Pooled over all avalanches, mean activity at age t should be flat in t at criticality. Drugs that move the branching ratio away from 1 should make it grow or decay as σ^t and cut off the power laws. Below the upper critical dimension (e.g. 2D directed percolation) activity is not conserved, and the reading predicts α_T ≠ 2.

decompositions.resource: Metabolic cost per avalanche, ∝ number of activations (q ∝ s)
decompositions.composition: Each activation costs a fixed amount of ATP, with equal cost per log size class
decompositions.independent_motivation: A brain on a fixed energy budget might spread spending evenly across scales.
decompositions.theory_agreement: No theory supports this; critical branching gives 3/2.
decompositions.testable_consequence: Rejected for LFP avalanches (1.5). Spike-based avalanches near 2.1 would fit (unverified), which would mean the two measurement modes see different resources.

cases.source: Beggs & Plenz 2003 J Neurosci 23:11167 (abstract, PMC6741045); Friedman et al. 2012 PRL 108:208102 (abstract and a 2022 summary of its scaling relation); reviews arXiv 1712.04499, 1010.2530; Frontiers Neural Circuits 2020 on subsampling.

cases.system: Taylor's power law of fluctuation scaling (insect, plant and animal counts; spatial and temporal)
cases.law_or_distribution: Var ∝ mean^b
cases.variable_k: mean abundance μ per sample unit
cases.reported_exponent: Taylor 1961 proposed b as a species-specific aggregation index. Empirically b often lies between 1 and 2 (some reviews say 1-3). Kilpatrick & Ives 2003: constant per-capita environmental variability gives b = 2; most species have b < 2, which negative interspecific interactions can explain. Cohen & Xu 2015: random sampling from skewed distributions yields Taylor's law with b proportional to skewness.
cases.alpha_uncertainty: Typically 1-2, sometimes up to about 3
cases.conversion: Scaling law, a = b. Implied resource exponent (d_log = d_lin): the size of independent fluctuation units (clusters) ∝ μ^(b-1), so d = b - 1 = 0.5.
cases.orthopolic_reading: Conserved total: the mean abundance μ in a sample unit. Units: independent clusters (cohorts, colonies, patches) whose number is Poisson. Var = λ·E[c²], with λ ∝ μ^(2-b) clusters each holding ∝ μ^(b-1) individuals. b = 1 means fixed-size units (individuals, Poisson). b = 2 means one coherent unit (multiplicative, Gibrat-type noise). b = 1.5 means √μ clusters of √μ individuals each. The population is discretely orthopolic: μ is shared equally among the clusters.

decompositions.resource: Cluster size in a compound Poisson (Tweedie) population
decompositions.composition: Tweedie power p = b with 1 < b < 2: Poisson rate λ = μ^(2-b)/(φ(2-b)) and gamma cluster mean ∝ μ^(b-1) (I checked the algebra numerically). So b = 1 + d_c, where d_c is the cluster-size exponent.
decompositions.predicted_exponent: any b in (1,2); the reading has content only if d_c is measured
decompositions.independent_motivation: Organisms are aggregated in clumps (egg masses, colonies, schools), so a sample count is a sum over a random number of clumps.
decompositions.theory_agreement: Jørgensen's Tweedie family. Kendal 2002 shows Colorado potato beetle counts fit a discrete compound Poisson model. The approach is criticized for lacking population dynamics and for failing when 0 < b < 1.
decompositions.testable_consequence: Zero-frequency test: P(empty sample) = exp(-λ), so -ln P0 ∝ μ^(2-b). With b estimated from the variances, the frequency of empty samples follows with no new parameter (for counts, use the discrete analogue).

decompositions.resource: Equal log-abundance variance per population (multiplicative noise)
decompositions.composition: Var(ln N) constant across populations gives Var ∝ μ^2: one coherent unit, d_c = 1
decompositions.independent_motivation: Environmental variation multiplies per-capita growth by the same factor regardless of population size (Gibrat).
decompositions.theory_agreement: Kilpatrick & Ives 2003 derive b = 2 for constant per-capita variability, and Cohen derives it for exponentially growing clones. Interactions or limited sampling move b (Giometto et al. 2015).
decompositions.testable_consequence: Communities with weaker competition should have b closer to 2, and removing competitors should raise b. Most observed b < 2, so the reading fails as a general rule.

cases.source: Taylor 1961 Nature 189:732; Kilpatrick & Ives 2003 Nature 422:65 (abstract); Cohen & Xu 2015 PNAS 112:7749 (abstract); Kendal 2002 and Tweedie criticism via Wikipedia (Taylor's law) and arXiv 0708.2053.

cases.system: Home-range area vs body mass (mammals; vertebrates generally)
cases.law_or_distribution: H ∝ M^about 1
cases.variable_k: body mass M (kg); y = home range area (km²)
cases.reported_exponent: Jetz et al. 2004 (supplement): mammal home-range slopes of about 1.03-1.06 across subsets (the retrieved table text was garbled). The home-range exponent is 0.26-0.39 steeper than the population-density exponent, interpreted as overlap rising with size (Pearce et al. 2013's summary). Over 90% of resources may be lost to neighbours in large mammals. Pike, within one species: 1.08. Tamburello et al. 2015 (569 vertebrates): exponents vary with locomotion, foraging dimension, trophic guild and prey size.
cases.alpha_uncertainty: 1.0-1.1 in mammals; wider across vertebrates
cases.conversion: Scaling law, a ≈ 1.03 = 3/4 (metabolic need) + about 0.28 (sharing). d_log = d_lin = 1.03 (area per individual).
cases.orthopolic_reading: Conserved total: the renewal rate of food per unit area R (a flux density). Units: individuals. Each individual needs B ∝ M^3/4, so an exclusive area of B/R would suffice. Neighbours take a share that grows with body size, so the area actually used is need divided by exclusivity. This is a flux reading with a sharing correction.

decompositions.resource: Area = metabolic need × sharing (inverse exclusivity)
decompositions.independent_motivation: Energy need comes from Kleiber. Large animals cannot defend proportionally larger ranges, because defence cost grows with perimeter and travel, so overlap rises with size.
decompositions.theory_agreement: Jetz, Carbone, Fulford & Brown 2004 (Science 306:266) propose this mechanistic model, and it agrees with the reading. The overlap exponent was inferred from the gap between density and home-range slopes rather than measured directly (Pearce et al. 2013).
decompositions.testable_consequence: Directly measured overlap (GPS) should scale as about M^0.25-0.39. Strictly territorial species should approach H ∝ M^3/4. Carnivores, whose prey supply per area falls with their own size, should scale more steeply.

decompositions.resource: Exclusive metabolic area only (no sharing)
decompositions.independent_motivation: Each individual uses only what it needs.
decompositions.theory_agreement: Jetz et al. show this underpredicts the observed slope.
decompositions.testable_consequence: Rejected for mammals in general. It should hold only for species with exclusive territories.

cases.source: Jetz et al. 2004 Science 306:266 (abstract and SOM snippet); Pearce et al. 2013 (via search summary); Rosten et al. 2016 (PMC4843214); Tamburello, Côté & Dulvy 2015 Am Nat (abstract).

cases.system: Predator vs prey biomass, and community production vs biomass, across ecosystems
cases.law_or_distribution: Predator biomass ∝ (prey biomass)^k, k about 3/4; community production ∝ biomass^about 3/4
cases.variable_k: prey biomass density B (kg/km²) across communities
cases.reported_exponent: Hatton et al. 2015 (2,260 communities of mammals, invertebrates, plants and plankton): predator–prey and production–biomass exponents are often near 3/4 (press reports about 0.75). Body size does not explain it, and the pattern appears only at whole-community level.
cases.alpha_uncertainty: About 0.7-0.8 across biomes; exact intervals not retrieved
cases.conversion: Scaling law across communities, a = k. Implied: production per unit prey biomass ∝ B^-0.25. d_log = d_lin = 0.75.
cases.orthopolic_reading: Conserved total: community production, a flux. Units: units of prey biomass. Denser communities give each unit of biomass a smaller share of production (∝ B^-1/4). Predators live on that production, so they scale as production. No individual-level resource has been identified.

decompositions.resource: Predator biomass ∝ prey production (an identity), with production ∝ B^3/4
decompositions.composition: k_pred = k_prod when transfer efficiency and predator turnover do not depend on B
decompositions.independent_motivation: Predators live on prey production, not on standing prey biomass.
decompositions.theory_agreement: Hatton et al. report both exponents near 3/4 and connect them through production. The origin of 3/4 itself is unknown.
decompositions.testable_consequence: Across the same ecosystems, the production–biomass exponent should predict the predator–prey exponent system by system. Where prey turnover is changed (harvest, enrichment), both exponents should shift together.

decompositions.resource: Organism-like supply network, Kleiber transferred to communities (3/(3+1))
decompositions.composition: Community production ∝ B^(D/(D+1)) with D = 3
decompositions.independent_motivation: None independent: a community has no single network supplying all its biomass, and body size does not track prey biomass.
decompositions.theory_agreement: No theory derives it. Hatton and colleagues suggest the echo of physiology may be coincidental.
decompositions.testable_consequence: If network geometry were the cause, two-dimensional communities (benthic films) and three-dimensional ones (pelagic) should differ (2/3 vs 3/4).

cases.source: Hatton, McCann, Fryxell et al. 2015 Science 349:aac6284 (abstract; Science News and University of Guelph coverage).

cases.system: Branching transport networks: mammalian arterial trees and tree branches
cases.law_or_distribution: r0^Δ = Σ ri^Δ at each bifurcation (Murray Δ = 3; Leonardo Δ = 2). For a self-similar tree, vessels per level N ∝ r^-Δ.
cases.variable_k: vessel or branch radius r
cases.reported_exponent: Murray 1926: Δ = 3 (laminar, minimum work). Turbulent: Δ = 7/3 (Uylings 1977, via secondary sources). Measured: small arteries 2.7-3.0; cat and chick arteries 2.49-2.59; coronary meta-analysis 2.39 (95% CI 2.24-2.54, I² = 99%); human pulmonary 2.31 ± 0.60. Trees: Leonardo Δ ≈ 2, with 1.8 < Δ < 2.3 for many species (Eloy 2011).
cases.alpha_uncertainty: α = Δ + 1: 3.3-4.0 for arteries, 2.8-3.3 for trees
cases.conversion: Self-similar tree with n daughters and radius ratio n^(-1/Δ) per level: N_k ∝ r_k^-Δ, and levels are equally spaced in ln r. So dN/d ln r ∝ r^-Δ and dN/dr ∝ r^-(Δ+1): α = Δ + 1, d_log = Δ, d_lin = Δ + 1. I use Δ ≈ 2.7 for arteries.
cases.orthopolic_reading: Conserved total: volumetric flow Q, a flux. Every level carries all the blood (mass conservation), so total flow per level, i.e. per log-radius step, is constant. The network is therefore exactly log-orthopolic in flow per vessel q(r) ∝ r^Δ. The content lies in the flow–radius law q ∝ r^Δ, which a cost optimization fixes. For trees the conserved quantity is cross-sectional area (pipe model) or bending stress.

decompositions.resource: Flow per vessel under laminar minimum work (Murray's law)
decompositions.composition: Minimize dissipation (∝ Q^a r^-c) plus blood-volume upkeep (∝ r^2), giving Q ∝ r^((c+2)/a). Poiseuille flow has a = 2 and c = 4, so Δ = (4+2)/2 = 3.
decompositions.independent_motivation: A vessel has two costs: viscous dissipation, and the metabolic upkeep of the blood it contains.
decompositions.theory_agreement: Murray 1926 derives exactly this, and the mechanism agrees.
decompositions.testable_consequence: Δ should fall as Reynolds number rises in larger vessels. The same reading, linear-orthopolic in hydraulic conductance ∝ r^4 (α = 4), is algebraically the same statement and not independent evidence.

decompositions.resource: Flow per vessel under turbulent minimum work
decompositions.composition: Fully rough turbulence: ΔP ∝ Q^2 r^-5, so power ∝ Q^3 r^-5 (a = 3, c = 5) and Δ = (5+2)/3 = 7/3. Blasius smooth turbulence gives (19/4 + 2)/(11/4) = 27/11 ≈ 2.45 (my calculation).
decompositions.independent_motivation: The same two costs as Murray's, with a different friction law.
decompositions.theory_agreement: Uylings 1977 (via secondary sources) agrees. The coronary pooled value 2.39 [2.24, 2.54] includes both values, and pulmonary trees average about 2.1-2.6.
decompositions.testable_consequence: Within one arterial tree, Δ should move from about 2.3-2.45 near the aorta to 3 in arterioles, crossing over at a definite Reynolds number. Microcirculation deviates because of the Fåhræus–Lindqvist effect.

decompositions.resource: Cross-sectional area (Leonardo; pipe model; uniform wind stress)
decompositions.composition: Area ∝ r^2: two transverse dimensions. In the pipe model each leaf is served by a pipe of fixed cross-section, so the number of pipes ∝ r^2.
decompositions.independent_motivation: Mechanically, fracture probability should be uniform under wind load (Eloy 2011); hydraulically, the pipe model.
decompositions.theory_agreement: Eloy 2011 (PRL) derives Δ = 2 from wind-induced stress on self-similar skeletons, and it agrees. The dual linear reading, d_lin = 3, is the bending section modulus ∝ r^3, which is the mechanical quantity in Eloy's argument. So both measure readings have physical names here.
decompositions.testable_consequence: Trees in sheltered understoreys, or with non-self-similar architecture, should deviate. In arteries, WBE predict area preservation (Δ = 2) in large pulsatile vessels and Δ = 3 in small ones, crossing where the Womersley number is about 1.

cases.source: Murray 1926; Uylings 1977 (via Wikipedia 'Murray's law' and arXiv adap-org/9909003); coronary meta-analysis 2024 and pulmonary/cat/chick values via search summary; Eloy 2011 PRL 107:258101 (arXiv 1105.2591).

cases.system: Lévy-flight foraging step lengths (marine predators, insects, birds, mammals)
cases.law_or_distribution: P(l) ∝ l^-μ for move-step lengths, μ ≈ 2 ('inverse-square Lévy walk')
cases.variable_k: move-step length l (m or km), or flight duration
cases.reported_exponent: Viswanathan et al. 1999: μ = 2 is optimal for sparse, revisitable targets, and data on insects, mammals and birds were consistent with it. Edwards et al. 2007: the albatross, deer and bumblebee Lévy claims are not supported (albatross flights are gamma-distributed). Sims et al. 2008: sharks, bony fishes, turtles and penguins show Lévy-like movement near the theoretical optimum (one basking shark has μ ≈ 2.3). Humphries et al. 2010: Lévy movement in low-productivity waters, Brownian in productive ones. Levernier et al. 2020: μ = 2 is not optimal in two or more dimensions.
cases.alpha_uncertainty: About 1.6-2.6 where a Lévy model fits; many datasets fit exponential or gamma instead
cases.conversion: Density; d_log = μ - 1 = 1 (resource ∝ l); d_lin = μ = 2.
cases.orthopolic_reading: Conserved total: the forager's travel budget (distance, or time at constant speed). Units: steps, sized by step length. The walk is log-orthopolic in distance: the total distance covered in steps of each log-length class is the same, so no search scale is favoured. This is a flux or time-budget reading.

decompositions.resource: Travel distance (time) per step ∝ l, equal per log scale
decompositions.composition: Equal effort per log scale: n_log(l) × l = constant
decompositions.independent_motivation: If prey have no characteristic spacing, a forager that cannot know the scale should spread its effort equally over scales.
decompositions.theory_agreement: Viswanathan 1999 derives μ = 2 from a different mechanism: the trade-off between revisiting and long flights for sparse targets that are not destroyed. Levernier et al. 2020 show that optimum holds only in one dimension, so in 2D or 3D no search-efficiency theory gives 2. The resource reading agrees with the exponent but not with any mechanism.
decompositions.testable_consequence: The equal-effort reading predicts μ = 2 regardless of prey density and dimension. Search optimization instead predicts Brownian movement (μ → 3) where prey are abundant, and μ → 1 for destructive foraging. Humphries et al. observed density-dependent switching, which favours optimization over equal effort.

decompositions.resource: Steps allocated in proportion to gaps in the prey field
decompositions.composition: μ_move = μ_gap: the walk reproduces the distribution of distances between prey patches
decompositions.predicted_exponent: μ_move equals the prey-gap exponent measured in the same habitat
decompositions.independent_motivation: Sims et al. report that prey density distributions are also Lévy-like.
decompositions.theory_agreement: Sims et al. 2008 suggest search patterns are adapted to landscape statistics. I could not verify a quantitative test of exponent equality.
decompositions.testable_consequence: Measure prey-gap and movement exponents in the same habitat: the reading predicts equality, with movement exponents shifting between habitats in step with prey statistics.

cases.source: Viswanathan et al. 1999 Nature 401:911 (abstract); Edwards et al. 2007 Nature 449:1044; Sims et al. 2008 Nature 451:1098 (abstract and figure caption); Humphries et al. 2010 Nature 465:1066 (abstract); Levernier, Textor, Bénichou & Voituriez 2020 PRL 124:080601.

catalogue.domain_patterns:
Methods note: WebFetch and curl were blocked by the network, so every 'verified' value comes from abstracts and reliable search summaries. Values marked 'from memory' were not confirmed: Preston's 0.26, the Clauset mammal species-per-genus value, and the dog-breed claim. I did not modify any repo files.

1. The final resource in ecology is usually an energy flux with resource exponent 3/4, plus one extra factor. Kleiber's 3/4 is itself a composition, D/(D+1) with D = 3 (Banavar, Maritan & Rinaldo; WBE), or 2/3 + 1/12 for capacity × velocity (Banavar et al. 2010). The ecological exponents in this set are built from it:
- Damuth density -3/4 = equal energy flux per species.
- Plant self-thinning -3/4 (EBW).
- Home range ≈ 1 = 3/4 (need) + 1/4 (sharing with neighbours).
- Sheldon spectrum: biomass d = 1 = 3/4 (metabolic flux) + 1/4 (trophic dilution, ln TE / ln PPMR = -1/4).
- Tree D^-2: 2 = (3/4)(8/3), a change of coordinate.
- Heartbeats per life ≈ 0: -1/4 + 1/4.

2. Stock vs flux is selected by the 1/4 turnover exponent. By the transport identity B = F/v with log-speed v ∝ M^-1/4, flux-orthopolic and stock-orthopolic readings differ by exactly 1/4. Within one trophic level the flux is flat: Damuth, so biomass per species ∝ M^1/4. Across trophic levels the stock is flat: Sheldon, so energy flux per log class ∝ m^-1/4. The selector can be tested: stock-orthopolity across sizes requires ln TE / ln PPMR = n - 1. A single trophic level should show α = 1.75 rather than 2.

3. Exponent arithmetic follows a few rules:
- Products of deterministic resources add exponents: rate × time for lifetime budgets, need × sharing for home range.
- Changing the size coordinate multiplies exponents: D to M for trees, s to T for avalanches.
- Cost optimizations give ratios: Murray's Q ∝ r^((c+2)/a) gives 3 for laminar flow, 7/3 for rough turbulence and 27/11 for Blasius flow.
- Packing gives dimension counts: Yoda 2/3, Leonardo 2, and Southwood, May & Sugihara's z = (3/2)(1/3)(1/2) = 1/4.
Integer and simple-ratio exponents tend to be capacity readings (packing, cross-sections). Quarter powers tend to be flux readings with a transport distance or turnover.

4. Every density exponent has two readings, d_lin = d_log + 1, and in several biological cases both have physical names:
- Arteries: Murray flow r^3 (log) vs Poiseuille conductance r^4 (linear).
- Tree branches: area r^2 vs bending section modulus r^3.
- Stems: D^1 vs basal area D^2.
The two readings are algebraically one statement, so a mechanism must pick one. In arteries and branches the log reading names the conserved flux. For stems only the linear reading has a name, which is a warning sign (point 7).

5. Count distributions behave like growth with entry. Gene-family sizes always show α ≥ 2, i.e. d_log = 1 + r/(1-r), the repo's prediction that ζ - 1 ≈ entry/growth. Species per genus in plants (α ≈ 1.45 < 2) violates this bound. Yule's growing clade (genus origination rate below speciation rate) is non-stationary, and orthopolity is not approached. The plant and mammal values (1.45 vs about 2.4) need two different Yule variants chosen after the fact. Gene-category scaling forms a ladder of exponents: 0 for the core, 1 additive, 2 combinatorial (toolbox reuse).

6. Critical systems are orthopolic in time. At branching ratio 1, expected activity is conserved (a martingale), so time is equally partitioned over log durations (α_T = 2). The size exponent then follows as 1 + 1/γ. This is the cleanest 'derived' case in which the exponent is not near 1 or 2 in the observed coordinate (3/2), because the natural resource is s^1/2.

7. Measure matters. 'Energetic equivalence' names three different hypotheses: discrete per species (Damuth), per log mass (α = 1.75, rejected for whole spectra), and per linear diameter (trees). Only the log version survives power reparameterization. The tree version holds only for dD, so it depends on the coordinate.

8. Counterexamples and failures:
- Community-level 3/4 (Hatton 2015) has no individual whose metabolism is shared; reading it as a network is numerology.
- The species–area z has no natural resource under random placement (abundance^0.27); only the Southwood–May–Sugihara capacity composition is plausible.
- Taylor's law fits as an exact Tweedie identity, but its exponent is free (b = 1 + cluster-size exponent) unless clusters or zero frequencies are measured.
- For Lévy μ = 2, the equal-effort-per-scale reading matches the exponent but no mechanism. The optimality derivation fails in two or more dimensions, and foragers switch exponents with prey density.
- Rate of living: the composition -1/4 + 1/4 holds allometrically, but the mechanism fails across birds and mammals and after phylogenetic control.

9. Overall pattern: of 32 readings, 7 are derived (Sheldon trophic composition, critical branching in time, Murray laminar and turbulent, Leonardo, toolbox gene-content, and arguably the Kleiber network). They share three ingredients: a conserved flux (energy, flow, expected activity, genes), a measurable per-unit cost law, and an exponent computed before looking at the distribution. Wherever one of these was missing, the reading graded suggestive or numerology. The program is strongest when the resource is a flux whose conservation holds level by level, and weakest for counts of taxa and for cross-community 3/4 coincidences.

checks.system: Whole-organism metabolic rate across species (Kleiber's law)
checks.corrected_alpha_uncertainty: I could not check this against sources. The WebSearch budget for this turn was used up before my first query, and fetch/curl to arxiv.org and doi.org were refused by the proxy. The values match what I remember: Kleiber 0.74; Savage et al. 2004, 0.737 for BMR and 0.749 for FMR; White & Seymour 2003, 0.686 uncorrected across 619 species and about 0.675 after temperature correction. The catalogue may have swapped which analysis gave 0.686. Studies range from 0.67 to 0.76, and the convex curvature (Kolokotrones 2010) means no single exponent holds. a is a scaling exponent, not a density exponent.
checks.algebra_note: Banavar et al. 1999: network volume C ∝ L^(D+1), with M ∝ C and B ∝ sites ∝ L^D, so B ∝ M^(D/(D+1)). This is correct. Tissue per site ∝ M^(1/(D+1)) = M^(1/4), also correct. Banavar et al. 2010: M^(2/3) × M^(1/12) = M^(3/4), correct. Writing d = 0.75 against a = 0.74 is cosmetic. A scaling law has no log/linear distinction, so the measure is discrete (per supply unit).
checks.best_reading:
The count of size-invariant terminal supply sites fed by a minimum-cost space-filling network (discrete measure; a flux reading): B ∝ sites ∝ M^(D/(D+1)) with D = 3. Three things weaken it:
- The 2D version of this reading predicts 2/3, the same as Rubner's surface law, so the proposed 2D test cannot tell the two apart.
- The convex curvature fits an ADDITIVE cost better, such as DEB-style maintenance B = aM^(2/3) + bM, whose local slope rises from 2/3 toward 1. A product composition of power laws cannot produce curvature.
- The capacity × velocity decomposition (velocity ∝ M^(1/12)) is numerology. In Banavar et al. 2010, 1/12 is the maximum allowed exponent, chosen to recover 3/4, and it was not measured independently.
checks.numerology_risk:
High. Two simple readings each fit a respectable dataset within its own error: 3/4 (network) fits Savage et al. and Kleiber, and 2/3 (surface) fits White & Seymour. The exponent therefore depends on how the data were processed (temperature, digestive state, phylogeny, binning). The 3/4 motivation is partly reverse-engineered, because the WBE assumptions (area-preserving, space-filling, invariant terminal units) were built to give 3/4. Banavar's argument is more general. Chance baseline, computed here: on [0.5, 3], fractions p/q with q ≤ 4 cover about 36% of the line at ±0.03 and 57% at ±0.05. Counterexamples outside mammals:
- DeLong et al. 2010: prokaryotes about 1.96, protists about 1.06.
- Reich et al. 2006: near-isometric plant respiration.
- Glazier 2005: intraspecific exponents 0.5-1.
checks.source: Catalogue sources (Kleiber 1932; Savage et al. 2004 Funct Ecol 18:257; White & Seymour 2003 PNAS 100:4046; Kolokotrones et al. 2010 Nature 464:753; Banavar, Maritan & Rinaldo 1999 Nature 399:130; Banavar et al. 2010 PNAS 107:15816), checked against my recollection only. Further sources I cite: Kooijman DEB theory; Glazier 2005 Biol Rev 80:611; DeLong et al. 2010 PNAS 107:12941; Reich et al. 2006 Nature 439:457. Web verification was impossible in this run.

checks.system: Resting heart rate and maximum lifespan across mammals (heartbeats per lifetime)
checks.corrected_alpha_uncertainty: Not checked against sources (web unavailable). From memory: heart rate is about -0.25 (Stahl 1967; Holt et al. 1968). Stahl's allometric equations WERE published (J Appl Physiol 22:453, 1967, f_H ≈ 241 M^-0.25 min^-1 with M in kg). The catalogue's 'never published' can only refer to his underlying data. The mammal lifespan exponent is usually 0.15-0.20, not 0.25, so heartbeats per life fall weakly with mass, about M^-0.05 to M^-0.10. Levine's 7.3 ± 5.6 × 10^8 beats per lifetime (CV about 77%) matches my memory.
checks.algebra_note: The composition (B/M) × T × M ∝ M^(-1/4+1/4+1) = M^1 is correct. The d fields (= 1) describe lifetime energy per individual, a different quantity from the reported a = -0.25 (heart rate), so the row mixes two variables. Both candidate invariants (energy per gram, beats per life) are fixed by the same two allometries, so the exponents cannot separate them. With a measured lifespan exponent of 0.15-0.20, both invariants scale as about M^-0.05 to M^-0.10 rather than M^0.
checks.best_reading:
Physiological-time invariance, not a budget being spent. Every biological duration scales with one clock ∝ M^(1/4), so the number of cardiac cycles per life is a dimensionless count, roughly size-invariant (discrete measure, d = 0). The rate-of-living reading (a fixed lifetime energy per gram) is contradicted on mechanism:
- Speakman 2005: after controlling for size and phylogeny, species with higher metabolic rates spend more lifetime energy per gram.
- Birds, bats and humans live far longer than their heart rates predict.
checks.numerology_risk: High. An exponent of 0 is the default for any ratio of two quantities that share an allometry, so matching it carries little information. The 'constant' holds only within an order of magnitude. The lifespan exponent (0.15-0.25) depends on clade and on phylogenetic control. No theory derives lifespan ∝ M^(1/4).
checks.source: Levine 1997 J Am Coll Cardiol 30:1104; Stahl 1967 J Appl Physiol 22:453; Holt, Rhode & Kines 1968; Speakman 2005 J Exp Biol 208:1717; Furness & Speakman 2008 Age 30:75 (number of species not checked); AnAge (de Magalhães). All from memory; web unavailable.

checks.system: Population density vs body mass (Damuth's rule) and plant self-thinning
checks.corrected_alpha_uncertainty: Not checked against sources (web unavailable). Damuth 1981 (307 species of mammalian primary consumers, slope -0.75) matches my memory. Carbone & Gittleman 2002 (about 90 kg of carnivore per 10,000 kg of prey; carnivore number per unit prey biomass ∝ M^-1) also matches. The -0.75 for prey productivity is not confirmed. Local community slopes are often much shallower than global ones (White et al. 2007 TREE 22:323). Sign convention: the field is a slope; the positive orthopolic d is 0.75.
checks.algebra_note: Discrete orthopolity, D ∝ 1/q̄ with q̄ ∝ M^0.75, gives d = 0.75: correct. Yoda's w ∝ N^-3/2 inverts to N ∝ w^-2/3: correct. EBW's N ∝ M^-3/4 inverts to w ∝ N^-4/3: correct. The one-dimensional packing test is also correct: N ∝ L^-1 and M ∝ L^3 give N ∝ M^-1/3, i.e. w ∝ N^-3. In a strip the flux reading still predicts -3/4, so this test separates flux from capacity.
checks.best_reading: Energetic equivalence: equal metabolic energy flux per species (discrete measure), D × M^(3/4) = constant. The animal case passes a genuinely independent check: Damuth's slope should equal minus the Kleiber exponent. Why each species takes an equal share is not derived; that is the orthopolity hypothesis itself. For plants, the Yoda capacity reading (2/3) and the EBW flux reading (3/4) each fit some stands, so the plant half is only suggestive.
checks.numerology_risk: Moderate. The ecological stock/flux readings differ by exactly 1/4 (turnover ∝ M^-1/4), and capacity and flux differ by 1/12. Carbone & Gittleman's carnivores fit a STOCK reading (equal carnivore biomass per unit prey biomass, M^-1) or a FLUX reading (M^-3/4 per unit prey productivity), depending on how they are normalized, and prey productivity was not measured independently. Kleiber's own spread (0.67-0.76) carries straight into the prediction. The global slope is a cross-community maximum-density relation, and local slopes do not follow it.
checks.source: Damuth 1981 Nature 290:699; Carbone & Gittleman 2002 Science 295:2273; Enquist, Brown & West 1998 Nature 395:163; Yoda et al. 1963; White, Ernest, Kerkhoff & Enquist 2007 TREE 22:323; Isaac, Storch & Carbone 2013 Glob Ecol Biogeogr. From memory; web unavailable.

checks.system: Pelagic size spectrum, bacteria to whales (Sheldon spectrum)
checks.corrected_alpha_uncertainty:
Confirmed from repo files read in this task:
- results/independent.json: GLOSSAQUA primary NBSS median slope -1.015 (study-block slope interval about [-1.100, -0.990]).
- docs/evidence.md: upper-ocean biomass-per-log-mass slope -0.0392 (90% interval [-0.058, -0.026]), i.e. abundance-per-log slope -1.039, α ≈ 2.04.
The external values (Sheldon 1972; Hatton 2021 at about 1 Gt per decade; Andersen & Beyer's 2.05; Platt & Denman's 1.22) match my memory but were not re-fetched. The repo also shows that individual spectra are NOT flat: only 7.9% (F = 1.25) and 24% (F = 2) of the 1,300 slopes fall within tolerance (verdict 'not supported'). With all method labels pooled, the median is -1.371. So flatness is an aggregate property, not a per-system one.
checks.algebra_note: NBSS and abundance per log mass are both m·n(m), so they share one slope, and α = 1 - slope is correct. B = F/v gives biomass per log mass ∝ m^((1-n) + ln TE/ln PPMR) and α = 1 + n - ln TE/ln PPMR. I checked: n = 3/4 and TE = 0.1 give α = 2.00 for PPMR = 10^4, 2.08 for PPMR = 10^3, and 2.25 for PPMR = 10^2.
