Andersen & Beyer's λ = 2 + q - n = 2.05 (q = 0.8) is a separate mechanism (encounter-rate self-consistency) that gives the same value.
checks.best_reading: Biomass stock is log-orthopolic (d = 1). It is an energy flux per log mass divided by the log-growth speed, d = 1 = 3/4 (metabolic turnover) + 1/4 (trophic dilution, ln TE / ln PPMR = -1/4); log measure. Brown & Gillooly 2003 and Jennings & Mackinson 2003 derive exactly this. Caveat: the quantitative match needs PPMR ≈ 10^4 at TE = 0.1. The PPMRs usually measured (10^2-10^3.5) predict α ≈ 2.1-2.25, which is Platt & Denman's 2.22, so the observed 2.04 sits at the low edge of the prediction band. The within-one-trophic-level corollary (α = 1.75) is supported by phytoplankton maximum densities ∝ M^-3/4 (Belgrano et al. 2002; Li 2002; from memory).
checks.numerology_risk: Low to moderate. The resource (biomass) is fixed by definition, which makes this the cleanest case. Two distinct published mechanisms (trophic transfer; encounter-rate q - n) both give about 2, and both are flux-based, so the stock-as-flux/residence reading survives either way. The risk lies in the inputs: PPMR = 10^4 is a convenient round choice, not a measured mean.
checks.source: Repo results/independent.json (glossaqua.subsets.primary_NBSS) and docs/evidence.md (read in this task). Sheldon, Prakash & Sutcliffe 1972 L&O 17:327; Hatton et al. 2021 Sci Adv 7:eabh3732; Brown & Gillooly 2003 PNAS 100:1467; Jennings & Mackinson 2003 Ecol Lett 6:971; Andersen & Beyer 2006 Am Nat 168:54; Platt & Denman 1978. The non-repo items are from memory.

checks.system: Tree stem-diameter distributions in forest stands
checks.corrected_alpha_uncertainty: Not checked against sources (web unavailable). From memory: Enquist & Niklas 2001 give about -2; Coomes et al. 2003 find power laws only for small stems, with exponents ≠ 2 that vary through time; Muller-Landau et al. 2006 find metabolic predictions inconsistent with 14 tropical plots. α ≈ 1.5-2.5 for small and medium stems; large stems fall off exponentially or with a hump. The exponent is not stable enough to select a resource.
checks.algebra_note: With M ∝ D^(8/3), dN/dM ∝ M^-11/8 (ζ_M = 3/8): correct. B ∝ M^(3/4) ∝ D^2: correct. dN/dh ∝ h^-5/2 for h ∝ D^(2/3): correct. Self-similar branching per level gives density ∝ r^-(Δ+1) = r^-3: correct. One reading was omitted: log-orthopolic in WBE crown area (∝ D^(4/3)) predicts α = 7/3, which also lies inside the empirical band.
checks.best_reading: Stand metabolic (xylem) flux ∝ D^2, equal per LINEAR diameter interval (Enquist & Niklas; WEB 2009 'energy equivalence'). The linear measure is what makes it fit: per log mass the same forest carries flux ∝ M^(3/8), so the reading fails under power reparameterization, which is the coordinate-selection problem concept.md §2 warns about. The defensible mechanism is demographic transport: stems flowing through D, with f(D) = F(D)/g(D) set by growth and mortality (Muller-Landau et al.; Kohyama). That reading is not orthopolic, because the stem flux declines with mortality.
checks.source: Enquist & Niklas 2001 Nature 410:655; West, Enquist & Brown 2009 PNAS 106:7040; Coomes et al. 2003 Ecol Lett 6:980; Muller-Landau et al. 2006 Ecol Lett 9:575, 9:589; Kohyama 1991. From memory; web unavailable.

checks.system: Species-area relationship S = cA^z
checks.corrected_alpha_uncertainty: z ≈ 0.25-0.27 (Preston 1962's canonical 0.262 matches my memory; Drakare et al. 2006's means were not re-checked; web unavailable). The density field is internally inconsistent. The catalogue lists alpha = 0.27 but d_log = 0.27 and d_lin = 1.27, which imply α_SAD = 1 + z = 1.27 under its own random-placement conversion. That conversion needs a Pareto species-abundance tail with ζ = z ≈ 0.27 < 1, which is top-heavy with infinite mean, and the entry itself rejects this. Real SADs (log-series, lognormal) have no density exponent to report.
checks.algebra_note:
For random placement with P(N_i ≥ n) ∝ n^-ζ and 0 < ζ < 1, S ∝ A^ζ is correct, and I verified it. The catalogue's entry is still inconsistent in three ways:
(i) The alpha field (0.27) contradicts the d fields (0.27 and 1.27), which need α = 1.27.
(ii) The reported d values rest on a conversion the entry rejects (no SAD has ζ ≈ 0.27).
(iii) The established derivation of z ≈ 1/4 (Preston 1962; May 1975) uses random sampling from a CANONICAL LOGNORMAL SAD, not a Pareto tail, so no d_log/d_lin pair follows from z.
checks.best_reading: Niche-slot capacity (Southwood, May & Sugihara 2006, discrete measure): species ∝ (extent of niche space)^D, with the size-axis extent set by the largest body the area supports. Its parts are independently measured allometries, but I could not verify the chain (3/2)(1/3)(1/2). The Preston-May sampling theory is the established derivation, and it is not orthopolic. Its condition is a 'canonical' crest in individuals per octave at the most abundant species, a boundary condition rather than equality.
checks.numerology_risk: High. z ≈ 1/4 is close to generic. May 1975 showed that lognormal SADs give z ≈ 0.2-0.3 over a wide range of parameters. Harte's self-similarity sets z by a free split probability. Neutral theory gives a triphasic, scale-dependent z. So several unrelated readings produce the same value, and z carries little information about any resource. z also varies with sampling design (nested vs island) and taxon.
checks.source: Preston 1962 Ecology 43:185, 43:410; May 1975 (in Cody & Diamond, Ecology and Evolution of Communities); Drakare, Lennon & Hillebrand 2006 Ecol Lett 9:215; Southwood, May & Sugihara 2006 PNAS 103:6931; Harte, Kinzig & Green 1999 Science 284:334; Irie & Tokita 2006. From memory; web unavailable.

checks.system: Species per genus (Willis & Yule plant families; mammals)
checks.corrected_alpha_uncertainty: Not checked against sources (web unavailable). Plants: α = 1 + 1/ρ = 1.41 for ρ = 2.457 (algebra checked); about 1.5 with finite clade age. Mammals: α = 2.40 ± 0.20 with x_min = 4 matches my recollection of the Clauset, Shalizi & Newman 2009 table, and the repo's zeta-compilation notes that the dataset (mammal species per genus) is in that paper. The two values sit on opposite sides of 2, and genus limits depend on taxonomic practice (lumping vs splitting).
checks.algebra_note: Yule: genus age density ∝ e^(-gt) and size ∝ e^(st) give P(n) ∝ n^-(1+g/s), i.e. α = 1 + g/s = 1 + 1/ρ: correct. Species per ln n ∝ n^(1-g/s), so d_log = g/s: correct. The Simon variant gives α = 2 + 1/m, so α = 2.4 needs m = 2.5: correct.
checks.best_reading: No natural resource reading. The Yule rate-ratio reading (d_log = g/s, with g genus origination and s speciation) is kinetic, not a resource. It holds only in a growing, non-stationary clade, and g/s is fitted from α. Plants (α < 2, top-heavy) and mammals (α > 2) need different model variants, each chosen after seeing α. 'Species' is a count of distinct taxa, not a quantity anything holds.
checks.numerology_risk: Very high. The single free parameter (g/s, or m) is fitted from the exponent. The exponent also reflects taxonomic convention. No independent estimate of g/s from dated phylogenies was presented.
checks.source: Willis & Yule 1922 Nature; Yule 1925 Phil Trans B 213:21; Simon 1955; Clauset, Shalizi & Newman 2009 SIAM Rev 51:661 (mammal value as recalled); repo docs/zeta-compilation.md (read in this task).

checks.system: Paralogous gene-family sizes in complete genomes
checks.corrected_alpha_uncertainty: Not checked against sources (web unavailable). The range is about 2-4 (Huynen & van Nimwegen 1998), flatter in larger genomes, and depends on the clustering threshold that defines a family. The entry contradicts itself: it cites Karev et al.'s BDIM asymptotic power of 1.9 (< 2) and then states that 'every reported α is at least 2'.
checks.algebra_note: Simon/Qian duplication-innovation model: ζ = 1/(1-r), α = 1 + 1/(1-r). r = 1/3 gives 2.5 and r = 2/3 gives 4: correct. d_log = 1 + r/(1-r): correct. The bound α ≥ 2 belongs to this model only. Birth-death-innovation models with gene loss (Karev et al. 2002) allow any α > 1, including α < 2.
checks.best_reading: Genes as an additive stock, log measure. Proportional duplication plus founding of new families gives α = 1 + 1/(1-r), which is log-orthopolic only in the limit r → 0 (the repo's 'ζ - 1 ≈ entry/growth'). Its content depends on measuring r independently from ORFan/singleton founding rates. Huynen & van Nimwegen argue that family-level (coherent) multiplicative fluctuations are needed, which is a Gibrat-type mechanism with no fixed exponent.
checks.numerology_risk: Moderate to high. r is solved from α. The α ≥ 2 'prediction' depends on the model and fails once deletion is included. The flattening with genome size has other explanations (more duplication in large genomes; HGT). Family definitions shift α.
checks.source: Huynen & van Nimwegen 1998 Mol Biol Evol 15:583; Qian, Luscombe & Gerstein 2001 J Mol Biol 313:673; Karev et al. 2002 BMC Evol Biol 2:18; Durrett & Schweinsberg 2005 (duplication model); repo docs/zeta-compilation.md. From memory; web unavailable.

checks.system: Functional gene-category content vs genome size in prokaryotes
checks.corrected_alpha_uncertainty: Not checked against sources (web unavailable). From memory: transcription regulators about 1.8-1.9 (van Nimwegen 2003); metabolism about 1; core processes (replication, translation, cell cycle) < 1. The quoted 99% interval of 1.72-1.95 excludes exactly 2.
checks.algebra_note: Pairs ∝ N^2 is correct. Toolbox: dN/dT ∝ 1/N gives T ∝ N^2, and regulators ∝ T ∝ N^2: correct. The share of genes per regulator, ∝ N^(1-1.85) = N^-0.85, is consistent.
checks.best_reading: The Maslov et al. 2009 toolbox: each acquired pathway needs fewer new enzymes as the enzyme toolbox grows (∝ 1/N), so pathways, and the regulators per pathway, scale as N^2 (d = 1 for genes + 1 for reuse; discrete measure). The motivation came first, and the model has an independent test (E. coli pathway branch lengths). The observed 1.72-1.95 lies just below the asymptote. Finite-size or topology corrections (Pang & Maslov 2011) might close the gap; I could not verify that. Because the exponent does not match within the stated error, I grade it below 'derived'.
checks.numerology_risk: Moderate. Pair counting predicts the same 2 (van Nimwegen judged it mechanistically implausible). van Nimwegen's own kinetic reading, exponent = ratio of category-specific to genome-wide gene gain/loss rates (Huxley allometry, like Yule's g/s), fits any value. The integer ladder 0/1/2 is attractive, but the observed core-process exponents are not 0.
checks.source: van Nimwegen 2003 Trends Genet 19:479; Molina & van Nimwegen 2008 Biol Direct; Maslov, Krishna, Pang & Sneppen 2009 PNAS 106:9743; Pang & Maslov 2011 PLoS Comput Biol; Grilli et al. 2012 NAR. From memory; web unavailable.

checks.system: Neuronal avalanches (cortical slices and cultures)
checks.corrected_alpha_uncertainty: Not checked against sources (web unavailable). LFP avalanches in slices: size 3/2 and duration about 2, branching ratio about 1 (Beggs & Plenz 2003), matching my memory. The catalogue misreads Friedman et al. 2012 as supporting MEAN-FIELD branching. As I recall, their spike-based data gave size exponents near 1.7 and a shape-collapse exponent 1/σνz ≈ 1.3, not 2. Fontenele et al. 2019 report about 1.28 across cortical states. Exponents also shift with time bin and subsampling (Priesemann), and in vivo dynamics look slightly subcritical (Wilting & Priesemann).
checks.algebra_note: Crackling relation: α_s = 1 + (α_T - 1)/γ = 3/2 for α_T = γ = 2, correct; the log-orthopolic resource in s is s^(1/2) ∝ T, also correct. One point was missed. The martingale states equivalently that total activations per unit DURATION interval are constant, n(T)·s̄(T) ∝ T^-α_T·T^γ = const, a linear-orthopolic reading in activations. It holds only if α_T = γ. Log-orthopolic in time needs only α_T = 2. In mean-field theory both hold. With γ ≈ 1.3 at most one can, which gives a discriminating test.
checks.best_reading: Conserved expected activity in a critical branching process (a martingale), log measure. Time is equally partitioned over log-duration classes (α_T = 2), or equivalently activations are linear-orthopolic across duration classes. The size exponent 3/2 follows as 1 + 1/γ. Critical Galton-Watson theory gives this exactly, and it fits LFP data from slices. It does not fit the spike data, whose γ ≈ 1.3 is non-mean-field.
checks.numerology_risk: Low for the mean-field case, because the exponents were predicted before the data. But the same (3/2, 2) pair also comes from non-critical mechanisms: neutral dynamics (Martinello et al. 2017 PRX) and thresholded correlated noise (Touboul & Destexhe). The pair therefore supports the resource reading without proving criticality. Avalanche size counts active sites, not a conserved stock.
checks.source: Beggs & Plenz 2003 J Neurosci 23:11167; Friedman et al. 2012 PRL 108:208102; Fontenele et al. 2019 PRL 122:208101; Martinello et al. 2017 PRX 7:041071; Touboul & Destexhe 2010 PLoS One; Priesemann et al. 2014; Harris 1963. From memory; web unavailable.

checks.system: Taylor's power law of fluctuation scaling
checks.corrected_alpha_uncertainty: Not checked against sources (web unavailable). b usually lies between 1 and 2. Taylor's original examples and later moth and aphid surveys include values below 1 and up to about 3 (from memory). b varies by species and by spatial vs temporal design, so 1.5 is a representative value, not a law.
checks.algebra_note: Tweedie compound Poisson-gamma with 1 < p < 2: λ = μ^(2-p)/(φ(2-p)), mean cluster = φ(2-p)μ^(p-1), and λ × cluster = μ. Correct. P0 = exp(-λ), so -ln P0 ∝ μ^(2-b): correct. d = b - 1 is consistent.
checks.best_reading: Mean abundance μ is shared equally among a Poisson number λ ∝ μ^(2-b) of independent clusters, each holding ∝ μ^(b-1) individuals (discrete measure). This is an exact distributional identity, not a resource law: it holds for any b in (1, 2). It cannot represent b < 1 or b > 2, both of which are reported. Its only content is the zero-frequency prediction.
checks.numerology_risk: High. The cluster exponent is defined as b - 1, so any b in (1, 2) 'fits'. Several unrelated mechanisms give TL with b in [1, 2]: random sampling of skewed distributions (Cohen & Xu 2015), species interactions (Kilpatrick & Ives 2003), reproductive correlation (Ballantyne & Kerkhoff), and the general independent-vs-driven bound of fluctuation scaling (Eisler, Bartos & Kertész 2008).
checks.source: Taylor 1961 Nature 189:732; Kilpatrick & Ives 2003 Nature 422:65; Cohen & Xu 2015 PNAS 112:7749; Kendal 2002; Eisler, Bartos & Kertész 2008 Adv Phys 57:89. From memory; web unavailable.

checks.system: Home-range area vs body mass
checks.corrected_alpha_uncertainty: Not checked against sources (web unavailable). Mammal home range ∝ M^1.0-1.1 matches my memory (Lindstedt et al. 1986; Kelt & Van Vuren 2001; Jetz et al. 2004). Carnivores are steeper. Across vertebrates the exponent varies with guild, locomotion and the dimension of foraging (Tamburello et al. 2015).
checks.algebra_note: H = overlap / D is an identity. With D ∝ M^-3/4, overlap ∝ H·D ∝ M^(1.03-0.75) = M^0.28. The arithmetic is correct, but the 'sharing' exponent is defined as the residual, so the composition 3/4 + 1/4 is fitted unless overlap is measured directly.
checks.best_reading:
Two simple readings fit equally well:
(a) Flux plus sharing (Jetz et al. 2004): metabolic need ∝ M^(3/4) per individual, divided by an exclusivity that falls as M^~1/4.
(b) A stock reading: land area shared equally per gram of animal (H ∝ M^1). Reading (b) needs no fitted term.
Only direct GPS-based overlap measurements, compared with day-range allometry (∝ M^~1/4), could separate them. Flux plus sharing is the better motivated mechanism, but at present it is not identified.
checks.numerology_risk: High. The ecological stock/flux readings always differ by exactly 1/4, because turnover ∝ M^-1/4. A slope near 1 is therefore matched by 'biomass stock' and by 'metabolic flux + 1/4' alike. The sharing exponent was inferred from the gap between the two slopes rather than measured.
checks.source: Jetz, Carbone, Fulford & Brown 2004 Science 306:266; Lindstedt, Miller & Buskirk 1986 J Mammal; Kelt & Van Vuren 2001 Am Nat 157:637; Tamburello, Côté & Dulvy 2015 Am Nat; Garland 1983 (day range). From memory; web unavailable.

checks.system: Predator vs prey biomass, and production vs biomass, across ecosystems (Hatton et al. 2015)
checks.corrected_alpha_uncertainty: Not checked against sources (web unavailable). From memory: Hatton et al. 2015 report predator ∝ prey^~0.75 and production ∝ biomass^~0.75 across about 2,000+ communities in many biomes. I did not retrieve per-biome intervals. Hatton et al. 2019 (PNAS) extend the 3/4 to growth across eukaryotes.
checks.algebra_note: Under constant transfer efficiency and constant predator turnover, k_pred = k_prod. Production per unit prey biomass ∝ B^-1/4 follows. Consistent.
checks.best_reading: Predator biomass is discretely orthopolic in prey PRODUCTION (a flux): a constant predator stock per unit prey production across ecosystems. This explains one 3/4 by the other, and the motivation (predators live on production) came first. The value 3/4 itself (production ∝ biomass^0.75 at community level, a density-dependence law with no single organism) has no resource reading. The network analogy is numerology.
checks.numerology_risk: Moderate for the link: both exponents come from the same ecosystems, and there is no independent production measurement. Very high for any explanation of the value 3/4, which matches Kleiber with no shared network. Social-insect colonies give a similar 3/4 without a network (Hou et al. 2010; Waters et al. 2010). This case is a counterexample to treating 3/4 as a signature of network geometry.
checks.source: Hatton, McCann, Fryxell et al. 2015 Science 349:aac6284; Hatton et al. 2019 PNAS 116:21616; Hou et al. 2010 PNAS 107:3634. From memory; web unavailable.

checks.system: Branching transport networks: arterial trees (Murray) and tree branches (Leonardo)
checks.corrected_alpha_uncertainty: Not checked against sources (web unavailable). Measured Δ: about 3 in small vessels, 2.3-2.6 in large and coronary arteries, and 1.8-2.3 in tree branches (Eloy 2011, as I recall). α = Δ + 1 is therefore 3.3-4 for arteries and 2.8-3.3 for trees. Using a single 3.7 for arteries hides a systematic crossover, not noise. I could not check the coronary meta-analysis value (2.39) or the pulmonary value.
checks.algebra_note:
I checked each step:
- Q ∝ r^((c+2)/a) from minimizing dissipation plus upkeep.
- Poiseuille (a = 2, c = 4) gives 3.
- Rough turbulence (a = 3, c = 5) gives 7/3.
- Blasius (a = 11/4, c = 19/4) gives 27/11 ≈ 2.45.
- A self-similar tree has N_k ∝ r_k^-Δ, evenly spaced in ln r, so α = Δ + 1.
Log-orthopolity in flow is an IDENTITY: mass conservation makes every generation carry the whole flow. All the content lies in the per-vessel law q ∝ r^Δ.
checks.best_reading: Volumetric flow per vessel, log measure. Each generation carries the full flow, and q ∝ r^3 follows from laminar minimum work (Murray), which fits small vessels where Δ ≈ 3. For coronary arteries (Δ ≈ 2.3-2.45), crediting the turbulent 7/3 is unjustified: coronary flow is laminar (Re of order 10^2). Huo & Kassab 2012 derive Q ∝ D^(7/3) for coronary trees from a laminar volume-length model (from memory), a different mechanism giving the same number. For tree branches, three derivations (pipe model, elastic similarity, Eloy's wind stress) all give Δ = 2 while naming different resources.
checks.numerology_risk: Low for laminar Δ = 3, which was derived in 1926 before the measurements. High for the 2.3-2.5 regime, where the turbulent and Huo-Kassab readings fit equally and turbulence is physically absent. For trees the exponent is robust but cannot select a resource (hydraulic pipes, cross-section or section modulus). Because the orthopolity here holds by construction, the case cannot test the program.
checks.source: Murray 1926 PNAS 12:207; Uylings 1977 Bull Math Biol 39:509; Sherman 1981 J Gen Physiol 78:431; LaBarbera 1990 Science 249:992; Huo & Kassab 2012 J R Soc Interface 9:190; Eloy 2011 PRL 107:258101; West, Brown & Enquist 1997 Science 276:122. From memory; web unavailable.

checks.system: Lévy-flight foraging step lengths
checks.corrected_alpha_uncertainty: Not checked against sources (web unavailable). Where a Lévy model is preferred, μ ≈ 1.6-2.6 (Sims et al. 2008; Humphries et al. 2010). Many datasets prefer exponential, gamma or composite Brownian models (Edwards et al. 2007). Pyke 2015 argues the Lévy foraging hypothesis should be abandoned.
checks.algebra_note: d_log = μ - 1 = 1: total distance per log length class, l·l^-2·l, is constant. d_lin = 2. Both correct.
checks.best_reading: Travel effort (distance or time) spread equally over log step-length classes (log measure): no search scale is favoured. The catalogue missed a theory that gives exactly this reading. Guinard & Korman 2021 (Sci Adv, from memory) show that intermittent inverse-square walks are near-optimal at once for targets of ALL sizes in 2D, i.e. equal effort per scale under scale ignorance. This rescues μ = 2 after Levernier et al. 2020 showed it is not optimal for a fixed target size in d ≥ 2. The data are weak: Lévy fits are contested, and foragers switch to Brownian movement where prey are dense (Humphries et al. 2010).
checks.numerology_risk: Moderate to high. Composite correlated random walks (mixtures of exponentials; Benhamou 2007) mimic μ ≈ 2 over 1-2 decades. Fits are sensitive to the method (Edwards et al. 2007). Density-dependent switching contradicts universal scale-free effort, which is the reading's own prediction.
checks.source: Viswanathan et al. 1999 Nature 401:911; Edwards et al. 2007 Nature 449:1044; Sims et al. 2008 Nature 451:1098; Humphries et al. 2010 Nature 465:1066; Levernier et al. 2020 PRL 124:080601; Guinard & Korman 2021 Sci Adv 7:eabe8211; Benhamou 2007 Ecology 88:1962; Pyke 2015 Methods Ecol Evol 6:1. From memory; web unavailable.

verification.missing_cases:
Methods note: web verification was impossible in this run. The per-turn WebSearch budget was used up before my first query, and fetch/curl to arxiv.org and doi.org were refused by the proxy. All external values above are checked against my recollection only. Only the Sheldon/GLOSSAQUA numbers were confirmed, from repo files.

A. Counterexamples and hard cases the catalogue omits:

(1) Metabolic scaling across the tree of life.
- DeLong et al. 2010 PNAS 107:12941: prokaryotes about 1.96 (super-linear), protists about 1.06, metazoans about 0.79. A supply-network or capacity reading cannot exceed 1.
- Reich et al. 2006 Nature 439:457: whole-plant respiration is near-isometric.
- Glazier 2005 Biol Rev 80:611: intraspecific exponents range from 0.5 to 1, and pelagic animals sit near 1.

(2) Curvature.
- Mammal BMR is convex in log-log (Kolokotrones 2010).
- An ADDITIVE cost (DEB: surface plus volume, B = aM^(2/3) + bM) predicts this. Products of power laws, the program's composition rule, cannot.
- The program needs a rule for sums of resources, which give crossovers rather than power laws.

(3) A 3/4 exponent with no network.
- Social-insect colonies (Hou et al. 2010 PNAS 107:3634; Waters et al. 2010 Am Nat) and Hatton 2015's community production both show 3/4.
- So 3/4 is not a signature of network geometry.

(4) Non-power-law cases.
- Hump-shaped maximum speed vs mass (Hirt et al. 2017 Nat Ecol Evol 1:1116).
- Species-abundance distributions (log-series, lognormal).
- Species body-size distributions (Clauset & Erwin 2008 Science 321:399).

(5) Degree is not a resource.
- Biological network degree distributions (metabolic, protein interaction; Jeong et al. 2000 Nature 407:651, α ≈ 2.2) are often cited as power laws.
- Broido & Clauset 2019 Nat Commun 10:1017 found strongly scale-free networks are rare.

(6) Contested fossil-record laws.
- Extinction-size P(s) ∝ s^-2 and genus lifetimes ∝ t^-2 (Solé et al. 1997; Newman & Sibani 1999) would read as log-orthopolic in time, like avalanches.
- Kirchner & Weil 1998 Nature 395:337 contested them.

(7) Epidemic sizes.
- Rhodes & Anderson 1996 Nature 381:600 (measles, Faroe Islands): α ≈ 1.28.
- No resource with d_log ≈ 0.28 suggests itself.

(8) Skeletal mass.
- Prange et al. 1979 Am Nat: skeletal mass ∝ M^1.08-1.09.
- Galilean stress similarity predicts 4/3, so a mechanical-resource reading made in advance fails. This is useful as an honest falsification.

(9) Brain-body allometry.
- About 2/3-3/4 across mammals but about 0.2-0.4 within orders.
- The exponent depends on the clade, so no single resource fits.

(10) Damuth's rule at local scale.
- Local size-density slopes are shallow or absent (White et al. 2007 TREE 22:323).

B. Cases that fit the program and should be added (motivation prior to the data):

(1) Seed size-number trade-off.
- Smith & Fretwell 1974; Henery & Westoby 2001 Oikos: seeds per unit reproductive biomass ∝ seed mass^-1.
- This is discrete orthopolity of reproductive allocation with d = 1.
- The leaf size-number trade-off has the same form (Kleiman & Aarssen 2007 J Ecol: leafing intensity ∝ leaf mass^-1).

(2) Fractal habitat and arthropod body lengths.
- Morse, Lawton, Dodson & Williamson 1985 Nature 314:731.
- Vegetation fractal dimension (about 1.5) × metabolic need predicted the abundance-length relation before the comparison: an explicit published 'final resource' combining habitat-slot capacity with an energy flux.

(3) Cortical white vs gray matter.
- Zhang & Sejnowski 2000 PNAS 97:5621: W ∝ G^(4/3), from wiring minimization.
- This is the same D/(D+1) family as Banavar's network.

(4) Gene-expression Zipf.
- Furusawa & Kaneko 2003 PRL 90:088102: rank exponent about -1, so α ≈ 2, log-orthopolic in mRNA copies.

(5) Further allometries and patterns.
- Growth ∝ M^0.75 across eukaryotes (Hatton et al. 2019 PNAS 116:21616).
- May's species-length relation, S ∝ L^-2 above about 1 cm.
- Animal group-size distributions, P(n) ∝ n^-1 e^(-n/n_p) (Bonabeau et al. 1999 PNAS 96:4472; Niwa 2003). Here d_log = 0: groups are flat per log size and no resource varies.

C. General findings for the program:

(i) Built-in ecological ambiguity.
- Turnover ∝ M^-1/4, so every ecological exponent has a STOCK reading and a FLUX reading that differ by exactly 1/4.
- Capacity (2/3) and flux (3/4) differ by 1/12.
- Damuth's carnivores (M^-1 per prey biomass vs M^-3/4 per prey productivity) and home range (M^1 as area per gram, or 3/4 + 1/4) are each matched by both.

(ii) Chance baseline (computed here).
- Fractions p/q with q ≤ 4 cover about 36% of [0.5, 3] at ±0.03, 57% at ±0.05 and 90% at ±0.1.
- So a match within typical ecological error is weak evidence unless the reading was written down first.

(iii) The catalogue's tally is off.
- There are 34 decompositions, not 32, and 6 are graded 'derived', not 7.
- One 'derived' grade (toolbox) sits on an exponent outside the stated 99% interval.

(iv) Orthopolic by construction.
- Murray/Leonardo trees, the critical-branching martingale and Tweedie clusters are orthopolic by identity (mass conservation, a martingale, a distributional identity).
- They show where the readings come from, but they cannot test the hypothesis.
- The informative cases are the ones where the resource is fixed by definition and the exponent could have failed, as in Sheldon's biomass, where per-system flatness in fact fails in the repo's own GLOSSAQUA analysis.

cases.system: Word tokens in written texts and corpora (English; Moby Dick; Google Books)
cases.law_or_distribution: Zipf: frequency of the r-th most common word f(r) ∝ r^-γ with γ ≈ 1. Equivalently, the number of word types with k occurrences is dN/dk ∝ k^-α, with α ≈ 2.
cases.variable_k: k = occurrences (tokens) of a word type in the text (dimensionless count)
cases.reported_exponent: Rank exponent γ ≈ 1 for frequent words (the 'kernel lexicon'). In large corpora, rare words have γ ≈ 2 (Ferrer i Cancho & Solé 2001, abstract; two regimes confirmed in Google Books by Petersen et al. 2012). For Moby Dick the MLE density exponent is α = 1.95 at x_min = 7 (Clauset et al. 2009, confirmed via the poweRlaw documentation and arXiv 2311.11200). Newman 2005 gets α = 2.20 for the same text with x_min = 1.
cases.alpha_uncertainty: 1.95 (x_min = 7) to 2.20 (x_min = 1) for the same text. The rare-word regime of large corpora has γ ≈ 2, i.e. α ≈ 1.5.
cases.conversion: Rank exponent γ: ζ = 1/γ, α = 1 + 1/γ. γ = 1 gives α = 2; γ = 2 gives α = 1.5. Then d_log = α − 1 and d_lin = α.
cases.orthopolic_reading: Conserved total: the N tokens of the text. Units: word types. Resource per unit: the type's token count. This is a stock within a fixed text and a usage flux in a growing corpus. d_log ≈ 1 means the resource is the token count itself: each factor-of-ten band of word frequency carries about the same share of the running text. In large corpora the rare-word regime has d_log ≈ 0.5 while the kernel regime keeps d_log ≈ 1. The linear reading (d_lin ≈ 2) makes the text linear-orthopolic in k², the number of same-type token pairs (coincidences).

decompositions.resource: Tokens (k itself), under proportional reuse with innovation
decompositions.composition: d = 1 (tokens) + a/(1−a) (innovation share). In Simon's model, each new token is a new word with probability a; otherwise it repeats an existing word chosen in proportion to that word's count. Log-frequency therefore grows at a rate independent of frequency, and the token flux is conserved (transport identity B = F/v with constant v).
decompositions.predicted_exponent: ζ = 1/(1−a). For Moby Dick, a = types/tokens ≈ (17,000–21,000)/(208,000–215,000) ≈ 0.08–0.10 (tokenization-dependent counts found in this task), so ζ ≈ 1.09–1.11 and α ≈ 2.1.
decompositions.independent_motivation: A text is a fixed budget of tokens written one at a time. An already-used word is more likely to be reused the more it has been used (priming, topic persistence). This fixes both the resource (tokens) and the log measure before the exponent is examined.
decompositions.theory_agreement: Simon (1955) derives exactly this reading, so the mechanism agrees with it. However, Simon's constant innovation rate implies vocabulary growing linearly with N, which Heaps' law (β ≈ 0.5) contradicts. The mechanism is therefore at best partial.
decompositions.testable_consequence: ζ − 1 ≈ a. Across many texts, with x_min fixed in advance, fitted ζ − 1 should track the type/token ratio V/N. An innovation rate that falls with N (Heaps) predicts a second, steeper-in-rank regime for rare words, and that regime is observed (γ ≈ 2).

decompositions.resource: Balance of speaker and hearer effort (least effort)
decompositions.composition: No resource product. In Ferrer i Cancho & Solé's (2003) signal–object optimization, an exponent near 1 appears only at a critical value λ* of the weight given to speaker versus hearer cost.
decompositions.predicted_exponent: Rank exponent ≈ 1 at λ*; no power law elsewhere
decompositions.independent_motivation: Speaker cost (few words) and hearer cost (unambiguous words) pull in opposite directions; Zipf proposed this before modern fits.
decompositions.theory_agreement: The PNAS 2003 simulations give z ≈ 1 at the transition (verified via abstract and reviews). Dickman, Moloney & Altmann (2012) dispute the optimization result. It is not a resource-allocation reading, and it does not explain the rare-word regime.
decompositions.testable_consequence: Because the exponent needs tuning to λ*, systems away from the transition should lose the power law rather than shift its exponent.

decompositions.resource: Same-type token pairs k(k−1)/2 (coincidences)
decompositions.composition: k² = k × k: tokens times the frequency of the same word
decompositions.independent_motivation: None found. No process in text production allocates coincidences equally per unit of frequency; this reading fits only because d_lin = d_log + 1 for every exponent.
decompositions.theory_agreement: No published theory
decompositions.testable_consequence: None independent of the token reading, from which it cannot be distinguished.

cases.source: Ferrer i Cancho & Solé (2001) J. Quant. Linguistics 8(3):165-173 (abstract); Clauset, Shalizi & Newman (2009) SIAM Rev. 51:661 (Moby Dick α = 1.95, via poweRlaw docs https://search.r-project.org/CRAN/refmans/poweRlaw/html/moby.html and arXiv 2311.11200); Newman (2005) Contemp. Phys. 46:323; Petersen et al. (2012) Sci. Rep. 2:943; Ferrer i Cancho & Solé (2003) PNAS 100:788; Simon (1955) Biometrika 42:425

cases.system: Vocabulary growth in texts and corpora (English corpora; Reuters RCV1; novels; Google Books)
cases.law_or_distribution: Heaps' law: V(N) ∝ N^β, where V is the number of distinct word types after N tokens
cases.variable_k: N = tokens read (text length); V = distinct types
cases.reported_exponent: β ≈ 0.4–0.6 for English corpora (encyclopedia summary). b = 0.49 for Reuters RCV1 (information-retrieval lecture fit). β ≈ 0.78 for individual English novels (review of statistical laws, arXiv 2407.19874). β → 1 at the start of a text. Large corpora show two regimes (Gerlach & Altmann 2013; Petersen et al. 2012, 'decreasing need for new words').
cases.alpha_uncertainty: 0.4–0.78 depending on corpus size and type
cases.conversion: Not a distribution. For a Zipf rank exponent γ > 1, β = 1/γ = ζ (Mandelbrot 1961 as cited by Petersen et al. 2012; Serrano et al.; Lü, Zhang & Zhou 2010 show this is asymptotic, with finite-size corrections). So β = 0.5 corresponds to ζ = 0.5 and α = 1.5 for the type-frequency tail that governs the discovery of new types. d_log = ζ and d_lin = α for that tail.
cases.orthopolic_reading: Conserved total: the N tokens. Units: word types. V(N) counts the types whose probability exceeds roughly 1/N, so V(N) is the survival function of type probabilities read at threshold 1/N, and β is the survival exponent ζ of the rare-word tail. Mean tokens per type, N/V ∝ N^(1−β), keeps growing: the text's budget is spread over a vocabulary that grows sublinearly. In resource terms, ζ = 0.5 means token mass per log-frequency band rises as p^0.5 inside the rare-word regime. That is top-heavy: the frequent (kernel) words hold most tokens. Vocabulary is a count of discovered slots (a capacity), not a stock.

decompositions.resource: Token mass per log-frequency band of the rare-word tail, inherited from Zipf
decompositions.composition: β = ζ_rare = 1/γ_rare. The rare-word regime has γ ≈ 2, so β ≈ 1/2.
decompositions.independent_motivation: Getting vocabulary size from the frequency distribution is a sampling identity, not a fit: a type is first seen once N·p ≳ 1.
decompositions.theory_agreement: Mandelbrot 1961; Serrano et al.; Lü, Zhang & Zhou 2010 (PLoS ONE; asymptotic for γ > 1, with finite-size corrections). They agree with this reading.
decompositions.testable_consequence: On the same corpus, β must equal the ζ fitted to the rare-word tail. Short texts dominated by the kernel regime (γ ≈ 1) must show β → 1 with a log correction (V ∝ N/ln N). This is consistent with β ≈ 0.78 for single novels and β → 1 early in a text.

decompositions.resource: Pairs of distinct types
decompositions.composition: If each new type arrives at a rate inversely proportional to the vocabulary already used, dV/dN ∝ 1/V, then V² ∝ N: tokens are linear-orthopolic in type pairs.
decompositions.independent_motivation: Weak. In Gerlach & Altmann's model, used noncore words lower the probability of a new word, but there the exponent is a fitted parameter, not 1/2 by construction.
decompositions.theory_agreement: Gerlach & Altmann 2013 (PRX) two-class model agrees only qualitatively; its parameters are language-dependent.
decompositions.testable_consequence: Predicts β = 1/2 for every language in the noncore regime. Language-dependent β, which Gerlach & Altmann report through language-specific parameters, argues against it.

cases.source: Lü, Zhang & Zhou (2010) PLoS ONE 5:e14139 (arXiv 1002.3861); Petersen, Tenenbaum, Havlin, Stanley & Perc (2012) Sci. Rep. 2:943 (arXiv 1212.2616); Gerlach & Altmann (2013) PRX 3:021006; typical β values via the Heaps' law encyclopedia entry and Manning et al. IR lecture (RCV1 b = 0.49); novels β = 0.78 via arXiv 2407.19874

cases.system: US metropolitan areas (135 largest MSAs, 1991) and 'natural' cities built by clustering populated cells (USA, Great Britain)
cases.law_or_distribution: P(S > s) ∝ s^-ζ (rank-size: ln rank = c − ζ ln s), with ζ ≈ 1
cases.variable_k: s = city population (persons)
cases.reported_exponent: ζ = 1.005 from OLS rank-size on 135 MSAs, R² = 0.986 (Gabaix 1999, via MIT lecture notes). Gabaix notes an OLS bias of about 0.05 and a true SE of about 0.1. The 135 largest US urban areas in 2010 give 1.019. Natural cities: ζ close to 1 down to 12,000 inhabitants (US) and 5,000 (GB) (Rozenfeld et al. 2011). Administrative US places give ζ ≈ 1.3–1.4 (repo compilation, not re-verified here).
cases.alpha_uncertainty: ζ ≈ 1.0 ± 0.1 for agglomerations; 1.3–1.4 for administrative places
cases.conversion: Survival ζ: α = ζ + 1
cases.orthopolic_reading: Conserved total: the national urban population. Units: cities. Resource per unit: residents (a stock). d_log ≈ 1 means residents themselves are the log-orthopolic resource: each factor-of-ten band of city size holds about the same number of people. The linear reading (d_lin ≈ 2) is resident pairs s²/2, the potential within-city contacts per unit of population.

decompositions.resource: Residents under proportional (Gibrat) growth with entry and a lower barrier
decompositions.composition: d = 1 + (ζ − 1), where ζ − 1 ≈ (population entering through new cities as a share of the total) / (resource-weighted log growth rate). The correction tends to 0 when entry is small and the floor is far below the mean (Gabaix: ζ = 1/(1 − s_min/s̄)).
decompositions.independent_motivation: Migration and natural increase act on a city roughly in proportion to its size, and people are conserved as cities move up the log-size axis. This fixes residents and the log measure before the data are seen.
decompositions.theory_agreement: Gabaix (1999) derives exactly ζ = 1 in this limit, so the theory agrees. Gibrat fails in the variance (small cities are more volatile), so near-Zipf tails appear despite a partial failure of the stated mechanism.
decompositions.testable_consequence: ζ depends on how a city is defined: administrative fragmentation steepens the tail to about 1.4, while clustering gives about 1. If area were a deterministic power of population, A ∝ P^c, then ζ_A = ζ_P/c. Rozenfeld et al. report ζ_A ≈ 1 as well, which implies c ≈ 1. This conflicts with the land-area exponent 2/3 of Bettencourt's (2013) framework, which would give ζ_A = 1.5. The tension is a direct test of either the deterministic map or that exponent.

decompositions.resource: Resident pairs (potential interactions)
decompositions.composition: s² = s × s
decompositions.independent_motivation: None. Urban scaling shows that realized per-capita interactions grow as s^δ with δ ≈ 0.15, not as s, so no process equalizes pairs.
decompositions.theory_agreement: No published theory
decompositions.testable_consequence: None beyond the resident reading

cases.source: Gabaix (1999) QJE 114:739 (slope 1.005 via MIT OCW 14.13 lecture 24; 2010 value 1.019 via LSBU Haplo paper); Rozenfeld, Rybski, Gabaix & Makse (2011) AER 101(5):2205 (NBER w15409 abstract); Bettencourt (2013) Science 340:1438

cases.system: Urban systems: US metropolitan statistical areas and other national urban systems
cases.law_or_distribution: Y = Y0 N^β. Socioeconomic outputs: β ≈ 1.15 (GDP), 1.12 (wages), 1.27 (new patents), 1.25 (inventors). Infrastructure: 0.87 (electrical cable length), 0.83 (road surface), 0.77 (gasoline stations). Individual needs (housing, employment, household electricity): ≈ 1.
cases.variable_k: N = metropolitan population; Y = annual output (flux) or infrastructure stock
cases.reported_exponent: Bettencourt et al. 2007 PNAS. Patents 1.27, inventors 1.25, GDP 1.15, wages 1.12 and cables 0.87 come from the table as reproduced in arXiv 0809.4994; roads 0.83 and gasoline stations 0.77 from a secondary summary. Theory gives 1 ± δ with δ = H/(D(D+H)) = 1/6 for D = 2, H = 1, i.e. 7/6 and 5/6 (Bettencourt 2013; formula verified via a 2016 European urban-scaling paper). Exponents depend on how cities are defined: most England & Wales indicators scale linearly (Arcaute et al. 2015), and many exponents are compatible with 1 once fluctuations are modelled (Leitão et al. 2016).
cases.alpha_uncertainty: US GDP 1.13–1.15 across definitions; patents up to 1.27; often compatible with 1 under other definitions
cases.conversion: Not a distribution. Combined with Zipf city sizes (ζ_N ≈ 1), a deterministic Y ∝ N^β gives P(Y > y) ∝ y^(−ζ_N/β). That predicts city GDP with ζ ≈ 0.87 (α ≈ 1.87) and road surface with ζ ≈ 1.2 (my derivation).
cases.orthopolic_reading: Conserved total: the city's socioeconomic output Y (a flux per year), or its network area (a stock). Units: residents. Resource per resident: y = Y/N ∝ N^δ with δ ≈ 0.15, so each resident's share grows with city size, while network per resident falls as N^(−δ). In Bettencourt's theory Y ∝ N²/A_n. The final resource is then the number of potential pairs N², divided between output and network, so that Y·A_n ∝ N². The log/linear measure distinction does not apply to a deterministic law; d_log and d_lin here both give the exponent of output in population.

decompositions.resource: Social interactions per resident = area swept per person (fixed by bounded daily effort) × population density on the network
decompositions.composition: d = 1 (residents) + δ, with δ = H/(D(D+H)) = (1/D)·(H/(D+H)). D = 2 (the urban plane) and H = 1 (fractal dimension of individual paths) give δ = 1/6.
decompositions.independent_motivation: Output arises from encounters. A person's daily travel covers a bounded area, so encounters scale with how densely people sit on the network, and networks grow incrementally to reach everyone. These assumptions precede the exponents.
decompositions.theory_agreement: Bettencourt (2013) derives exactly this dimension-based δ, so the theory agrees. It matches GDP 1.15, wages 1.12, roads 0.83 and cables 0.87, but not patents 1.27 or gasoline stations 0.77. Empirical exponents depend on city definition.
decompositions.testable_consequence: Dimension dependence with H = 1: D = 1 (ribbon or linear cities) gives δ = 1/2 and β = 1.5; D = 3 gives δ = 1/12 and β ≈ 1.08. Within one urban system, GDP across cities should have a survival exponent ζ ≈ 1/1.15 ≈ 0.87 if populations are Zipf.

decompositions.resource: Potential pairs N², shared between socioeconomic output and network area
decompositions.composition: Y × A_n ∝ N², so β_Y + β_network = 2 for any δ (my rearrangement of Y = G N²/A_n)
decompositions.independent_motivation: Follows from the interaction assumption (output ∝ N × density on the network = N²/A_n) without choosing D or H.
decompositions.theory_agreement: Implied by Bettencourt (2013); the symmetric 1 ± δ form is its signature. The pairing of specific variables (GDP with roads, wages with cables) is mine. Published US values give 1.15 + 0.83 = 1.98 and 1.12 + 0.87 = 1.99.
decompositions.testable_consequence: Parameter-free: across urban systems or city definitions (e.g. Arcaute-style boundary ensembles), any shift in the network exponent must be mirrored by an opposite shift in the output exponent.

cases.source: Bettencourt, Lobo, Helbing, Kühnert & West (2007) PNAS 104:7301 (values via arXiv 0809.4994, Table I); Bettencourt (2013) Science 340:1438 (δ formula via arXiv 1510.00902); Arcaute et al. (2015) J. R. Soc. Interface (arXiv 1301.1674); Leitão, Miotto, Gerlach & Altmann (2016) R. Soc. Open Sci. (arXiv 1604.02872)

cases.system: US firms with employees (about 5.5 million tax-paying firms, Census 1997)
cases.law_or_distribution: P(S > s) ∝ s^-ζ with ζ ≈ 1 (Zipf)
cases.variable_k: s = employees per firm
cases.reported_exponent: ζ = 1.059, with density slope 2.059, fitted on power-of-three bins over nearly six decades (Axtell 2001 Science, verified via arXiv cond-mat/0401053 and secondary sources). Receipts ζ ≈ 0.99 and 2011 SBA data ζ = 1.097 ± 0.002 come from the repo compilation (not re-verified here).
cases.alpha_uncertainty: ζ about 1.06 (SE not verified); other size measures 0.89–1.10
cases.conversion: Survival ζ: α = ζ + 1
cases.orthopolic_reading: Conserved total: private-sector employment. Units: firms. Resource per unit: workers (a stock). d_log ≈ 1.06 means employment per log size band is almost equal and slightly bottom-heavy: small and medium firms hold a little more employment per band than the largest. The linear reading is worker pairs.

decompositions.resource: Workers under proportional growth with entry and exit
decompositions.composition: d = 1 + φ/m, where ζ − 1 ≈ J_R/(Q·m): annual employment created by entrants as a fraction of total employment, divided by the employment-weighted log growth rate. ζ − 1 = 0.059 implies m·τ_res ≈ 17.
decompositions.independent_motivation: Firm growth is roughly proportional to size (Gibrat), jobs are conserved as firms grow, and entry adds jobs at the bottom. This fixes workers and the log measure.
decompositions.theory_agreement: Luttmer 2007, Reed 2001 and Gabaix 1999 (the research-program exponent equation) derive this; the theory agrees. Gibrat fails in the variance (see the firm-volatility case), so the agreement is approximate.
decompositions.testable_consequence: Panel data (BDS-type) giving the entrant employment share and growth rates should predict ζ − 1 ≈ 0.06 out of sample. Periods of high entry should show steeper tails.

decompositions.resource: Receipts = workers × revenue per worker
decompositions.composition: If receipts R ∝ L^(1+c) deterministically, then ζ_R = ζ_L/(1+c). Receipts ζ ≈ 0.99 against employees ζ = 1.059 implies c ≈ 0.07.
decompositions.predicted_exponent: Elasticity of revenue per worker to firm size ≈ 0.07
decompositions.independent_motivation: Larger firms are somewhat more productive. But c is backed out from the two exponents, not measured.
decompositions.theory_agreement: No published theory derives c. If productivity varied independently of size with a lighter tail, both measures would share the same ζ instead.
decompositions.testable_consequence: A cross-sectional regression of ln(receipts/employee) on ln(employees) should give about 0.07. Large scatter at fixed size would break the deterministic map.

cases.source: Axtell (2001) Science 293:1818, doi:10.1126/science.1062081 (1.059 via arXiv cond-mat/0401053 and fgeerolf Pareto slides); Luttmer (2007) QJE; Reed (2001) Econ. Lett.

cases.system: Growth-rate volatility of firms (US publicly traded manufacturing firms, Compustat 1975–1991; pharmaceutical firms by product)
cases.law_or_distribution: σ(g | S) ∝ S^(−β): standard deviation of the annual log growth rate g at firm size S
cases.variable_k: S = sales (also employees, assets)
cases.reported_exponent: β = 0.20 ± 0.03 over about seven orders of magnitude of sales (Stanley et al. 1996 Nature, as restated by a 2017 re-analysis and arXiv 2404.15226). β = 0.14–0.2 depending on the average number of units per firm (Riccaboni et al. 2008 PNAS). Pure diversification over independent equal units would give 0.5.
cases.conversion: Not a distribution. Absolute growth variance Var(ΔS) = σ²S² ∝ S^(2−2β) = S^1.6. The effective number of independent units is n_eff ∝ S^(2β) = S^0.4.
cases.orthopolic_reading: Conserved total: the firm's absolute growth variance, which is additive over independent components. Units: effectively independent sub-units (products, divisions, plants). Resource per unit: each unit's variance, ∝ (unit size)². With n_eff ∝ S^0.4 units, each of size S/n_eff ∝ S^0.6, total variance ∝ S^0.4 × (S^0.6)² = S^1.6. The firm is a container whose size is shared among a slowly growing number of units, and β is half the exponent of that unit count.

decompositions.resource: Absolute growth variance = (number of effective independent units) × (unit size)²
decompositions.composition: 2 − 2β = 2β + 2(1 − 2β), i.e. 1.6 = 0.4 + 2 × 0.6 (deterministic exponents add)
decompositions.predicted_exponent: β = 1/2 if units are equal-sized and n ∝ S. β = 1 − 1/μ if unit sizes are Pareto with 1 < μ < 2 (Wyart & Bouchaud 2003, via a 2024 review); β = 0.2 then needs μ ≈ 1.25. Riccaboni et al. (2008): β crosses over from 0 for small firms to 1/2 for very large ones, staying at 0.14–0.2 for realistic numbers of units.
decompositions.independent_motivation: Firms are portfolios of products and divisions whose shocks are partly independent, and the variance of a sum of independent parts adds. This fixes the resource before β is examined.
decompositions.theory_agreement: Wyart & Bouchaud (2003), using Pareto sub-units, and Riccaboni et al. (2008), using proportional growth of sub-units, both derive exactly this 'effective number of units' reading; they agree with it.
decompositions.testable_consequence: Within firms, the Herfindahl effective number of products (ΣS_i)²/ΣS_i² should scale as S^0.4. Under Wyart–Bouchaud, the product-size tail should have μ ≈ 1/(1−β) ≈ 1.25. β should rise toward 1/2 for the largest, most diversified firms.

cases.source: Stanley et al. (1996) Nature 379:804; Amaral et al. (1997) J. Phys. I 7:621 (arXiv cond-mat/9702082); Riccaboni, Pammolli, Buldyrev, Ponta & Stanley (2008) PNAS (arXiv 0904.1404); Wyart & Bouchaud (2003) Physica A (arXiv cond-mat/0210479; exponent form via arXiv 2404.07935); Moran, Secchi & Bouchaud arXiv 2404.15226

cases.system: Richest US individuals (Forbes 400 lists, 1988–2003)
cases.law_or_distribution: P(W > w) ∝ w^-ζ in the top tail
cases.variable_k: w = net worth (US dollars)
cases.reported_exponent: ζ = 1.49, averaged over Forbes 400 lists 1988–2003 (Klass et al. 2006 Econ. Lett. 90:290). Other estimates on similar lists, 1.09–1.36 (Newman 2005; Levy & Solomon 1997), come from the repo compilation and were not re-verified. A fixed-k tail regression (arXiv 2105.10007) finds that top marginal income-tax rates of 30–40% correspond to ζ ≈ 1.5–1.8. The 80/20 rule corresponds to ζ = ln 5/ln 4 ≈ 1.16.
cases.alpha_uncertainty: ζ 1.1–1.5 across estimators and years; 1.5–1.8 at higher tax rates
cases.conversion: Survival ζ: α = ζ + 1
cases.orthopolic_reading: Conserved total: wealth held by the top group (a stock). Units: persons or families. Resource: net worth. ζ ≈ 1.5 means wealth per log band falls as w^(−0.5) within the tail: bottom-heavy, with more total wealth near the entry threshold than among the very richest. Formally the log-orthopolic resource is w^1.5. The natural reading, though, is wealth itself plus a turnover correction of +0.5.

decompositions.resource: Wealth under multiplicative returns with exit (death, estate division, consumption, taxation, dropping off the list)
decompositions.composition: d = 1 + φ/m ≈ 1 + 1/(m·τ_res). ζ − 1 = 0.49 implies m·τ_res ≈ 2: a unit of top wealth climbs only about two e-folds before it leaves the tail.
decompositions.predicted_exponent: ζ > 1, rising with turnover and taxation
decompositions.independent_motivation: Fortunes grow by returns roughly proportional to their size (Kesten/Gibrat), while exit events occur roughly independently of size. The motivation precedes the fit.
decompositions.theory_agreement: Levy & Solomon (Kesten processes), Klass et al. 2007 (efficient-market investor model), Benhabib et al.: the mechanism agrees, but none predicts the exponent without measured rates.
decompositions.testable_consequence: Taxation shortens residence and should raise ζ. The fixed-k tail regression finds ζ rising to 1.5–1.8 at 30–40% top rates, confirming the direction. A prediction from measured return dispersion and list turnover should reproduce ζ ≈ 1.5.

decompositions.resource: Liquidation cost under square-root market impact
decompositions.composition: w^1.5 = w × w^(1/2): wealth times the square-root price impact of selling it
decompositions.independent_motivation: None for the distribution of fortunes. No process allocates liquidation cost equally per log band.
decompositions.theory_agreement: No published theory
decompositions.testable_consequence: Would fix ζ at 1.5 regardless of taxation, which the observed tax dependence contradicts.

cases.source: Klass, Biham, Levy, Malcai & Solomon (2006) Econ. Lett. 90(2):290-295; fixed-k tail regression arXiv 2105.10007; Newman (2005); Levy & Solomon (1997)

cases.system: US top personal incomes from IRS tabulations, 1916–2019, split into labor and capital income
cases.law_or_distribution: P(Y > y) ∝ y^-ζ in the top tail
cases.variable_k: y = annual income (US dollars per year), a flux
cases.reported_exponent: Labor income ζ ≈ 2 and capital income ζ ≈ 1.2, both stable since about 1985 (Lee, Sasaki, Toda & Wang 2022, arXiv 2206.04257, abstract). Total top income ζ ≈ 1.4–1.8 since 1985 (Toda & Wang, arXiv 1901.02471).
cases.alpha_uncertainty: Labor ζ ≈ 2 (α ≈ 3); capital ζ ≈ 1.2 (α ≈ 2.2); total 1.4–1.8
cases.conversion: Survival ζ: α = ζ + 1 (labor income shown)
cases.orthopolic_reading: Conserved total: income received by top earners per year (a flux). Units: taxpayers. Capital income is a flux drawn from a wealth stock (y_K = r·W) and inherits that stock's nearly log-orthopolic allocation (ζ ≈ 1.2). Labor income, with ζ ≈ 2, is far from orthopolic in itself. Its log-orthopolic quantity is y_L², i.e. labor income behaves like the square root of a Zipf-distributed stock.

decompositions.resource: The size S of the organization or market an earner's talent is applied to (Zipf, ζ_S ≈ 1), with pay y ∝ S^κ
decompositions.composition: ζ_y = ζ_S/κ, so d_log(y) = 1/κ. Labor ζ ≈ 2 corresponds to κ ≈ 1/2. For CEOs, Roberts' law gives κ ≈ 1/3, so ζ_CEO pay ≈ 3.
decompositions.predicted_exponent: ζ_labor = 2 if κ = 1/2; ζ_CEO pay = 3 (my derivation from the Gabaix–Landier inputs)
decompositions.independent_motivation: In assignment models (Rosen's superstars; Gabaix & Landier 2008), pay is an increasing power of the scale an earner controls, and firm size is independently Zipf (Axtell). However, κ = 1/2 is backed out from the labor exponent.
decompositions.theory_agreement: Gabaix & Landier (2008): pay elasticity to own-firm size ≈ 1/3 and β/α ≈ 2/3 (verified via survey and follow-up). The mechanism agrees for CEOs; κ = 1/2 for all top labor income is not derived.
decompositions.testable_consequence: The CEO-pay tail should have ζ ≈ 3. Among top labor earners generally, the elasticity of pay to the scale they control should be about ζ_S/ζ_y ≈ 0.5.

decompositions.resource: Capital income as a flux: return × wealth stock
decompositions.composition: y_K = r·W with r ∝ W^ε gives ζ_K = ζ_W/(1+ε)
decompositions.predicted_exponent: ζ_K = ζ_W ≈ 1.1–1.5 for size-independent returns; ζ_K < ζ_W if returns rise with wealth
decompositions.independent_motivation: Capital income is mechanically a rate times a stock.
decompositions.theory_agreement: Standard, and it agrees. The populations differ (IRS top filers versus the Forbes 400), so the 1.2 versus 1.49 gap does not yet pin down ε (it would need ε ≈ 0.25 if the populations were the same).
decompositions.testable_consequence: The measured elasticity of realized returns to wealth, in one population, should equal ζ_W/ζ_K − 1.

decompositions.resource: Income squared
decompositions.composition: y² = y × y (e.g. a variance contribution)
decompositions.independent_motivation: None
decompositions.theory_agreement: No published theory
decompositions.testable_consequence: None

cases.source: Lee, Sasaki, Toda & Wang (2022) arXiv 2206.04257; Toda & Wang arXiv 1901.02471; Gabaix & Landier (2008) QJE 123:49 (1/3 elasticity and β/α ≈ 2/3 via survey and NBER w13372)

cases.system: Citations to scientific papers (ISI 1981 cohort, about 783,000 papers; Physical Review D volumes 11–50, 24,296 papers)
cases.law_or_distribution: N(x) ∝ x^-α in the high-citation tail, α ≈ 3
cases.variable_k: x = citations received per paper (count)
cases.reported_exponent: α ≈ 3, inferred from a rank slope of about 1/2 for top papers (Redner 1998 EPJ B 4:131). α = 3.16 ± 0.06 (Clauset et al. 2009) and 3.15 (Golosovsky & Solomon 2012) come from the repo compilation and were not re-verified here. Later work prefers double power laws (Lehmann et al.).
cases.conversion: Density α taken directly; equivalently rank slope 1/2, ζ = 2, α = 3
cases.orthopolic_reading: Conserved total: the references made by citing papers. Each reference is one unit of credit, so the total is m times the number of citing papers. Units: cited papers. Resource per unit: citations received (a count of credit units, not a held stock). ζ = 2 means citations per log band fall as x^(−1): strongly bottom-heavy, with most credit going to moderately cited papers.

decompositions.resource: Citations plus initial attractiveness under cumulative advantage (Price model; Dorogovtsev–Mendes–Samukhin)
decompositions.composition: d_log = 1 + A/m, i.e. ζ − 1 = A/m: the ratio of non-preferential attachment (initial attractiveness A) to preferential attachment per new paper carrying m references. α = 3 means A = m. Equivalently, in-degree grows as (t/t_i)^(m/(m+A)) = (t/t_i)^(1/2), and the system is log-orthopolic in relative age t/t_i ∝ x².
decompositions.predicted_exponent: α = 2 + A/m; α = 3 when A = m (also the undirected Barabási–Albert value)
decompositions.independent_motivation: Scientists find papers partly through other papers' reference lists (proportional to existing citations) and partly by direct search (independent of citations). This is motivated before the exponent is seen.
decompositions.theory_agreement: Price 1976 and DMS 2000 (γ = 2 + A/m, verified via reviews and Wikipedia's 'Initial attractiveness') derive this, so the mechanism agrees. Aging, obsolescence and paper fitness are known to matter and are omitted here.
decompositions.testable_consequence: Measure the attachment kernel Π(x) ∝ x + A in a citation panel: A/m must equal α − 2 ≈ 1. Fields with more references per paper, at similar A, should have flatter tails.

decompositions.resource: Citations × relative age
decompositions.composition: x³ = x × x², under the linear measure
decompositions.independent_motivation: None beyond restating the first reading in a different measure
decompositions.theory_agreement: No published theory
decompositions.testable_consequence: None independent

cases.source: Redner (1998) EPJ B 4:131-134, arXiv cond-mat/9804163; Dorogovtsev, Mendes & Samukhin (2000) PRL 85:4633 (γ = 2 + A/m via arXiv cond-mat/0409154 and reviews); Price (1976)

cases.system: Authors of scientific papers (Chemical Abstracts 1907–1916; Auerbach's physics index; later bibliographies)
cases.law_or_distribution: Lotka's law: y(n) ∝ n^-a, the number of authors with n papers, with a ≈ 2 (the 'inverse square law')
cases.variable_k: n = papers per author (count)
cases.reported_exponent: Lotka's least-squares slopes: 1.888 (Chemical Abstracts, senior authors only) and 2.021 (Auerbach) (via arXiv 1601.04950). The exponent varies by field and period; a 2026 sustainability-science study finds a higher exponent and prefers a lognormal. Clauset et al. 2009 report a MathSciNet tail α = 4.3 above n = 133 (repo compilation, from memory, not verified).
cases.alpha_uncertainty: 1.89–2.02 in Lotka's data; field-dependent and often steeper in tails
cases.conversion: Discrete density exponent used directly
cases.orthopolic_reading: Conserved total: author–paper credits (each paper counted once per credited author). Units: authors. Resource per unit: papers. d_log ≈ 1 means each factor-of-ten productivity band (1–10 papers, 10–100 papers) contributes about the same number of papers.

decompositions.resource: Papers under cumulative advantage with newcomer entry (Simon/Price 'success breeds success')
decompositions.composition: d = 1 + a/(1−a), where a = share of papers by first-time authors = authors/papers. Lotka's own law truncated at n_max = 100–1000 implies mean productivity of 3.2–4.6, hence a ≈ 0.22–0.32 and ζ ≈ 1.28–1.46 (my computation).
decompositions.predicted_exponent: Asymptotic tail α ≈ 2.3–2.5. The Yule–Simon local slope over n = 1–10 is 1.7–2.2 (my computation), matching the small-n range Lotka fitted.
decompositions.independent_motivation: Productive authors gain resources, students and visibility in proportion to their past output, and newcomers enter constantly; both facts precede the fit.
decompositions.theory_agreement: Simon 1955 and Price 1976 agree with the resource reading. The inverse-square value is then a small-n crossover, not the asymptotic exponent.
decompositions.testable_consequence: Tails fitted above a theory-set n_min should be steeper than 2, by a/(1−a) computed from the same bibliography's authors/papers ratio. MathSciNet's steep tail points this way; finite careers would steepen it further.

decompositions.resource: Productivity as a product of independent personal factors (Shockley 1957)
decompositions.composition: Papers = Π f_i over several independent abilities, so log(papers) is a sum and the distribution is lognormal. Tail exponents of independent random factors do not add.
decompositions.independent_motivation: Research output requires several distinct abilities and resources jointly.
decompositions.theory_agreement: Shockley 1957 (not re-verified here). It gives no power law, so it cannot account for α ≈ 2. Some recent bibliographies do prefer a lognormal (2026 study, abstract).
decompositions.testable_consequence: A likelihood-ratio test of lognormal against power law on large bibliographies, with n_min fixed in advance

cases.source: Lotka (1926) J. Wash. Acad. Sci. 16:317 (slopes via arXiv 1601.04950); Pao (1985) IP&M 21:305; Chalmers 2026 sustainability-science study (research.chalmers.se/publication/552701); Simon (1955); Price (1976)

cases.system: Journals contributing articles on a subject (Bradford's 1934 bibliographies and later subject bibliographies)
cases.law_or_distribution: Bradford's law, verbal form: ranked journals split into a core and zones that each yield the same number of articles, with journal counts in successive zones in the ratio 1 : n : n². Leimkuhler's form: cumulative articles F(x) = ln(1 + βx)/ln(1 + β).
cases.variable_k: k = relevant articles per journal; journals ranked r = 1, 2, … by productivity
cases.reported_exponent: The multiplier n is set empirically for each bibliography; there is no universal value. The verbal Bradford law, Leimkuhler's law and Lotka's law with exponent 2 are equivalent (Egghe 1988; Chen & Leimkuhler); the graphical form differs (Egghe). Real bibliographies deviate, and a 2021 polymer bibliography fails the verbal law but fits Leimkuhler.
cases.alpha_uncertainty: Exact in the verbal form; empirical fits vary
cases.conversion: Equal articles per zone with geometric zone boundaries means cumulative articles ∝ ln r, so articles per journal ∝ 1/r (rank exponent 1), ζ = 1 and α = 2 for the density of journals over articles per journal.
cases.orthopolic_reading: Conserved total: the articles on the subject. Units: journals. Resource per unit: relevant articles. Bradford's verbal law is literally discrete orthopolity: the resource (articles) is equal per class, where the classes are geometric bands of journal rank, so articles are equal per log rank. It is the bibliometric statement of log-orthopolity with d = 1.

decompositions.resource: Articles per journal, discretely orthopolic over geometric rank zones
decompositions.composition: Zone j spans ranks n^j to n^(j+1). With articles per journal ∝ r^(−1/ζ), articles in zone j ∝ n^(j(1 − 1/ζ)), so equal yields across zones hold if and only if ζ = 1.
decompositions.predicted_exponent: Equal articles per zone; the ratio of successive zone yields is n^(1 − 1/ζ)
decompositions.independent_motivation: Authors send papers to journals already publishing on the topic (cumulative advantage of journals), and a subject's literature is a finite set of articles to be shared.
decompositions.theory_agreement: Egghe (1988) proves the equivalence of verbal Bradford, Leimkuhler and Lotka(2); the orthopolic reading is the law itself. The cumulative-advantage mechanism is Price's, and the 1:n:n² equality requires its entry correction to be negligible.
decompositions.testable_consequence: If new journals keep entering (ζ = 1.1), then with n = 5 each zone should hold about 16% more articles than the previous one (5^(1 − 1/1.1) ≈ 1.16, my arithmetic). A Groos droop (fewer articles in the outer zones) points the other way, toward a lower cutoff or incomplete coverage.

cases.source: Bradford (1934) Engineering 137:85; Leimkuhler (1967) J. Documentation; Egghe (1988) J. Documentation 44(1):53-62 (via Emerald abstract); INFLIBNET module on Bradford distributions; Brookes (1981) commentary

cases.system: World Wide Web pages (AltaVista crawls of 1999, over 200 million pages and 1.5 billion links; nd.edu domain 1999)
cases.law_or_distribution: P(k_in) ∝ k_in^(−γ_in) with γ_in ≈ 2.1; out-degree γ_out ≈ 2.45–2.7
cases.variable_k: k = in-links per page (count)
cases.reported_exponent: γ_in = 2.1 (Broder et al. 2000, agreeing with earlier studies at smaller scales; Newman's 2001 review cites τ_in = 2.1). γ_out ≈ 2.7 for the AltaVista crawl (Broder et al., via Newman's review) and 2.45 for nd.edu (Albert, Jeong & Barabási 1999). Clauset et al. 2009 reject a pure power law for in-links (repo compilation, not re-verified).
cases.alpha_uncertainty: About ±0.1 (not stated); out-degree 2.45–2.72
cases.conversion: Density exponent used directly
cases.orthopolic_reading: Conserved total: hyperlinks (total in-degree = total out-degree). Units: pages. Resource per page: links received, i.e. attention conferred by other authors (a count of credit units). d_log ≈ 1.1 means links are almost log-orthopolic: each factor-of-ten band of popularity receives about the same number of links, with a 10% bottom-heavy correction. Out-degree is chosen by the page's own author, so its exponent has no comparable reading.

decompositions.resource: In-links under preferential attachment with initial attractiveness
decompositions.composition: d_log = 1 + A/m; γ = 2 + A/m, so A/m ≈ 0.1
decompositions.independent_motivation: Pages are found mostly by following links (finding probability ∝ in-links) and rarely by other routes, so a new page starts nearly invisible. This is motivated before the fit, but A has not been measured independently here.
decompositions.theory_agreement: The DMS 2000 / Price model (γ = 2 + A/m) agrees with the link-credit reading.
decompositions.testable_consequence: The Web's measured attachment kernel should be nearly linear with offset A ≈ 0.1·m. Citations (A ≈ m) should differ from the Web (A ≈ 0.1·m) because direct search matters more for papers.

decompositions.resource: Out-links as authoring effort (same lens applied to out-degree)
decompositions.composition: No accepted proportional-growth mechanism exists for a page's own outgoing links. Any reading q ∝ k^1.7 would be built from the exponent itself.
decompositions.independent_motivation: None found
decompositions.theory_agreement: No published theory derives γ_out ≈ 2.7 from a resource
decompositions.testable_consequence: None. That absence is what makes this a counterexample.

cases.source: Broder et al. (2000) Computer Networks 33:309 (WWW9; γ_in = 2.1 via Cornell excerpt and Newman arXiv cond-mat/0007235, which also gives τ_out = 2.7); Albert, Jeong & Barabási (1999) Nature 401:130 (γ_out = 2.45); Dorogovtsev, Mendes & Samukhin (2000) PRL 85:4633

cases.system: US stocks (every trade on NYSE, AMEX and Nasdaq, 1994–1995; 40 million data points), plus LSE and Paris for volume
cases.law_or_distribution: Inverse cubic law: P(|r| > x) ∝ x^(−ζ_r) with ζ_r ≈ 3. Half-cubic law for trading volume: P(V > v) ∝ v^(−3/2).
cases.variable_k: r = normalized price change (return) over short intervals; V = shares traded
cases.reported_exponent: ζ_r ≈ 3. Fits give 3.1 ± 0.03 (positive tail) and 2.84 ± 0.12 (negative tail) over 2–100 standard deviations; extrapolation gives 2.84 ± 0.12 and 2.73 ± 0.13, with tail labels inconsistent in the preprint (Gopikrishnan et al. 1998). Volume ζ_V ≈ 3/2 (Gopikrishnan et al. 2000; LSE, 262 stocks, ≈ 3/2, consistent with NYSE and Paris per Plerou et al. 2004).
cases.conversion: Survival ζ: α = ζ + 1
cases.orthopolic_reading: Returns are not a resource. The orthopolic stock behind them is the assets S of the institutions whose trades move prices. Fund sizes are roughly Zipf (ζ_S ≈ 1), i.e. log-orthopolic in assets. The chain V ∝ S^(2/3) (optimal trade size) and r ∝ V^(1/2) (square-root impact) gives r ∝ S^(1/3), so the log-orthopolic resource written in the return coordinate is S ∝ r³, and d_log = 3. The cubic law says the assets behind a trade scale as the cube of the return it causes. The linear reading is equal contributions to the fourth moment per unit return, so kurtosis diverges.

decompositions.resource: Assets under management of the trading institution (a Zipf stock) seen through two deterministic maps
decompositions.composition: Nested maps multiply exponents: d_log(r) = ζ_S × (d ln S/d ln V) × (d ln V/d ln r) = 1 × 3/2 × 2 = 3, and d_log(V) = 1 × 3/2 = 3/2. With a general impact exponent δ, ζ_r = ζ_S(1+δ)/δ and ζ_V = ζ_S(1+δ) (my generalization of the chain).
decompositions.independent_motivation: Large funds must trade large blocks, impact costs limit how fast they trade, and fund sizes are independently Zipf-like. These inputs are measured separately from returns.
decompositions.theory_agreement: Gabaix, Gopikrishnan, Plerou & Stanley (2003, Nature 423:267) derive exactly this, so the theory agrees. It is contested: Farmer & Lillo (2004) find impact growing more slowly than a square root, and Schwarzkopf & Farmer (2010) find US mutual-fund sizes lognormal rather than Zipf.
decompositions.testable_consequence: ζ_r = 2ζ_V wherever impact is square-root, independent of the fund-size distribution. The LSE volume ζ_V ≈ 3/2 supports the volume link. Markets with a different impact exponent δ should show ζ_r/ζ_V = 1/δ. The theory also predicts a number-of-trades exponent of about 3.4 (not verified here).

decompositions.resource: Volatility as a multiplicatively reinvested stock (GARCH/Kesten)
decompositions.composition: σ²_t = ω + (a·z²_(t−1) + b)·σ²_(t−1); ζ solves E[(a·z² + b)^(ζ/2)] = 1
decompositions.predicted_exponent: ζ ≈ 3–4 for typical fitted (a, b) (not verified here)
decompositions.independent_motivation: Volatility clustering is documented independently of tail fits.
decompositions.theory_agreement: Kesten 1973 and Goldie 1991. The mechanism is multiplicative feedback, not resource allocation, and the exponent depends on fitted parameters.
decompositions.testable_consequence: ζ should vary with the fitted persistence a + b across assets and periods, whereas the fund-size reading ties it to ζ_V. Both readings currently fit.

cases.source: Gopikrishnan, Meyer, Amaral & Stanley (1998) EPJ B 3:139, arXiv cond-mat/9803374; Gopikrishnan, Plerou, Gabaix & Stanley (2000) PRE 62:R4493, arXiv cond-mat/0008113; Plerou, Gopikrishnan, Gabaix & Stanley (2004) Quant. Finance 4:C11, arXiv cond-mat/0403067; Gabaix et al. (2003) Nature 423:267; Schwarzkopf & Farmer (2010) arXiv 1005.4976

cases.system: Interstate wars, Correlates of War 1823–2003 (95 wars)
cases.law_or_distribution: Richardson's law: P(x) ∝ x^(−α) for battle deaths x ≥ x_min
cases.variable_k: x = battle deaths per war
cases.reported_exponent: α = 1.53 ± 0.07 for x ≥ 7,061 (51 of 95 wars; p_KS = 0.78 ± 0.03) (Clauset 2018 Sci. Adv. and 2019 chapter, arXiv 1901.05086). Per-capita intensity α = 1.7 ± 0.2 (Clauset et al. 2009) and 1.80 (Newman 2005) come from the repo compilation and were not re-verified.
cases.alpha_uncertainty: ± 0.07 for deaths; 1.7–1.8 per capita
cases.conversion: Density α used directly; ζ = α − 1 = 0.53
cases.orthopolic_reading: An event total (deaths in one war), not a held stock. Conserved total: battle deaths over the observation window. Units: wars. ζ ≈ 0.5 means deaths per log band rise as x^0.47: strongly top-heavy, with the total dominated by the largest wars (WWII, 16.6 million). The log-orthopolic resource is about x^(1/2).

decompositions.resource: War duration (generations of escalation) in a critical branching cascade
decompositions.composition: Mean-field critical branching gives P(T) ∝ T^(−2) (ζ_T = 1, i.e. log-orthopolic in duration) and size s ∝ T², hence α_s = 3/2. The resource is T ∝ s^(1/2).
decompositions.independent_motivation: Weak. Wars spread by drawing in further combatants and fronts, which suggests branching, but no branching ratio has been measured.
decompositions.theory_agreement: Mean-field branching gives exactly 3/2 (size) and 2 (duration) (verified via reviews), and SOC-type war models exist (Cederman 2003). The 2025 escalation study supports a different mechanism.
decompositions.testable_consequence: War durations should follow P(T) ∝ T^(−2), with deaths ∝ duration². Instead 79% of wars end within two years, and civil wars last longer while being smaller, which does not support it.

decompositions.resource: Coalition mass under source-driven coagulation with a constant kernel (ν = 0)
decompositions.independent_motivation: None specific to wars; ν = 0 is chosen to fit.
decompositions.theory_agreement: Smoluchowski coagulation with a source; there is no war-specific derivation.
decompositions.testable_consequence: The same family gives ζ = 1 for ν = 1 and 3/2 for ν = 2. ν would have to be measured from how conflicts merge.

decompositions.resource: Severity under year-to-year multiplicative escalation, stopped at random ('killed' multiplicative growth)
decompositions.composition: Transport identity with growth outpacing termination: ζ − 1 = φ/m < 0. ζ ≈ 0.5 means the log-growth of severity dominates exit, giving a top-heavy allocation; the exponent is a rate ratio, not a dimension.
decompositions.predicted_exponent: α between 1 and 2, set by the distribution of escalation factors and the hazard of ending
decompositions.independent_motivation: Within-war annual escalation factors are measured from different data (1946–2008) than the size distribution.
decompositions.theory_agreement: Clauset, Walter, Cederman & Gleditsch (arXiv 2503.03945; Sci. Adv. 2026) argue that unconditioned escalation is a plausible mechanism for Richardson's law. This agrees with a flux (escalation) reading rather than a stock reading. Checked only via abstracts.
decompositions.testable_consequence: Civil wars, which de-escalate once large, should have steeper tails than interstate wars; this is reported qualitatively. Per-capita normalization changes α (1.53 → 1.7), so the resource definition must be fixed in advance.

cases.source: Clauset (2018) Sci. Adv. 4:eaao3580; Clauset (2019) chapter arXiv 1901.05086 (α = 1.53 ± 0.07, x_min = 7,061; 79% of wars end within two years); Clauset, Walter, Cederman & Gleditsch arXiv 2503.03945; Cederman (2003) APSR 97:135

cases.system: Terrorist attacks worldwide (MIPT database 1968–2006, about 9,000 events); insurgent attacks in Iraq, Colombia, Afghanistan and other conflicts
cases.law_or_distribution: P(x) ∝ x^(−α) for deaths per attack, x ≥ x_min
cases.variable_k: x = deaths per attack
cases.reported_exponent: MLE α ≈ 2.4. In this task this was confirmed only through Mohler's published discussion of Clauset & Woodard 2013, which also notes bootstrap estimates clustering near 2.2. The Clauset et al. 2009 table value 2.4 ± 0.2 at x_min = 12 comes from the repo compilation. Insurgent-event size exponents cluster around 2.5, and extensions span 1.9–4.5 (as stated in a later paper citing Bohorquez et al. 2009 and Johnson et al. 2013). Lognormal and stretched-exponential fits are also plausible.
cases.conversion: Density α used directly; ζ = 1.4
cases.orthopolic_reading: An event total. Units: attacks. ζ ≈ 1.4 means deaths per log band fall as x^(−0.4): bottom-heavy, so most deaths come from small and medium attacks, unlike interstate wars. The log-orthopolic resource is x^1.4–1.5.

decompositions.resource: Attack-unit size under coalescence–fragmentation with size-proportional merging
decompositions.composition: A mean-field merging rate ∝ s_i·s_j (kernel homogeneity ν = 2) gives group sizes n_s ∝ s^(−5/2). Transport reading: a constant member flux through sizes divided by the log-speed v ∝ s^((ν−1)/2) = s^(1/2), so d_log = 1 (members) + 1/2 (merger log-speed) = 3/2. Deaths are assumed ∝ unit strength.
decompositions.independent_motivation: Insurgent and terrorist cells form and split, and larger groups are more likely to join because they have more members who can meet. This is motivated before the casualty data.
decompositions.theory_agreement: Johnson et al. 2006 and Bohorquez et al. 2009 derive 5/2 from coalescence–fragmentation (Eguíluz–Zimmermann type), so the theory agrees. But the assumption deaths ∝ group size is untested, and the same framework was later extended to cover 1.9–4.5.
decompositions.testable_consequence: Where group sizes can be observed, they should show density exponent 5/2. Within the same family, the contrast with wars (ν = 0, giving 3/2) requires interstate coalitions to merge at size-independent rates, which can be checked.

decompositions.resource: Deaths under proportional growth with entry
decompositions.independent_motivation: None; φ/m is read off the exponent.
decompositions.theory_agreement: No published theory for attacks
decompositions.testable_consequence: None

cases.source: Clauset, Young & Gleditsch (2007) J. Conflict Resolution 51:58 (arXiv physics/0606007); Clauset & Woodard (2013) Ann. Appl. Stat. 7:1838 and Mohler discussion (arXiv 1209.0089, 1401.2308); Johnson et al. (2006) arXiv physics/0605035; Bohorquez et al. (2009) Nature 462:911; Clauset et al. (2009) SIAM Rev.

catalogue.domain_patterns:
The 15 cases fall into four groups, and each group has its own kind of "final resource".

(1) d_log ≈ 1, and the resource is the counted unit itself. Examples:
- word tokens in the kernel lexicon (0.95–1.2)
- residents of clustered cities and US metro areas (1.00)
- workers per firm (1.06)
- articles per journal (Bradford; exactly 1 in the verbal form, which is literally discrete orthopolity over geometric rank zones)
- papers per author at small n (Lotka ≈ 1)
- web in-links (1.1)

Every one is a stock or a credit built up by proportional, rich-get-richer growth. The deviation from 1 is additive and small: d_log = 1 + (non-proportional share), i.e. a/(1−a) in Simon's model, A/m in Price/DMS, 1/(m·τ_res) for Gibrat growth with entry. That correction is a ratio of rates, not a dimension.

(2) The same additive form with a large correction:
- citations: d_log = 2 = 1 + A/m with A ≈ m
- top wealth: 1.5 = 1 + 1/(m·τ_res) with m·τ_res ≈ 2. The predicted direction is confirmed: higher top tax rates go with higher ζ.
- terrorism: 1.4–1.5 = 1 (members) + 1/2 (merger log-speed under a product coagulation kernel)

(3) Exponents well above 1, often integers, come from deterministic maps of a Zipf stock. If y ∝ S^c and S is log-orthopolic, then d_log(y) = 1/c:
- returns: c = 1/3, so 3
- volume: c = 2/3, so 3/2
- CEO pay: c = 1/3, so 3 (predicted)
- labor income: c ≈ 1/2, so 2 (backed out)
- city GDP: 1/1.15, so 0.87 (predicted)

Here the authors' reading of p ∝ k^−α works literally. The cubic law says the underlying resource, fund assets, scales as the cube of the return.

Two composition rules emerged:
