- Products of deterministic factors add exponents. Urban output is 1 + δ; firm growth variance is 0.4 + 2 × 0.6 = 1.6, i.e. number of independent units times unit size squared.
- Nested maps multiply exponents. Returns: 1 × 3/2 × 2 = 3.
- Products of independent random factors do neither: they give lognormals (Shockley's productivity model).

(4) Spatial dimension appears explicitly only in urban scaling: δ = H/(D(D+H)) = 1/6, giving 7/6 and 5/6. The final resource there is N² potential pairs, split between output and network. That implies a parameter-free sum rule, β_output + β_network = 2; published US values give 1.98–1.99.

Regularities:
- Stocks and credits sit at d_log ≥ 1 (flat or bottom-heavy). Event totals split by mechanism: wars ≈ 0.5 (top-heavy, escalation) and terrorism ≈ 1.4 (bottom-heavy, fragmentation).
- The coagulation family ζ = (1+ν)/2 puts wars (ν = 0), Zipf (ν = 1) and terrorism (ν = 2) on one line. ν is fitted, so this stays numerology until merger rates are measured.
- Linear-measure readings (d_lin = d_log + 1: token coincidence pairs, resident pairs, r⁴) never had independent motivation in this domain. Here the log measure is the one supplied by proportional-growth mechanisms.

Counterexamples and cautions:
- Web out-degree (ζ ≈ 1.7) has no reading.
- Heaps' β ≈ 0.5 has no resource of its own; it inherits the rare-word ζ. Its V² ∝ N (type-pairs) reading is numerology.
- The exponent depends on how the unit is defined: administrative places ζ ≈ 1.4 against clustered cities ≈ 1.0; firm assets 0.89 against employees 1.06.
- Many urban exponents become compatible with 1 under other city definitions.
- Labor and capital income differ (2 against 1.2) within the same flux.
- Lotka's inverse square looks like a small-n crossover of a Yule–Simon law whose tail should be about 2.3–2.5.

The authors see choosing the resource after seeing the data as a strength of the framework. The readings that earned "derived" or "motivated" all tie the chosen resource to a mechanism whose rates can be measured separately: A/m, a, m·τ_res, δ, the impact exponent, n_eff(S). Readings without such a tie (w^1.5, y², x³, out-degree) were graded numerology.

Verification: exponents were checked against search-engine extracts, abstracts and reliable secondary summaries in this task, because direct fetching of arXiv, PMC and publisher pages was blocked by the network proxy. Values marked in the cases as coming from the repo compilation were not re-verified here.

checks.system: Word tokens in written texts and corpora (English; Moby Dick; Google Books)
checks.corrected_alpha_uncertainty: Clauset et al. 2009 give 1.95 ± 0.02 at x_min = 7 ± 2 (18,855 types). Newman 2005 gives 2.20 ± 0.01 at x_min = 1. The kernel lexicon has rank exponent ≈ 1. In large corpora the rare-word regime has rank exponent ≈ 2, i.e. density ≈ 1.5. Confirmed from my recollection of the primary sources and from docs/zeta-compilation.md. Web tools did not work in this task: the search budget was exhausted, WebFetch failed on DNS, and the proxy blocked arXiv.
checks.algebra_note: α = 1 + 1/γ, d_log = 0.95 and d_lin = 1.95 are correct. Simon's ζ = 1/(1−a) = 1.09–1.11 for a = 0.08–0.10 (recomputed). However, Simon's model forces α > 2 for any a > 0. The x_min = 7 fit (1.95 ± 0.02) lies below 2, and the prediction (2.1) sits between two fits that each have small stated errors: 7σ from one and 5σ from the other. 'Matches within error' holds only if the x_min systematic is counted as the error. The pairs reading is just the identity d_lin = d_log + 1.
checks.best_reading: The tokens themselves (q = k), under the log measure. Resource is fixed by definition, so nothing was chosen to fit: d_log ≈ 1 means each factor-of-ten frequency band carries about the same token mass. The mechanism is Simon/Yule reuse with innovation. Equivalently, types enter at a steady rate, so relative age t/t_i is exactly log-orthopolic (P(u) > u = 1/u), and counts grow as (t/t_i)^(1−a), giving ζ = 1/(1−a).
checks.numerology_risk: Low for d_log ≈ 1 with q = k, because nothing is adjustable and the motivation (Zipf, Simon 1955) is genuinely prior. High for the correction a/(1−a) ≈ 0.1: it is smaller than the x_min systematic (ζ = 0.95–1.20), so it is untested. Simon also predicts linear vocabulary growth, which Heaps' law contradicts. The least-effort reading stays suggestive, since it needs tuning to a critical point. The coincidence-pairs reading is numerology, as the catalogue says.
checks.source: Clauset, Shalizi & Newman (2009) SIAM Rev. 51:661, Table 6.1; Newman (2005) Contemp. Phys. 46:323; Ferrer i Cancho & Solé (2001) J. Quant. Linguist. 8:165; Simon (1955) Biometrika 42:425. All checked from recollection and the repo compilation, not web-verified in this task.

checks.system: Vocabulary growth in texts and corpora (Heaps' law)
checks.corrected_alpha_uncertainty: β ≈ 0.4–0.6 for English corpora. RCV1 gives b = 0.49 with k ≈ 44 (Manning, Raghavan & Schütze, IR textbook; recollection). Single texts and early growth give higher values, about 0.7–1. The implied rare-tail density exponent is α = 1 + β ≈ 1.4–1.6. The catalogue's alpha_density field holds β = 0.5, which is not a density exponent; I report 1.5. The 0.78 value for novels (arXiv 2407.19874) was not verified.
checks.algebra_note: This is an error in one field only. d_log = 0.5 and d_lin = 1.5 are correct for the implied rare-word tail (ζ = β, α = 1.5). As recorded, though, alpha_density = 0.5 makes d_log = α − 1 fail; set it to 1.5 or N/A. β = 1/γ holds only for γ > 1; for γ ≤ 1, β → 1 (V ∝ N/ln N at γ = 1). The reading N/V ∝ N^(1−β) is consistent. The type-pairs model dV/dN ∝ 1/V gives V ∝ N^(1/2) correctly, but nothing motivates it.
checks.best_reading: Heaps' law has no resource of its own. It is the sampling transform of the rare-word Zipf tail: V(N) counts the types with p ≳ 1/N, so β = ζ_rare. Its orthopolic content is the rare-word tail, where token mass per log-frequency band rises as p^0.5 (top-heavy). This is a derived identity (Mandelbrot; Lü, Zhang & Zhou 2010).
checks.numerology_risk: The identity has no free parameter. It is only approximate in real texts: topical burstiness makes vocabulary grow more slowly than in a shuffled text, so β and ζ_rare must be fitted on the same corpus with x_min set in advance. The V² ∝ N type-pairs reading is numerology. Because ζ_rare ≈ 0.5 < 1, a stock (tokens) can be top-heavy, which contradicts the catalogue's own 'stocks sit at d_log ≥ 1' regularity.
checks.source: Lü, Zhang & Zhou (2010) PLoS ONE 5:e14139; Manning, Raghavan & Schütze (2008) Introduction to Information Retrieval, ch. 5 (RCV1 b = 0.49); Gerlach & Altmann (2013) PRX 3:021006. Checked from recollection; web unavailable.

checks.system: US metropolitan areas (Gabaix 1999) and natural cities (Rozenfeld et al. 2011)
checks.corrected_alpha_uncertainty: The OLS rank-size fit gives ζ = 1.005 with reported SE 0.010 and R² = 0.986 (135 MSAs, 1991). The correct SE is about ζ√(2/n) ≈ 0.12 (Gabaix & Ibragimov 2011). Administrative US places give α = 2.37 ± 0.08 (Clauset 2009) or 2.30 (Newman 2005), i.e. ζ ≈ 1.3–1.4. Dispersion across countries is large: Soo (2005) rejects Zipf by OLS in 53 of 73 countries.
checks.algebra_note: α = ζ + 1 and d_log = 1.005 are correct. Gabaix's ζ = 1/(1 − s_min/s̄) is correct. ζ_A = ζ_P/c under a deterministic A ∝ P^c is correct.
checks.best_reading: Residents (q = k) under the log measure, with Gibrat growth and a lower barrier or entry. Gabaix (1999) derives ζ → 1 when s_min/s̄ → 0: people are conserved as cities move up the log-size axis.
checks.numerology_risk: Low for the resident reading, because the resource is fixed by definition. The resident-pairs reading is numerology. Caveats: the statement concerns a defined upper tail of agglomerations. Over all places the distribution is lognormal (Eeckhout 2004), and ζ depends on how a city is defined. The catalogue's area-versus-Bettencourt test is weak. Rozenfeld's natural-city area is built from populated cells, so area ∝ population is partly true by construction. Built-up land from satellite data would be a cleaner test.
checks.source: Gabaix (1999) QJE 114:739; Gabaix & Ibragimov (2011) JBES; Rozenfeld, Rybski, Gabaix & Makse (2011) AER 101:2205; Eeckhout (2004) AER 94:1429; Soo (2005) RSUE 35:239 (via repo compilation). Checked from recollection; web unavailable.

checks.system: Urban scaling (Bettencourt et al. 2007; Bettencourt 2013)
checks.corrected_alpha_uncertainty: The exponents are right, but several are attributed to the wrong country. In Bettencourt et al. 2007, Table 1 (recollection): GDP 1.15 [1.06, 1.23] is China 2002. The same table gives GDP 1.26 for the EU and 1.13 [1.03, 1.23] for Germany 2003. Wages 1.12 (USA 2002), patents 1.27, inventors 1.25 and private R&D employment 1.34 are US values. All the infrastructure values are Germany 2001–2002, not US: cables 0.87 [0.82, 0.92], road surface 0.83 [0.74, 0.92], gasoline stations 0.77, gasoline sales 0.79. Later work puts US MSA GDP at about 1.13.
checks.algebra_note: ζ_Y = ζ_N/β is correct for a deterministic map. δ = H/(D(D+H)) gives 1/6 (D = 2), 1/2 (D = 1) and 1/12 (D = 3); all correct. Y·A_n ∝ N² is an exact rearrangement of Y = G·N²/A_n. The catalogue's sum-rule check ('US values give 1.98–1.99'), however, pairs Chinese GDP or US wages with German infrastructure. Within Germany alone: GDP 1.13 + roads 0.83 = 1.96 and GDP 1.13 + cables 0.87 = 2.00, each with CIs of about ±0.1. The sum rule is consistent but only weakly tested.
checks.best_reading: Output per resident equals social interactions per resident, so d = 1 + δ with δ = H/(D(D+H)). The final resource is the N² potential pairs, shared between output and network area: Y·A_n ∝ N².
checks.numerology_risk: Medium. The theory came before the data and gives exactly this reading, but H = 1 is assumed rather than measured. Patents and R&D (1.25–1.34) and gasoline stations (0.77) fall outside 7/6 and 5/6. The exponents shift with how cities are defined (Arcaute et al. 2015; Leitão et al. 2016; Cottineau et al. 2017). The sum rule is an identity of the model. It tests the model only when output and network are measured for the same cities with the same boundaries. I downgraded the grade from 'derived' for these reasons.
checks.source: Bettencourt, Lobo, Helbing, Kühnert & West (2007) PNAS 104:7301, Table 1 (country labels from recollection); Bettencourt (2013) Science 340:1438; Arcaute et al. (2015) J. R. Soc. Interface; Leitão et al. (2016) R. Soc. Open Sci. Not web-verified in this task.

checks.system: US firms by employees (Axtell 2001)
checks.corrected_alpha_uncertainty: ζ = 1.059 (s.e. 0.054, adjusted R² 0.992) from a log-binned fit to 1997 Census data. Receipts give ζ ≈ 0.99 (s.e. ≈ 0.06) in the same paper (recollection). The 2011 SBA binned MLE, 1.097 ± 0.002, comes from the repo compilation.
checks.algebra_note: α = ζ + 1 is correct. The receipts decomposition gives c = 1.059/0.994 − 1 ≈ 0.065, but both SEs are about 0.06, so c = 0.07 ± 0.09, consistent with 0. The decomposition is not identified.
checks.best_reading: Workers (q = k) under the log measure, with Gibrat growth plus entry and exit. d_log ≈ 1, with a small bottom-heavy correction set by entrant job flux / (total employment × log growth rate).
checks.numerology_risk: Low for the workers reading. The correction ζ − 1 = 0.06 is about one SE from 0, so the rate reading (m·τ ≈ 17) is not yet constrained. The receipts decomposition, with c backed out and indistinguishable from 0, is at best suggestive and closer to numerology.
checks.source: Axtell (2001) Science 293:1818; Luttmer (2007) QJE; repo docs/zeta-compilation.md. Checked from recollection; web unavailable.

checks.system: Firm growth-rate volatility versus size (Compustat)
checks.corrected_alpha_uncertainty: This field holds −β, a scaling exponent, not a density exponent. Stanley et al. 1996 (Nature) give β ≈ 0.15 ± 0.03 on Compustat 1974–1993. Amaral et al. 1997 (J. Phys. I), on the same database, give 0.20 ± 0.03 for sales and 0.18 ± 0.03 for employees and assets (recollection). The catalogue's '0.20 ± 0.03, Stanley 1996, 1975–1991' merges the two papers. Across papers β ranges 0.14–0.20.
checks.algebra_note: Var(ΔS) = σ²S² ∝ S^(2−2β). Define n_eff = S²/ΣS_i². Then n_eff·(S/n_eff)² = S²/n_eff exactly, so n_eff ∝ S^(2β). The catalogue's 1.6 = 0.4 + 2×0.6 is correct for β = 0.2; β = 0.15 gives 1.7 = 0.3 + 1.4. Wyart–Bouchaud's β = 1 − 1/μ gives μ ≈ 1.18–1.25.
checks.best_reading: Absolute growth variance is additive over effectively independent sub-units. The firm's size is spread over n_eff ∝ S^(0.3–0.4) units of size S^(0.6–0.7). Wyart & Bouchaud (2003), Sutton (2002) and Riccaboni et al. (2008) all derive this reading.
checks.numerology_risk: Low for the reading: additivity of variance is forced by statistics, and the decomposition is an identity once n_eff is defined by a Herfindahl index. The empirical content is n_eff ∝ S^(2β) measured at product level. Why 2β ≈ 0.3–0.4 has several competing derivations: Pareto sub-unit sizes, proportional growth of sub-units, and a hierarchical-tree model. So the reading is robust but the mechanism is not unique.
checks.source: Stanley et al. (1996) Nature 379:804; Amaral et al. (1997) J. Phys. I 7:621; Wyart & Bouchaud (2003) Physica A; Riccaboni et al. (2008) PNAS; Sutton (2002) Physica A. Recollection; not web-verified.

checks.system: Richest US individuals (Forbes 400)
checks.corrected_alpha_uncertainty: Klass et al. 2006 give an average ζ = 1.49 over the 1988–2003 lists (recollection; the repo agrees). The same kind of data gives other values: Levy & Solomon 1997, 1.36; Newman 2005, α = 2.09 (ζ = 1.09, x_min = $600M); Clauset 2009, α = 2.3 ± 0.1, with the pure power law rejected (p ≈ 0). So ζ ranges 1.1–1.5 by estimator and year. The fixed-k tax result (ζ 1.5–1.8) was not verified.
checks.algebra_note: α = ζ + 1 is correct. One interpretation slip: from stationary resource accounting with deterministic growth m and size-independent exit rate δ, ζ = δ/m = 1 + J_R/(Q·m). So ζ − 1 = 0.49 means Q/J_R (resource turnover time via entry) ≈ 2/m. It does not mean a unit of wealth 'climbs about two e-folds before it leaves'. The mean climb before exit is m/δ = 1/ζ ≈ 0.67 e-folds.
checks.best_reading: Wealth (q = k) under multiplicative returns with size-independent exit (Kesten/Gibrat). d_log = 1 plus a turnover correction that measured growth and exit rates should predict.
checks.numerology_risk: Low for the choice of resource. The 0.49 correction is backed out, and the ζ estimate itself spans 1.1–1.5, so the rate interpretation has not been tested. The w^1.5 liquidation-cost reading is numerology. The tax-direction evidence would be qualitative support, but I did not verify it here.
checks.source: Klass, Biham, Levy, Malcai & Solomon (2006) Econ. Lett. 90:290; Levy & Solomon (1997) Physica A; Newman (2005); Clauset et al. (2009). Recollection and repo compilation; web unavailable.

checks.system: US top incomes, labor versus capital (IRS 1916–2019)
checks.corrected_alpha_uncertainty: Labor ζ ≈ 2 and capital ζ ≈ 1.2, both stable for about three decades (abstract of Lee, Sasaki, Toda & Wang; recollection). Total top income ζ ≈ 1.4–1.8 (Toda & Wang) was not verified.
checks.algebra_note: ζ_y = ζ_S/κ and ζ_K = ζ_W/(1+ε) are correct. 1.49/1.2 − 1 ≈ 0.24 if the populations matched, but they do not (Forbes 400 versus IRS filers).
checks.best_reading: For capital income: a flux r·W drawn from the near-Zipf wealth stock (motivated; that returns rise with wealth, ε > 0, is independently supported in direction by Fagereng et al. 2020 and Bach, Calvet & Sodini 2020; recollection). For labor income ζ ≈ 2, the exponent shown here, no reading rises above suggestive.
checks.numerology_risk: High for labor. At least two prior mechanisms fit ζ = 2 without fixing it. One is assignment to a Zipf-distributed scale with κ = 1/2, where κ is backed out from the exponent; only the CEO value κ = 1/3 is measured. The other is random earnings growth with exit or creative destruction (Jones & Kim 2018; Gabaix, Lasry, Lions & Moll 2016), which fits any ζ > 1. The y² reading is numerology. The CEO-pay ζ ≈ 3 prediction is a real out-of-sample test that has not been checked.
checks.source: Lee, Sasaki, Toda & Wang (2022) arXiv 2206.04257; Gabaix & Landier (2008) QJE 123:49; Jones & Kim (2018) JPE. Recollection; not web-verified.

checks.system: Citations to scientific papers
checks.corrected_alpha_uncertainty: Redner 1998 gives α ≈ 3 (rank slope ≈ 1/2). Clauset 2009 gives 3.16 ± 0.06 at x_min = 160 (recollection; the repo agrees). Golosovsky & Solomon 2012 give ≈ 3.15. The power-law form is contested: field-normalized distributions collapse onto a lognormal (Radicchi, Fortunato & Castellano 2008), and Redner (2005) found a lognormal fits Physical Review data better.
checks.algebra_note: γ = 2 + A/m is correct, so A = m gives 3. With steady arrival, P(t/t_i > u) = 1/u exactly, so the system is log-orthopolic in relative age u. x ∝ u^(m/(m+A)) = u^(1/2) then gives ζ_x = 2. The linear x³ reading only restates the log reading in another measure.
checks.best_reading: Relative age (exposure time) is exactly log-orthopolic because papers enter at a steady rate. Citations are a deterministic power of it, x ∝ u^θ with θ = m/(m+A), so d_log(x) = 1/θ = 2. The same structure underlies Simon's model (θ = 1 − a), the web (θ = m/(m+A)) and Lotka.
checks.numerology_risk: Medium. I downgraded the grade from 'derived'. The mechanism is prior (Price, DMS), but A = m is read off the exponent: Price's A ≈ 1 with m ≈ 20 references would give α ≈ 2.05. One prior argument for A = m exists: visibility proportional to total degree (k_in + m), as when papers are found by following links in both directions. It is not established. Aging and fitness (Wang, Song & Barabási 2013) change the tail, and lognormal alternatives fit.
checks.source: Redner (1998) EPJ B 4:131; Clauset et al. (2009); Dorogovtsev, Mendes & Samukhin (2000) PRL 85:4633; Radicchi, Fortunato & Castellano (2008) PNAS 105:17268. Recollection; web unavailable.

checks.system: Authors' productivity (Lotka's law)
checks.corrected_alpha_uncertainty: Lotka 1926: 1.888 (Chemical Abstracts) and 2.021 (Auerbach), fitted over roughly n = 1 to 10–30 (recollection). The MathSciNet tail is α = 4.3 ± 0.1 above n = 133 (Clauset 2009; recollection; the repo marks it as memory).
checks.algebra_note: Recomputed: Lotka(2) truncated at n_max = 100–1000 gives mean productivity 3.17–4.55, a = 0.22–0.32, ζ = 1.28–1.46 and α = 2.28–2.46 (agrees). The Yule–Simon local slope for ρ = 1.28–1.46 is 1.92–2.03 over n = 1–10 and 2.23–2.39 over n = 10–100. The catalogue's '1.7–2.2' is too wide, and the true match to Lotka's values is closer than stated.
checks.best_reading: Papers (q = k) under the log measure, with cumulative advantage and steady newcomer entry. d_log ≈ 1 holds only over the first decade of n.
checks.numerology_risk: Medium-high. Over one decade almost any right-skewed distribution has a local slope near 2, and a lognormal (Shockley) fits comparably. The Simon asymptote (2.3–2.5) is contradicted by the MathSciNet tail (4.3), where finite careers dominate, so the mechanism fails exactly where it could be tested. The Shockley alternative is a counter-reading (no power law), suggestive.
checks.source: Lotka (1926) J. Wash. Acad. Sci. 16:317; Clauset et al. (2009); Simon (1955); Price (1976). Recollection; web unavailable.

checks.system: Journals contributing articles on a subject (Bradford's law)
checks.corrected_alpha_uncertainty: The verbal law is exact by construction. The empirical multiplier n is set per bibliography. Bradford's geophysics data were roughly 9 : 59 : 258 journals giving 429 : 499 : 404 articles (approximate recollection). The Groos droop is a common deviation.
checks.algebra_note: Equal articles per geometric zone gives cumulative articles ∝ ln r, so articles per journal ∝ 1/r, ζ = 1 and α = 2. The zone-yield ratio n^(1−1/ζ) is correct; 5^(1−1/1.1) = 1.158 (recomputed).
checks.best_reading: Discrete log-orthopolity of articles over geometric rank zones. Bradford's verbal law is itself the orthopolic statement with d = 1. Egghe proved it equivalent to Lotka(2) and Zipf(1).
checks.numerology_risk: No freedom in the resource, but there are three caveats. First, it is not independent evidence: it is equivalent to Lotka(2)/Zipf(1) for the same data and should not be counted as a separate confirmation. Second, analysts choose the number of zones and the equal-yield boundaries and then report n, so the testable content is only the constancy of the zone multipliers. Third, the Groos droop and core curvature are frequent failures.
checks.source: Bradford (1934) Engineering 137:85; Egghe (1988) J. Documentation 44:53; Leimkuhler (1967). Recollection; web unavailable.

checks.system: World Wide Web in-degree (Broder et al. 2000; Albert, Jeong & Barabási 1999)
checks.corrected_alpha_uncertainty: 2.1 is the published full-range in-degree value (Broder et al.; Albert et al.); out-degree is 2.72 (Broder) or 2.45 (nd.edu). A tail MLE gives α = 2.336 ± 0.009 at x_min = 3,684 with the pure power law rejected (p ≈ 0) (Clauset 2009; recollection; the repo marks this as tentative). So α = 2.1–2.34, d_log = 1.1–1.34 and A/m = 0.1–0.34.
checks.algebra_note: d_log = 1.1 and d_lin = 2.1 are correct, and γ = 2 + A/m is correct.
checks.best_reading: In-links (q = k) under the log measure, with preferential attachment and small initial attractiveness. d_log ≈ 1.1–1.3, so links are nearly log-orthopolic.
checks.numerology_risk: Medium. A/m is read off the exponent, and the exponent itself depends on x_min (2.1 versus 2.34). Measured attachment kernels in online networks are often sublinear (recollection, not verified), and a pure power law is rejected in the tail. For out-degree the right grade is 'none' (no reading), not 'numerology'. It is a genuine counterexample.
checks.source: Broder et al. (2000) Comput. Netw. 33:309; Albert, Jeong & Barabási (1999) Nature 401:130; Clauset et al. (2009). Recollection; web unavailable.

checks.system: US stock returns and trading volume (inverse cubic and half-cubic laws)
checks.corrected_alpha_uncertainty: ζ_r = 3.10 ± 0.03 (positive tail) and 2.84 ± 0.12 (negative tail) for about 1,000 US stocks, 1994–95, over 2–100 SD (recollection). ζ_V ≈ 1.5 (Gopikrishnan et al. 2000; Plerou & Stanley 2007 across NYSE, LSE and Paris). This is disputed: Rácz, Eisler & Kertész (2009) find volume exponents that differ by stock and are often higher. Return tails vary roughly 2–5 across markets and horizons.
checks.algebra_note: V ∝ S^(1/(1+δ)) and r ∝ V^δ give ζ_V = ζ_S(1+δ) and ζ_r = ζ_S(1+δ)/δ. For δ = 1/2 these are 3/2 and 3. Correct.
checks.best_reading: The assets of trading institutions, a stock assumed to be Zipf, seen through the optimal trade size V ∝ S^(2/3) and square-root impact r ∝ V^(1/2). The log-orthopolic resource in the return coordinate is S ∝ r³ (Gabaix, Gopikrishnan, Plerou & Stanley 2003).
checks.numerology_risk: Low-medium. The inputs are measured separately from returns, and square-root impact of metaorders is now well supported (Tóth et al. 2011; recollection). But fund sizes may be lognormal rather than Zipf (Schwarzkopf & Farmer 2010), and large returns are often driven by order-book gaps rather than large orders (Farmer et al. 2004). GARCH/Kesten also gives 3–4 with fitted parameters. A clean test: ζ_r/ζ_V = 1/δ across markets with different impact exponents.
checks.source: Gopikrishnan et al. (1998) EPJ B 3:139; Plerou et al. (1999) PRE 60:6519; Gopikrishnan et al. (2000) PRE 62:R4493; Gabaix et al. (2003) Nature 423:267; Schwarzkopf & Farmer (2010). Recollection; web unavailable.

checks.system: Interstate wars, Correlates of War 1823–2003 (Richardson's law)
checks.corrected_alpha_uncertainty: 1.53 ± 0.07 at x_min = 7,061, from 95 wars with 51 in the tail (Clauset 2018; recollection). Per-capita intensity gives α = 1.7 ± 0.2 (Clauset 2009) and 1.80 (Newman 2005).
checks.algebra_note: d_log = 0.53 and ζ = 0.53 are correct. Mean-field branching gives sizes s^(−3/2) and durations T^(−2) with s ∝ T². The coagulation family gives ζ = (1+ν)/2. Both are correct. Because α < 2, the mean diverges.
checks.best_reading: α = 3/2 is equivalent to ζ = 1/2, i.e. war severity is log-orthopolic in √x. Three mechanisms give exactly this: critical branching (log-orthopolic in duration, with x ∝ T²), constant-kernel coagulation, and stopped multiplicative escalation. The escalation (flux) reading has the most data behind it, but its exponent is a fitted rate ratio.
checks.numerology_risk: High. I downgraded the grade from 'motivated': at least three simple mechanisms give 3/2, so matching 1.53 does not tell them apart. The branching reading fails its own test, because durations are not T^(−2). With α < 2 the total is dominated by the largest war (WWII), so the 'conserved total' does not average out. The escalation paper (arXiv 2503.03945) could not be verified here.
checks.source: Clauset (2018) Sci. Adv. 4:eaao3580; Clauset et al. (2009); Newman (2005); Cederman (2003) APSR 97:135. Recollection; web unavailable.

checks.system: Terrorist and insurgent attacks (deaths per attack)
checks.corrected_alpha_uncertainty: 2.4 ± 0.2 at x_min = 12 ± 4 with p = 0.68 (Clauset 2009; recollection; the repo agrees). Clauset, Young & Gleditsch (2007) give ≈ 2.38, and insurgencies give ≈ 2.5 (Johnson et al. 2006; Bohorquez et al. 2009).
checks.algebra_note: n_s ∝ s^(−(3+ν)/2), so ν = 2 gives 5/2. Then B = s²n ∝ s^((1−ν)/2) and v ∝ s^((ν−1)/2) = s^(1/2), so q = members × merger log-speed = s^(3/2) and d_log = 1.5. Verified. 'Deaths ∝ unit size' adds a deterministic map whose exponent is assumed to be 1.
checks.best_reading: Coalescence–fragmentation of attack units. The final resource is members × merger log-speed = s^(3/2), with deaths assumed proportional to unit size.
checks.numerology_risk: Medium-high. I downgraded the grade from 'motivated'. Within 2.4 ± 0.2, 5/2 fits, but so does Gibrat with entry (any α > 2) and a lognormal. The deaths ∝ size map is untested. The model family was later tuned to cover α ≈ 1.9–4.5, so 5/2 is not a sharp prediction. Grading this ζ = (1+ν)/2 family 'motivated' here and 'numerology' for wars is inconsistent unless ν is measured in both.
checks.source: Clauset et al. (2009); Clauset, Young & Gleditsch (2007) JCR 51:58; Johnson et al. (2006) arXiv physics/0605035; Bohorquez et al. (2009) Nature 462:911. Recollection; web unavailable.

verification.missing_cases:
Verification note: I could not use web tools in this task. WebSearch reported the per-turn search budget already exhausted, WebFetch failed on DNS, and the proxy rejected arXiv. All 'confirmed' statuses rest on my recollection of the primary sources, cross-checked against docs/zeta-compilation.md. Treat them as not web-verified.

Omitted cases in this domain:

(1) Spatial-interaction laws, the most direct tests of a dimensional resource:
- Gravity laws of trade and migration. The distance exponent is about 1 for trade (Disdier & Head 2008 meta-analysis) and varies for migration.
- Stouffer's intervening opportunities and the radiation model (Simini et al. 2012). Flow is shared equally per intervening opportunity, and the number of opportunities within r grows with r² in 2D. This is an explicitly orthopolic, parameter-free reading.
- Human mobility. Banknote dispersal p(r) ∝ r^(−1.59) (Brockmann et al. 2006); phone displacements ∝ (r + r0)^(−1.75) (González et al. 2008). Converting radial to areal density shifts the exponent by D − 1, so these test 'which dimension'.

(2) Clauset et al. (2009) social and technological tails, each a test of the 'stocks sit at d_log ≥ 1' regularity:
- religious followers: α ≈ 1.8, d_log ≈ 0.8, a top-heavy stock
- web hits: α ≈ 1.81, power law rejected
- book sales: α ≈ 3.7 ± 0.3; email address books: α ≈ 3.5 ± 0.6. Both are large exponents with no natural composite resource.
- telephone calls: α ≈ 2.09
- surnames: α ≈ 2.5 ± 0.2 (Newman 2005: 1.94)
- Internet AS degree: α ≈ 2.1

Together with Moby Dick (ζ = 0.95) and the rare-word regime (ζ ≈ 0.5), these contradict the catalogue's claim that stocks and credits sit at d_log ≥ 1.

(3) Bursty human waiting times. Email gives α ≈ 1; letters give 3/2 (Barabási 2005; Oliveira & Barabási 2005). Priority-queue models produce discrete exponents.

(4) Social networks:
- sexual-contact degree (Liljeros et al. 2001)
- coauthorship and actor networks (power law with cutoff)
- chess-opening popularity, a Zipf law derived from branching (Blasius & Tönjes 2009)

(5) Deterministic social scaling laws:
- Metcalfe's law (value ∝ n²) against Odlyzko's n·log n. This is the one place where the pairs reading the catalogue dismisses is argued in advance.
- Hirsch's relation N_c ≈ (3–5)·h², a square-root map.
- Price's square-root law, a corollary of Lotka.
- Zipf's meaning–frequency law, meanings ∝ f^(1/2).
- Taylor's law and fluctuation scaling in traded value and web traffic, with exponents between 1/2 and 1 (Eisler, Bartos & Kertész 2008).
- Number of trades, ζ_N ≈ 3.4 (Plerou et al. 2000).
- Social-brain group layers 5/15/50/150 with a discrete ratio of about 3 (Zhou, Sornette, Hill & Dunbar 2005), a candidate for discrete orthopolity of a time budget.

Counterexamples to the program:
- Lognormal rather than power-law data, which leave no exponent to read: all US places (Eeckhout 2004); mutual-fund sizes (Schwarzkopf & Farmer 2010); Compustat firm sizes (Stanley et al. 1995); field-normalized citations (Radicchi et al. 2008); online popularity (Digg and YouTube votes and views); Shockley productivity.
- Exponent heterogeneity: city ζ across 73 countries (Soo 2005), and urban-scaling exponents that shift with city boundaries (Cottineau et al. 2017). The 'resource' must be argued per system, not per domain.

Regularities the catalogue missed or misstated:

(a) A single final resource underlies every cumulative-advantage case. When objects enter at a constant rate, relative age u = t/t_i is exactly log-orthopolic (P(U > u) = 1/u). Any deterministic growth k ∝ u^θ then gives ζ = 1/θ:
- Simon words: θ = 1 − a
- Price/DMS citations and the web: θ = m/(m+A)
- Barabási–Albert: θ = 1/2
So 'exposure time' is the shared log-orthopolic stock, and the exponent measures how fast the resource accrues with age.

(b) α = 3/2 laws are equivalent to Zipf in √k. This covers war severity, mean-field critical branching sizes (log-orthopolic in duration), first-passage times of a random walk (log-orthopolic in excursion extent) and constant-kernel coagulation. Matching 3/2 therefore never selects among them.

(c) The 'deterministic map of a Zipf stock' group (d_log = 1/c) can produce any exponent. A reading counts as evidence only when c is measured independently, as for impact and trade size, Roberts' law, and urban β.

(d) When α < 2 (wars, rare words, religions, web hits), the total is dominated by the largest object, so the orthopolic constant does not average out.

(e) Correct the catalogue's sum-rule evidence. The US 1.98–1.99 pairs Chinese GDP and US wages with German infrastructure. Within Germany the sums are 1.96–2.00 with CIs of about ±0.1.

regularities.statement: TERRITORY (CAPACITY) RULE. When objects tile a support of dimension d_s without systematic gaps, the count per ln L scales as L^-d_s. The orthopolic final resource is then the territory L^d_s, not the object's own content. For any content k ∝ L^D_k this gives zeta_k = d_s/D_k, i.e. alpha_k = 1 + d_s/D_k. Exponents well above 2 are a dimension count, and fractional values are ratios of dimensions.
supporting_cases: Craters in equilibrium (geo-astro): d_s=2, D_k=1, zeta=2. Derived (Gault; Richardson).
Fracture networks, dense regime (geo-astro): a = D+1, with D measured from centre positions. Derived (Davy et al. 2010 UFM; Bour et al. 2002).

Critical percolation (physics): tau-1 = d/D_f gives 2D 187/91 and 3D 1+3/2.5229 = 2.1891 (verifier-corrected). The rule fails above d_c=6, which is exactly where clusters stop packing space, so the failure is predicted.
Dark-matter field halos (geo-astro): Lagrangian volume, zeta→1, tilted by the spectral slope to alpha = 2-(n+3)/6. Derived.
IMF above the turnover (geo-astro): 3D turbulent territory with core mass ∝ L^(4-beta), giving Gamma = 3/(4-beta) ≈ 1.33-1.36. Motivated.
Earthquakes below Mw ~6.7 (geo-astro): 2D fault territory with M0 ∝ L^3 gives zeta_M0 = 2/3 and b=1. Verifier grade: suggestive.
Lakes (geo-astro): territory L^2 with water area ∝ L^(91/48) gives 2.055, against 2.14 observed. Verifier downgraded to motivated.
Inverse-square laws (physics): the number of area cells ∝ r^(d-1) is the counted capacity. Derived.
Rayleigh-Jeans, Debye, Bloch and Stefan-Boltzmann (physics): the number of active modes ∝ T^(d/s) is a k-space capacity. Derived.
Rivers (geo-astro): channel sites tile the basin at spacing W(a) ∝ a^(1-h), so beta = 1-h. The Scheidegger network (h=2/3) moves beta to 1/3 as predicted. Derived.
counterexamples: Earthquakes above width saturation: rupture-area orthopolity predicts b = 0.75, but USGS data give b ≈ 1.0-1.1 up to M7, rising to 1.3 ± 0.15 above M7.5.

Event catalogues are rates, not capacities. With recurrence ∝ slip ∝ L, slot counting gives b = 1.5, not 1, so the earthquake and flare readings need an extra assumption: a per-slot rate independent of size.
3D fracture networks: 3-3.6 observed against a = 4 predicted for the dense regime (convention unchecked).
Hartmann's crater equilibrium slope of -1.83 against -2 is unexplained.
Landslides: 2D territory (alpha_A = 2) fails outright.

GMC/clump mass spectra, inner Galaxy, 1.5-1.8 (verifier, from memory): with Larson's M ∝ R^2 this fails both the 3D prediction (2.5) and the 2D one (2.0), in the same medium where the IMF reading is claimed.
Rock fragmentation, D ≈ 2.5-2.6 (Turcotte; Sammis): a 3D packing that does not fill space.
Electrons in metals (C ∝ T in every dimension) and Dirac electrons (T^2): the slot exponent is the density-of-states exponent plus 1, not a spatial dimension.
Graphite T^2 has two slot geometries that give the same 2.
Wildfires: no territory reading fits.
regularities.how_to_test: Pre-register d_s from geometry and D_k from an independently measured content scaling before looking at the distribution. Candidates not yet examined: Euclidean source counts (d_s=3, flux ∝ r^-2, so N(>S) ∝ S^-3/2); planetary ring particles (cross-section-limited, q ≈ 3?); volumetric or swarm seismicity (d_s=3 predicts b = 1.5, while FD-SOC predicts 1); lake radius of gyration (N(>L) ∝ L^-2 exactly, independent of D_f); hedgerow or strip plant packing (N ∝ M^-1/3); filament-dominated core mass functions (2/(4-beta) ≈ 0.9); 3D fault-disc exponent (4 in the dense regime). The rule is falsifiable, as the GMC failure shows, but it is only informative when D_k is measured rather than fitted. Stereological identities (crater transects, a_3D = a_2D + 1, scanlines) hold for any mechanism and do not test it.

regularities.statement: CASCADE / TRANSPORT RULE. Where a conserved quantity moves through size, scale or energy, the primitive orthopolic quantity is the FLUX F, which is constant per log class. The standing stock per log class is B = F/v, so d_stock = d_flux + z, where v ∝ k^z is the log-speed (turnover, disruption, escape or growth rate). Measured flat stocks are the special case z = 0.
supporting_cases: K41 turbulence (physics): energy flux eps is constant, and d_log = 2/3 is exactly the exponent of the eddy-turnover rate. The 4/5 law, an exact flux statement, holds without intermittency correction while the spectrum (the stock) carries about +0.03. Derived.

2D enstrophy cascade (physics): z = 0 (non-local strain), so both the enstrophy stock and the enstrophy flux are flat and E ∝ k^-3. Drag breaks flux conservation and steepens the spectrum, a predicted failure mode. Derived.
Batchelor passive scalar (physics): z = 0 (uniform strain below the Kolmogorov scale), so variance per ln k is flat (k^-1), with level ∝ chi(nu/eps)^1/2. Derived.
Dohnanyi asteroids (geo-astro): mass × disruption rate, D^3 × D^-0.5 = D^2.5, so alpha = 3.5. Strength dependence (21+s)/(6+s) gives a second prediction. Derived.
Sheldon spectrum (bio-eco): biomass per log mass = energy flux/log-growth speed. d = 1 = 3/4 (metabolic turnover) + 1/4 (trophic dilution, ln TE/ln PPMR). Derived.
Cosmic rays (geo-astro): leaky box, N = Q × tau_esc, with delta = 1/3 measured independently (AMS-02 B/C). The structure is derived; the source index is not.
Wind waves (physics): the Zakharov-Filonenko omega^-4 range with level ∝ P^(1/3) for four-wave transfer (v ∝ B^2), and the capillary branch omega^(-17/6) with level ∝ P^(1/2) for three-wave transfer.
Terrorism coagulation (social-info): members × merger log-speed s^(1/2), giving d_log = 3/2 (suggestive).
Gibrat growth in social systems (cities, firms, wealth): proportional growth means v is independent of size, so flux flatness appears as stock flatness, ζ ≈ 1.
counterexamples: Cosmic rays: DSA source 2.0 plus delta 0.333 gives 2.33, not the observed 2.7, or 2.85 for protons (verifier). The source index must be fitted (r ≈ 3.0-3.2), so it is matched after the fact.
Capillary wave turbulence: the exponent matches but the predicted level ∝ P^(1/2) fails in both regimes (Falcon et al. 2007). The flux reading is only half confirmed.
Gravity waves: Phillips' local input-dissipation balance gives the same omega^-4 and the same level ∝ u_*, so neither the exponent nor the level discriminates the cascade reading.
Sheldon flatness holds only in aggregate. In the repo's GLOSSAQUA analysis only 7.9-24% of 1,300 individual spectra are flat within tolerance.
Main-belt asteroids above 100 km are primordial, not collisionally relaxed, and debris-disk grain indices (q ≈ 3.36) are shallower than the strength-regime prediction (3.6-3.7).
MRN dust: 3.5 is the generic number for any steady fragmentation cascade, so matching it does not single out ISM shattering (suggestive).
Beta-model 'fewer active slots' correction to K41 overshoots (mu/3 against mu/9).
regularities.how_to_test: For each cascade, write down the conserved quantity, its locality in scale, and the log-speed exponent z from an independent measurement. Then predict both the stock exponent and the dependence of the spectral level on the flux (prefactor), before fitting. Discriminating tests: the 2D inverse cascade must give k^-5/3; flat-stock ranges (z=0) must show exponential pair separation, while z>0 ranges show power-law separation (Richardson); drag or sinks must steepen spectra by a computable amount; the Dohnanyi slope must track measured strength s; a single trophic level must give alpha = 1.75 rather than 2. Unexamined targets: inverse wave-action cascade (omega^-11/3); Kelvin-wave and MHD (Iroshnikov-Kraichnan k^-3/2 against Goldreich-Sridhar) cascades; sediment grain-size spectra under steady abrasion.

regularities.statement: EXPONENT ARITHMETIC (COMPOSITION CALCULUS). (a) Products of deterministic cost laws ADD resource exponents. (b) A deterministic change of coordinate y ∝ x^c DIVIDES survival exponents (zeta_y = zeta_x/c). Nested maps multiply. (c) Cost optimisations give ratios such as (c+2)/a, D/(D+1) and H/(D(D+H)). (d) Products of independent random factors do not compose this way: they give lognormals. Sums of power-law costs give crossovers, not new power laws.
supporting_cases: Additive: Stefan-Boltzmann d+1 = d slots + 1 energy per slot; Richardson 3 = 1 + 2; Brownian 1/f^2 = white (0) + integrator gain (2); urban output 1 + delta (delta = 1/6 from D=2, H=1); firm growth variance 0.3-0.4 (number of units) + 2 × 0.6-0.7 (unit size squared); Kleiber D/(D+1) as D spatial dimensions + 1 transport dimension; Sheldon 3/4 + 1/4; earthquake moment L^1 (slip) × L^2 (area) = L^3.

Coordinate change: earthquakes zeta_M0 = 2/3 from zeta_L = 2 and M0 ∝ L^3; inverse cubic law zeta_r = 1 × 3/2 × 2 (fund assets → trade volume → square-root impact) and zeta_V = 3/2, with zeta_r = 2 zeta_V a separable check; GSMF zeta_* = 0.9/(5/3) ≈ 0.54 against 0.47-0.50 observed; river energy 0.45/0.5 = 0.90 (observed); random-walk span to duration (×1/2); branching duration to size (×1/2); lakes d/D_f; Heaps beta = zeta of the rare-word tail; city GDP survival exponent ≈ 1/1.15.
Ratios from optimisation: Murray Q ∝ r^((c+2)/a), giving 3 (laminar), 7/3 (rough turbulent) and 27/11 (Blasius); Banavar C ∝ N^(1+1/D); Padoan-Nordlund 3/(4-beta); Bettencourt delta = H/(D(D+H)).

Sum rules from a shared budget: urban Y·A_n ∝ N², so beta_output + beta_network = 2. Within Germany the sums are 1.96-2.00 with CIs of about ±0.1 (verifier: the catalogue's US pairing mixed Chinese, US and German values).
counterexamples: Kleiber curvature (Kolokotrones 2010): a product of power laws cannot produce a convex log-log relation; an additive cost (B = aM^(2/3) + bM) can.
Earthquake width saturation and the asteroid strength-gravity transition: crossovers between additive regimes, where no single composed exponent holds.
Shockley productivity (Lotka): a product of independent random abilities gives a lognormal, not added exponents.
Sparre Andersen: the 1D first-return exponent 1/2 is universal even for Levy flights, so 'span × diffusion' is not the real reason for it.
Capacity × velocity for Kleiber (2/3 + 1/12): the 1/12 is the maximal exponent chosen to recover 3/4, not measured, so the composition is numerology.
Home range 3/4 + ~1/4: the sharing term is defined as the residual.
Receipts per worker c = 0.07 ± 0.09 for firms: backed out and indistinguishable from 0.
regularities.how_to_test: The calculus is algebra and always holds; its empirical content lies entirely in whether each factor exponent is measured independently. Test by requiring every component (slip-length, Hanks-Bakun M0-A, Larson M-R, impact exponent delta, SHMR slope, Hack's h, PPMR and TE) to come from a different dataset than the target distribution, and by predicting the composed exponent before fitting. For sums of costs, predict the crossover location (e.g. the mass where the local Kleiber slope passes 0.7; Mw ≈ 6.7 for seismogenic-width saturation; the strength-gravity transition at ~0.1-1 km for asteroids) instead of a single exponent. For sum rules, measure output and network for the same cities with the same boundaries.

regularities.statement: PROPORTIONAL-GROWTH ZIPF RULE. Counted stocks and credits that grow by proportional (Gibrat or rich-get-richer) accumulation with entry sit near d_log = 1 (zeta ≈ 1). The deviation is an additive RATE RATIO, zeta - 1 ≈ entry/growth, not a dimension. Unified form: with steady entry, relative age u = t/t_i is exactly log-orthopolic, P(U>u) = 1/u. Any deterministic accrual k ∝ u^theta then gives zeta = 1/theta.
supporting_cases: US metro areas and natural cities, zeta = 1.005 (SE ≈ 0.12): Gabaix limit, derived.
US firms by employees, zeta = 1.059 ± 0.054: derived.
Bradford's verbal law: literally discrete orthopolity over geometric rank zones (d=1). Equivalent to Lotka(2) and Zipf(1), so it is not independent evidence.
Moby Dick and kernel words, zeta ≈ 0.95-1.2: Simon reuse, theta = 1 - a.
Web in-links, alpha = 2.1-2.34: theta = m/(m+A).
Citations, alpha ≈ 3.0-3.16: theta = 1/2 requires A = m.
Gene-family sizes, alpha ≥ 2 in the duplication-innovation model.
Forbes 400 wealth, zeta 1.1-1.5: Kesten growth with exit; higher top tax rates go with higher zeta (direction not verified here).
counterexamples: Rare-word regime in large corpora, zeta ≈ 0.5: a top-heavy stock, contradicting 'stocks sit at d_log ≥ 1'.
Religious followers (alpha ≈ 1.8) and web hits: top-heavy stocks.
Species per genus in plants (alpha ≈ 1.45 < 2): a growing, non-stationary Yule clade; the plant and mammal (2.4) values need different model variants chosen after the fact. Numerology.
MathSciNet authors, tail 4.3 above n = 133: finite careers break cumulative advantage exactly where the Simon asymptote (2.3-2.5) could be tested.
Lognormal populations that leave no exponent: all US places (Eeckhout), mutual-fund sizes, Compustat firms, field-normalised citations.
Administrative cities, zeta ≈ 1.3-1.4: the exponent depends on how a unit is defined.
Birth-death-innovation models with gene loss allow alpha < 2 (Karev's 1.9).
regularities.how_to_test: The zeta ≈ 1 part is robust. The correction is only meaningful if entry and growth rates are measured before fitting. For each case, predict zeta - 1 from panel data: the entrant employment share and employment-weighted log growth (BDS) for firms; the type/token ratio for texts (Simon gives zeta - 1 ≈ a); the attachment-kernel offset A/m measured from citation or link panels; the ORFan founding rate for gene families; list turnover and return dispersion for Forbes. Unexamined targets: app or software-package downloads, GitHub stars, patent forward citations, surname frequencies (alpha ≈ 1.94-2.5), Wikipedia edit counts per article.

regularities.statement: LOG MEASURE FOR MULTIPLICATIVE SIZE TRANSFER; LINEAR MEASURE FOR ADDITIVE COORDINATES TRAVERSED AT A CONSTANT RATE. In the k^-3 ambiguity (log-orthopolic in k^2 against linear-orthopolic in k^3), every case with a known mechanism takes the log reading. Linear readings created only by d_lin = d_log + 1 (volume for area, pairs k², x³, r⁴, coincidences) never acquired independent motivation, apart from the FD-SOC postulate.
supporting_cases: Log with a mechanism: craters, fractures, lakes, Dohnanyi, K41, Kraichnan, Batchelor, Sheldon, Murray, percolation, cities, firms, words, citations, web, avalanches (in duration), 1/f and Omori (in time).

In spectra, the k^-3 'k^2' is a squared-gradient weight (enstrophy, wave slope variance), not an area. Kraichnan and Phillips both give log-orthopolic in k^2. The 2D mode count per ln k (∝ k^2) coincides with it, but in 3D the gradient weight stays k^2 while the mode count becomes k^3, so 3D separates them.

Linear readings with a mechanism: radiation energy per shell dr = P/c (constant speed); white noise per Hz (equipartition); dark-matter halos, equal mass per unit peak height nu (excursion set); Richardson, energy delivered per dt; critical branching, activations per linear duration interval (holds only if alpha_T = gamma); random walk d ≥ 3, explored volume; Kepler II, time per swept area.
Arrhenius bridge: a uniformly distributed linear variable (barrier energy, rate-state stress) maps into log-uniform time. This gives 1/f (Dutta-Horn) and Omori p ≈ 1 (Dieterich).
counterexamples: FD-SOC (flares, earthquakes): linear-orthopolic in Euclidean volume L^3, with joint predictions (5/3, 9/5, 2, 7/3). It fits as well as the 2D-log reading, though only as a postulate. Flare exponents are also waveband-dependent (GOES soft X-ray fluence ≈ 2.0; verifier).
Trees, dN/dD ∝ D^-2: linear-orthopolic in basal-area flux only per dD, which fails under reparameterisation (flux per log mass ∝ M^(3/8)). Verifier grade: numerology.
Tree branches and arteries: both measures have physical names (area r^2 against section modulus r^3; flow r^3 against conductance r^4), so the measure cannot be selected from the exponent there.
regularities.how_to_test: The rule predicts which reading survives a change of support dimension. 3D fracture discs: log gives a = 4, linear volume gives 3. Volumetric seismicity: log/territory gives b = 1.5, FD-SOC gives b = 1. 2D against 3D turbulence spectra of gradient quantities. Flare ribbon areas: log gives 2.0, FD-SOC gives 7/3. Before examining a new system, ask whether the variable is a size under multiplicative transfer (predict log) or an additive coordinate traversed at constant speed or with equipartition (predict linear).

regularities.statement: MARTINGALE / CRITICAL RULE. A conserved expectation (branching ratio 1, a fair random walk) makes the carrier variable Zipf (zeta = 1 in duration or span). A deterministic coordinate change then gives the ubiquitous density exponent 3/2 (zeta = 1/2). Equivalently, any alpha = 3/2 law is Zipf in sqrt(k).
supporting_cases: Critical Galton-Watson and mean-field avalanches: P(T) ∝ T^-2, s ∝ T^2, P(s) ∝ s^-3/2, with the crackling relation holding jointly. Derived.
Neuronal LFP avalanches in slices: 1.5 ± 0.1 and 2.0 ± 0.1. Derived for the model.
1D random-walk first return: the span martingale gives P(reach L) = 1/L, and L ∝ t^(1/2).
Bethe-lattice (mean-field) percolation per site: tau = 5/2.
Wars, alpha = 1.53 ± 0.07: suggestive only.
counterexamples: At least three unrelated mechanisms give 3/2: 3D explored volume for random walks, constant-kernel coagulation, and stopped multiplicative escalation. Matching 3/2 therefore never selects among them.
Sparre Andersen: 1D first passage is 1/2 for Levy flights too, so the real invariant is combinatorial, not a span resource.
Spike-based avalanches: gamma ≈ 1.3 and size exponents ≈ 1.3-1.7 (Friedman; Fontenele), which is non-mean-field.
War durations are not T^-2: 79% of wars end within two years.
Neutral dynamics and thresholded noise reproduce the (3/2, 2) pair without criticality.
regularities.how_to_test: Never test the size exponent alone. Test the joint triple (alpha_T, alpha_s, gamma) through the crackling relation. For the linear-in-activation form, test whether alpha_T = gamma. Measure the branching ratio independently, and check the predicted exponential cutoff at T ~ 1/|ln m| when the ratio is moved by drugs. Unexamined targets: epidemic chain sizes near R0 = 1 (subcritical clusters), retweet cascades, power-grid blackouts (alpha ≈ 1.5-2), and Barkhausen noise in the mean-field class.

regularities.statement: EXPONENTIAL-COMPETITION BRIDGE. A power law whose exponent is a ratio of two exponential rates (growth against killing, energy gain against escape, speciation against genus origination) carries no dimensional resource. The orthopolic reading reduces to 'equal resource per log time or per log size' only when the two rates are equal.
supporting_cases: DSA: d_log = 3/(r-1) = escape probability per cycle / fractional energy gain, which is 1 at r = 4. Derived, but a kinematic coincidence rather than a conservation law.
Omori p = 1: rate-state nucleation, log-uniform failure times. Motivated.
1/f: Arrhenius map of flat barrier densities. Motivated; the DDH temperature relation is the discriminating test.
Yule species per genus: alpha = 1 + g/s.
Forbes wealth: zeta - 1 from the ratio of exit to growth.
War escalation: growth outpacing termination gives zeta ≈ 0.5.
counterexamples: Omori p ranges 0.7-1.8 with only ad hoc readings (heat-flow correlation disputed).
Yule: g/s is fitted from alpha.
Cosmic-ray source index: effective r is fitted.
regularities.how_to_test: Measure both rates independently, then predict the exponent. Examples: speciation and genus-origination rates from dated phylogenies; return dispersion and list turnover for Forbes; Omori p against loading rate and crustal temperature; the DDH slope-temperature relation for 1/f noise; compression ratio from SNR shock observations. If the rates are not measured, grade the reading numerology by default.

regularities.statement: SUPPLY-NETWORK D/(D+1) FAMILY AND THE 1/4 TURNOVER EXPONENT IN BIOLOGY. Space-filling supply to D-dimensional tissue gives B ∝ M^(D/(D+1)), with turnover ∝ M^-1/4. Ecological exponents compose from 3/4 and ±1/4. Every ecological stock reading and flux reading therefore differ by exactly 1/4, an ambiguity built into the domain.
supporting_cases: Damuth D ∝ M^-3/4 (equal energy flux per species), with the independent check Damuth slope = -Kleiber exponent. Motivated.
Sheldon: d = 3/4 + 1/4 = 1.
Carbone and Gittleman carnivores: M^-1 per unit prey biomass, M^-3/4 per unit prey productivity.
Home range ≈ M^1 = 3/4 + ~1/4.
Cortical white against gray matter, W ∝ G^(4/3) (verifier, missing case).
Urban delta: the same dimension logic in social systems.
counterexamples: Mammal BMR varies 0.67-0.76 across studies; White and Seymour find 2/3, which matches Rubner's surface law, and the D=2 network prediction also equals 2/3.
Kleiber curvature.
DeLong et al. 2010: prokaryotes ≈ 1.96, protists ≈ 1.06.
Near-isometric plant respiration (Reich 2006).
Intraspecific exponents 0.5-1 (Glazier).
3/4 in communities with no shared network (Hatton 2015 production-biomass) and in social-insect colonies, so 3/4 is not a signature of network geometry.
Rate of living (heartbeats per life): the exponents cancel but the mechanism fails (Speakman).
regularities.how_to_test: Predict D/(D+1) for organisms whose supply geometry is measured before metabolic data are collected: planar colonies and benthic films should give 2/3, filamentous organisms 1/2. Measure terminal blood velocity against mass (the reading needs M^(1/12)). Use within-single-trophic-level size spectra (alpha = 1.75) and strip-planted stands (flux reading -3/4 against capacity reading -1/3) to separate stock, flux and capacity.

regularities.statement: NO-READING CLASS. Natural orthopolic readings are absent when (i) no quantity is conserved at intermediate scales (sinks or forcing at every scale, non-stationary drivers), (ii) the exponent is a renormalisation-group eigenvalue or an irrational fractal dimension, (iii) the law is a sampling or distributional identity whose exponent is a free parameter, or (iv) the per-unit cost is cheaper than the budget everywhere or dearer than it everywhere (exponential regimes).
supporting_cases: (i) Wildfires: 1.3-1.8 by ecoregion, 2.2 at high xmin, driven by weather and suppression. Web out-degree (≈ 2.45-2.7). Labor income zeta ≈ 2. Multipole and dispersion laws (r^-3, r^-6, r^-7): the total flux through a sphere around a dipole is zero, and the exponents come from differentiation and squaring.
(ii) 3D Ising (nu ≈ 0.630, eta ≈ 0.036); DLA D_f ≈ 1.71; 3D percolation D_f. Hyperscaling and the territory rule only move the irrational content into D_f.
(iii) Taylor's law (b = 1 + cluster exponent by definition, Tweedie); Heaps' law (inherits zeta_rare); species-area z ≈ 1/4, which lognormal SADs give generically (May 1975).
(iv) Wien tail, gapped excitations, superconductors: Boltzmann exponentials. Electron C ∝ T arises from a Fermi shell, not a dimension.
counterexamples: Kraichnan steepening under drag is a predicted, quantifiable failure, not a no-reading case.
The hyperscaling breakdown above d_c = 6 (and above 4 for Ising) is itself predicted by the slot reading.
regularities.how_to_test: Before analysing a new system, classify it on (i)-(iv). The prediction is that systems failing (i) will show exponents that drift with region, period or cutoff (as wildfires do), while systems passing (i) with measured inputs will have stable exponents. Check on forest-fire models with and without suppression, on traffic-jam sizes, on blackout sizes, and on online popularity (often lognormal).

regularities.statement: UNDERDETERMINATION. A single exponent rarely identifies a resource. The same number recurs with unrelated resources, and the same system carries different resources in adjacent ranges. In every domain, the discriminating evidence came from dimension series, prefactor or flux scaling, joint exponent sets, or independently measured inputs, never from a matching exponent alone.
supporting_cases: 3/2: random walk 1D and 3D, branching, wars, Euclidean counts.
k^-3: area-log, volume-lin, enstrophy, slope saturation, crater equilibrium.
b = 1: three readings.
Kleiber 2/3 against 3/4.
Landslides: 2.5 from 3D territory equals gamma = 1.5.
Graphite T^2: two slot geometries.
Same system, adjacent ranges: ocean waves omega^-4 (flux) and omega^-5 (capacity); 2D turbulence k^-5/3 and k^-3.
Flares: three readings, each fitting some waveband.

Dimension series that did discriminate: percolation 2D, 3D and 6D; T^(d+1) confirmed by the 1D thermal conductance quantum; line sources giving 1/r; rivers (Scheidegger against OCN); Debye d/s across phonons and magnons.
counterexamples: Craters and Gauss's law: the resource is fixed in advance and no rival reading has a mechanism, so underdetermination is minimal.
regularities.how_to_test: Require each reading to state a second consequence in a different observable before the comparison: a dimension change, a related variable, a prefactor or flux dependence, or a joint scaling relation. Count a case as support only if that second consequence passes.

patterns.log_vs_linear:
I compiled the four verified catalogues (59 systems, using the verifier's grades) by hand.

**Which measure wins**
- **Log wins for size distributions.** The log measure is the only one with an independent mechanism in nearly every density case where the variable is a size or content moved by multiplicative transfer, packing or proportional growth. Examples:
  - craters and dense fractures (territory per ln L)
  - lakes and percolation (territory per ln L)
  - Dohnanyi and MRN dust (mass flux per ln D)
  - K41 (energy flux per ln k)
  - Kraichnan and Phillips (enstrophy or slope variance per ln k, which is the k^-3 case)
  - Batchelor (variance per ln k)
  - Sheldon (biomass per ln m)
  - Murray and Leonardo trees (flow or area per log-radius generation)
  - critical avalanches (time per ln T)
  - cities, firms, words, Bradford, web in-links, citations (Gibrat/Simon accumulation per ln k)
  - 1/f and Omori (log time)
- **Linear wins in a smaller, coherent group.** The variable is an additive coordinate traversed at a constant rate, or one on which equipartition or Gaussian diffusion lives:
  - radiation energy per dr = P/c (constant speed)
  - white noise, equal power per Hz (Johnson-Nyquist)
  - equipartition kT per mode, with modes counted linearly in k-space
  - dark-matter halos, equal mass per unit peak height nu (excursion set; explicitly not per ln M)
  - Richardson pairs, energy delivered per dt
  - critical branching, activations per linear duration interval (only if alpha_T = gamma)
  - random-walk return in d >= 3 (explored volume)
  - Kepler II (time per swept area)
- **Discrete classes for cross-species scaling laws.** Damuth, Kleiber's supply sites, Taylor's clusters and Bradford zones are naturally discrete (per species, per site, per cluster, per zone). For aggregate laws (Stefan-Boltzmann, Kepler, Debye) no abundance density exists, so the log/linear choice does not apply.

**The bridge between the two.** An exponential map converts linear-orthopolic allocation in an energy-like variable into log-orthopolic allocation in time:
- Arrhenius barriers give 1/f.
- Rate-state stress gives Omori p ≈ 1.
- DSA escape against energy gain gives E^-2.

**The k^-3 ambiguity.** Every k^-3 case with a mechanism takes the log reading: crater obliteration, the fracture exclusion rule, percolation hyperscaling, and enstrophy and slope weights (k^2 as a squared gradient, not an area). The linear-in-volume reading rests only on Aschwanden's FD-SOC postulate, which fits flares and earthquakes no better than the 2D-log reading. The linear partners that d_lin = d_log + 1 generates automatically never had independent motivation:
- token coincidences k^2
- resident pairs s^2
- citations × age x^3
- returns r^4
- 'linear in k^3 volume' for 2D turbulence

The verifier graded all of these numerology.

**Where it cannot be decided.**
- Tree branches: area r^2 vs section modulus r^3.
- Arteries: Murray flow r^3 vs conductance r^4.

In both, each measure names a physical quantity, and the two readings are algebraically one statement, so a mechanism has to choose.

**Coordinate dependence.** Trees per linear dD (dN/dD ∝ D^-2) shows that a linear-measure claim depends on the coordinate: per log mass, the same forest is top-heavy in flux. Only log-measure claims survive a power reparameterisation, so a linear reading needs a physically privileged coordinate (time, distance from a source, frequency with equipartition, peak height).

**Heuristic to fix before looking.** If the variable is a size under multiplicative transfer, predict log. If it is a privileged additive coordinate traversed at a constant rate, predict linear.
patterns.stock_flux_capacity:
Across the 38 cases graded derived or motivated after verification, the primitive orthopolic quantity is most often a flux. Capacity comes second and dominates geometric and territorial systems. A pure stock is rarely primitive.

**Flux (about 15 cases).**
- Physics and astrophysics cascades: K41, enstrophy, wave turbulence, Dohnanyi, cosmic-ray escape.
- Physiological and ecological energy flows: Kleiber supply sites, Damuth (energy per species), Murray (flow per vessel), Hatton (predators per prey production).
- Time budgets: avalanches, Omori, Richardson.

**Capacity / slot count (about 14 cases).**
- Craters, fractures, lakes, percolation, halos (Lagrangian volume).
- IMF parent volume, rivers (drained-width spacing).
- Inverse-square area cells, Rayleigh-Jeans, Debye, Bloch active modes.
- Phillips saturation, the urban network.

**Stock (about 9 cases).**
- Cities, firms, words, Bradford, web, citations, wealth.
- Sheldon biomass, Batchelor variance.

**Most flat stocks are flux orthopolity in disguise.** The transport identity B = F/v says a stock is flat per log class exactly when the log-speed is independent of size:
- Gibrat/Simon growth in cities, firms, words and wealth.
- The uniform strain rate in Batchelor's range and in the enstrophy cascade.

When the log-speed scales, the stock carries the rate exponent:
- K41: d_log = 2/3 is the turnover-rate exponent.
- Dohnanyi: the stock is D^2.5 = mass × D^-0.5 disruption rate.
- Ecology: turnover ∝ M^-1/4 makes stock and flux readings differ by exactly 1/4 (Damuth's flux is flat while biomass ∝ M^1/4; Sheldon's biomass is flat while energy flux ∝ m^-1/4).

The stock reading is directly refuted where the cascade is steady: Dohnanyi stock mass predicts alpha = 4, observed 3.5.

**Capacity readings have two traps.**
1. A slot count is a capacity, but event catalogues are rates. For earthquakes and flares the territory reading needs a per-slot event rate independent of size. With recurrence ∝ slip ∝ L, slot counting gives b = 1.5, not 1, an assumption the catalogues left implicit.
2. For sharing laws (inverse square), the exponent identifies the number of sharers (area cells ∝ r^(d-1)), not the shared quantity. For aggregate laws (Stefan-Boltzmann, Debye) it factors as slots ∝ T^d × per-slot share ∝ T. The orthopolic statement is equal share per slot, with exponent 0.

**Time budgets are a fourth kind**, a time-integrated flux:
- avalanche duration
- aftershocks per log time
- Levy travel distance
- heartbeats per life

The well-graded ones are those with a conservation law in time (the martingale E[Z_t] = 1). The rest are suggestive.

**Domain split.** Physics and geo/astro are dominated by flux and capacity. Social systems look stock-dominated only because proportional growth makes the log-speed constant. Ecology is intrinsically ambiguous by 1/4.
patterns.composition_rules:
Recurring ways final resources combine:

**1. Deterministic products add exponents: q = q1·q2 gives d = d1 + d2.**
- Seismic moment: slip L^1 × area L^2.
- Stefan-Boltzmann: T^d slots × kT per slot.
- Richardson: 1 (energy delivered at constant rate) + 2 (ballistic conversion).
- Brown noise: 0 (white) + 2 (integrator gain).
- Kraichnan and Phillips: 2 (squared-gradient weight) + 0 (scale-free rate).
- Urban output: 1 + delta.
- Firm growth variance: n_eff ∝ S^(2β) × (unit size)^2.
- Sheldon: 3/4 + 1/4.
- Kleiber as D spatial dimensions + 1 transport dimension.

**2. A deterministic change of coordinate y ∝ x^c divides survival exponents (zeta_y = zeta_x/c); nested maps multiply.**
- Earthquakes: zeta_M0 = zeta_L/3.
- Lakes: d/D_f.
- IMF: 3/(4-beta).
- GSMF: zeta_h/(5/3).
- Inverse cubic law: zeta_r = 1 × 3/2 × 2.
- Volume: zeta_V = 3/2.
- River energy: 0.45/0.5.
- Heaps: beta = zeta_rare.
- Random-walk and branching durations to spans or sizes: ×1/2.
- Landslide area to volume: gamma.

**3. Territory rule (1 and 2 combined): zeta_k = d_s/D_k.** d_s is the support dimension and D_k the content-length exponent. This is where small-denominator rationals come from mechanistically: 2/3, 5/3, 187/91, 3/2 for Euclidean counts.

**4. Transport identity: d_stock = d_flux + z, with log-speed v ∝ k^z.**
- K41: z = 2/3.
- Dohnanyi: z = -1/2.
- Cosmic rays: alpha = source index + delta.
- Ecology: z = -1/4.
- If the rate depends on the stock (wave turbulence, v ∝ B^(N-2) for N-wave interactions), the level scales as F^(1/(N-1)): P^(1/3) for four-wave and P^(1/2) for three-wave interactions.

**5. Entry/exit corrections add a rate ratio: zeta = 1 + entry/growth.**
- Simon: a/(1-a).
- Price/DMS: A/m.
- Gibrat with exit: 1/(m·tau).
- Equivalently, steady entry makes relative age exactly log-orthopolic, and accrual k ∝ u^theta gives zeta = 1/theta.

**6. Cost optimisation gives ratios.**
- Murray: (c+2)/a gives 3, 7/3 and 27/11.
- Banavar: D/(D+1).
- Bettencourt: delta = H/(D(D+H)).
- Padoan-Nordlund: 4 - beta.

**7. Shared pair budgets give sum rules.** Urban Y·A_n ∝ N², so beta_out + beta_net = 2.

**8. A martingale or conserved expectation gives zeta = 1 in the carrier variable,** followed by rule 2 (the 3/2 family).

**9. Exponential competition gives exponent = rate ratio:** DSA 3/(r-1), Yule g/s, Arrhenius bridges.

**10. Marginal cases, where a slot exponent equals a dynamical one, give logarithms:** Kraichnan's ln^(-1/3), 2D random-walk return, V ∝ N/ln N.

**Rules that do not hold:**
- Products of independent random factors give lognormals; their tails do not add (Shockley).
- Sums of power-law costs give crossovers, not power laws: Kleiber curvature, width saturation, the strength-gravity transition. The framework still needs a rule for sums.
- Composition is pure algebra. Its empirical content is only as good as the independent measurement of each factor exponent. Several catalogue compositions back out one factor as a residual: capacity × velocity 1/12, home-range sharing 1/4, receipts c = 0.07, labor-income kappa = 1/2. Those are numerology.
patterns.numerology_assessment:
**Chance coverage.** I computed this in this task. Simple fractions p/q cover the range 1.5-4 densely:

| Denominator | ±0.03 | ±0.05 | ±0.1 |
|---|---|---|---|
| q ≤ 2 | 12% | 20% | 40% |
| q ≤ 3 | 24% | 40% | 73% |
| q ≤ 4 | 36% | 57% | 90% |
| q ≤ 6 | 65% | 87% | 100% |

The verifier got similar figures on [0.5, 3]. Every exponent also comes with two readings (d_lin = d_log + 1), and most cases offered 2-4 candidate resources. So the chance that some simple reading fits within ±0.1 is close to 1. A match at typical empirical precision (±0.05-0.3 for geophysical, ecological and social exponents) is near-zero evidence on its own.

**Mechanism also lands on simple rationals.** Dimension ratios d_s/D_k, (c+2)/a and D/(D+1) produce small-denominator numbers too. Even a correct mechanism therefore cannot be told apart from coincidence by the number alone.

**Patterns that could plausibly arise by chance, or are already shown to be generic:**
- '3/4 everywhere': Kleiber, Damuth, plant thinning, Hatton communities, social insects. A 3/4 with no network shows the value is not diagnostic, and Kleiber itself spans 0.67-0.76 by data processing.
- 3/2: at least three unrelated mechanisms produce it (random walk, branching, coagulation/escalation, Euclidean volume).
- k^-3 and b = 1: multiple readings.
- MRN 3.5: the generic number for any steady cascade.
- Landslides 2.4: gamma in 1.1-1.6 maps onto most of the observed range.
- Islands B = 1 - H/2: any H in [0, 1] covers every reported B.
- Species-area z ≈ 1/4: generic for lognormal SADs.
- Trees D^-2: five readings fit within 1.5-2.5.
- Levy mu = 2.
- Flare 5/3: waveband-dependent; GOES fluence is about 2.0.
- IMF 2.35 against 2.36: Hennebelle-Chabrier and competitive accretion give similar values.
- The integer ladder 0/1/2 for gene categories: core exponents are not 0, and the regulator interval 1.72-1.95 excludes 2.
- Every 'zeta - 1 = entry/growth' correction where the rate is backed out: cities 0.005, firms 0.06, wealth 0.49, citations A = m, web A/m.
- The ecological 1/4 stock/flux offset, which lets both readings fit (carnivores; home range).

**Patterns unlikely to be chance**, because the motivation came first and a second prediction was tested:
- Percolation hyperscaling across 2D, 3D and 6D, including the predicted failure above d_c.
- T^(d+1), confirmed by the 1D thermal conductance quantum.
- Debye d/s across phonons and ferro/antiferromagnets.
- Line-source 1/r and extra-dimension bounds for inverse square.
- Rivers: beta = 1 - h holds across Scheidegger and optimal networks, and the energy exponent 0.90 is predicted.
- K41 with the exact 4/5 flux law.
- Batchelor's prefactor chi(nu/eps)^(1/2).
- Crater equilibrium appearing only when production is steeper than -2.
- Dohnanyi's strength dependence.
- Crackling relations in mean-field avalanches.
- Halo slopes tracking the power-spectrum index in scale-free simulations.

**Overall verdict.** The verifier's grade counts across 59 systems: about 23 derived, 15 motivated, 18 suggestive, 3 numerology or none. The derived cases cluster where established theory already is a conservation or packing argument. Mainly in physics, orthopolity there re-expresses known derivations rather than predicting new exponents. The newly proposed readings, mostly in biology and social systems, grade suggestive or worse once inputs are checked for independence. The verifier downgraded several catalogue grades: earthquakes, lakes, islands, flares, MRN, urban scaling, citations, Kleiber, wars and terrorism.

**Method caveat.** Most verification in these catalogues used abstracts, search summaries and the checkers' recollection, because web budgets were exhausted. I did no new web verification in this synthesis.

**Rule for the paper.** A within-±0.1 match counts as evidence only if:
- the resource and its inputs were fixed before the exponent was seen, and
- the reading makes a second prediction (dimension series, prefactor or flux scaling, joint exponents, related variable) that also passes.

Otherwise grade it numerology, however natural the story.
most_promising_directions: Use the authors' own 'super power' (choosing the resource after seeing the data) in two steps. Exploration: read any exponent as a candidate resource. Confirmation: before fitting a new case, state the support dimension d_s, the content scaling D_k, any rate exponent z, the measure (log, linear or discrete) and one second consequence, and archive this. Test it on cases nobody has examined: Euclidean source counts (3/2), planetary ring particles, volumetric or swarm seismicity (b = 1.5 vs 1), 3D fault-disc exponents (a = 4 vs 3), lake radius of gyration (N(>L) ∝ L^-2), GMC mass spectra (known to fail), rock fragmentation (D = 3 predicted vs 2.58), seed size-number trade-offs (d = 1), Morse et al. arthropods on fractal vegetation, and inverse wave-action cascades (omega^-11/3).

Make dimension series the main discriminator. Look for the same mechanism in different embedding or support dimensions: point vs line sources, 2D vs 3D turbulence and fractures, map vs volume packing, hedgerow vs area plant thinning (N ∝ M^-1/3 vs M^-2/3), sheet vs volume core fragmentation (2/(4-beta)), planar vs 3D supply networks (2/3 vs 3/4), and 1D/2D/3D urban forms (beta = 1.5, 1.167, 1.08). This is the one kind of test that repeatedly separated readings the exponent alone could not.

Treat the transport identity B = F/v as the organising principle of the paper. Flux is primitive; a stock is flat exactly when the log-speed is independent of size; capacity applies where packing binds. For each case report the flux, the log-speed exponent and the predicted dependence of the level on the flux, not just the slope. This turns 'which resource' into a measurable question: Sheldon per-system flatness against measured PPMR and TE, wave-spectrum level ∝ P^(1/3), cosmic-ray source index = observed index minus delta, Dohnanyi slope against strength s.

Turn the near-Zipf corrections into out-of-sample predictions. Measure entry and growth rates independently, then predict zeta - 1: BDS entrant employment for firms, type/token ratio for texts, attachment-kernel offsets A/m from citation and link panels, ORFan rates for gene families, Forbes turnover and return dispersion. Apply the 'relative age is exactly log-orthopolic, zeta = 1/theta' unification to new growing systems (software packages, patents, Wikipedia).

Extend the composition calculus to sums of costs. Products give power laws; sums give crossovers whose location is predictable. Predict where crossovers fall rather than a single exponent: Kleiber curvature from surface plus volume costs, seismogenic-width saturation near Mw 6.7, the asteroid strength-gravity transition, and the Murray turbulent-to-laminar crossover inside one arterial tree. This also handles the cases where single-exponent readings currently fail.

Fix the rate assumption in event catalogues. For earthquakes and flares, state the per-slot event rate explicitly and test it independently. For earthquakes, aftershock productivity ∝ 10^(alpha M) with alpha ≈ b implies productivity ∝ rupture area, which tests the area reading better than b itself. Explain why recurrence ∝ slip does not give b = 1.5. Explain the stress dependence of b (0.7-1.2) with the same resource.

Use sum rules and joint relations as tests, because they need no fitted parameters: beta_output + beta_network = 2 for the same cities and boundaries; zeta_r/zeta_V = 1/delta across markets with different impact exponents; crackling relations for avalanches; the FD-SOC joint set against flare ribbon areas (2.0 vs 7/3); natural-city area against population (zeta_A = zeta_P/c).

Report the no-reading class as a result: no conserved quantity at intermediate scales, RG-irrational exponents, sampling or distributional identities, exponential (gapped) regimes. Predict that exponents in this class drift with region, period or cutoff, while those passing the conservation test stay stable. This makes the framework falsifiable at the level of whole systems.

State the paper's claim honestly. In physics, orthopolity mostly unifies known derivations under one vocabulary (slots × per-slot share, flux/rate, coordinate change, territory d_s/D_k). Its new content lies in cross-system predictions (dimension series, prefactors, sum rules) and in classifying failures. Novel exponent predictions so far come mainly from the territory and transport rules applied with independently measured inputs. The quarter-power, species-area, Taylor and Levy cases should be presented as open or numerology-risk examples.
